News.title: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
News.content:
The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News.

Diesel prices in the UK reached a new high on Monday due to supply pressures springing from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Fuel prices are rising globally and US President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports, stating at the weekend: "We're thinking about it very seriously."

Healey, who admitted that UK diesel prices are "extreme", said the government was in discussions with the US, adding: "We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK."

Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Healey said: "We work very closely with the Americans.

"In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran."

The UK depends on the US for around a third of its diesel imports and a ban would send prices even higher.

US sources suggest that Trump is considering a ban to attempt to bring down prices for domestic consumers ahead of the critical midterm elections.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In the UK, the average price for a litre of diesel reached 199.33p on Monday, according to the RAC motoring organisation, surpassing a previous high of 199.09p in June 2022 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.23p.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

Healey said he was "very aware" of these cost of living pressures as he prepared what he called a "breathing space" Budget on 28 October.

A freeze on fuel duty, first implemented by the Conservative government in 2022, is due to expire at the end of the year. Duty is scheduled to increase by 3p in January and a further 2p in March.

Healey said: "Fundamentally, what we need is a settlement in the Middle East. We need an easing of the pressure of costs on business, the costs on households and on ordinary families that we see at the pumps in the most extreme level today for diesel."

News.title: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
News.content:
The chancellor has warned against allowing Britain's benefits bill to balloon while not offering young people opportunities.

John Healey told Labour's annual conference in Liverpool that cutting welfare spending was "more than an economic must - it's a moral duty".

"The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage," he said.

He announced the expansion of a Local Apprenticeships Service for mayors in England, which he said would deliver thousands more apprenticeships for young people.

Healey's speech comes as he faces pressure to cut public spending or raise taxes ahead of next month's Budget to bring down government borrowing costs.

In an attempt to reassure the markets, he said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" with him and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "united on meeting the fiscal rules".

Fiscal rules are the government's self-imposed constraints to manage decisions on spending and tax.

The Budget would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space", the chancellor said.

And he admitted that "the money New Labour had in the '90s is simply not there now".

Healey blamed the Conservative Party's time in government for leaving Britain spending more on debt than on the Home Office, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Justice combined.

Tory shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said in response to the speech that "Labour MPs will never support cutting the out-of-control welfare bill" and "with Labour, it's always more taxes if you work and more benefits if you don't".

Healey praised young people as "digital natives, whip-smart, questioning, ambitious, brave" who could move from "generation jeopardy to generation hope".

But he pointed to the million young people not in education, employment or training - known as Neets - which he said created a necessity to make benefits a bridge into work, rather than a "trap".

"It is not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill, and a system which offers an income but doesn't offer a future," he said.

Asked how quickly the bill might come down, when he appeared on the BBC's Newscast, Healey would not commit to the benefits bill falling, saying he "won't set a timeline" for the UK's benefits bill coming down by the time of the next election.

News.title: Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test
News.content:
SpaceX's Starship rocket has splashed down in the Pacific Ocean after orbiting the Earth for about three hours. The mission was supposed to last about 10 hours, but the SpaceX team decided to end it early. The ship deployed 26 "next generation" Starlink V3 satellites, joining the existing constellation which deliver broadband internet on Earth. SpaceX describes Starship as "the world's most powerful launch vehicle ever developed" and says it will eventually carry crew and cargo "to Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars and beyond". The aim of the spacecraft is to be able to carry up to 100 people on "long-duration, inter-planetary flights".

Read more on the launch

News.title: Mahmood signals rethink on migrants' right to remain
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has signalled she is willing to rethink plans to make it harder for foreign workers to claim permanent residence in the UK.

The home secretary has been under pressure to water down the proposals from a significant number of Labour MPs, including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, and trade unions.

In a speech to Labour's annual conference, Mahmood acknowledged "some have said elements of these reforms are not fair".

And she said the government would "come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country".

Permanent residence, or indefinite leave to remain, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

Mahmood suggested doubling the time it takes for most migrants to qualify for the right from five to 10 years.

Under the proposals, people who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years.

Earlier this year, when Rayner was a backbench MP, she accused the government of "moving the goalposts", branding Mahmood's plans "un-British" - and then stuck with her criticisms when she re-joined the cabinet.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of Unison, said the proposed changes would unfairly penalise overseas care workers.

Home Office sources insist no final decision on changes to the immigration rules have been taken, and Mahmood was setting out the principles that would guide her in her conference speech.

The home secretary told delegates: "As we restore control and fairness to our asylum system, we must do the same for legal migration too.

"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did, and fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young.

"That same principle underpins my reforms to the right to live here indefinitely, ensuring settled status is earned by those who have shown a consistent commitment to this country."

And she vowed to come up with a policy that was fair to those who "came here legally" and to British citizens.

A Conservative spokesperson said: "Shabana Mahmood has caved in to pressure from Angela Rayner and her open borders MPs and will shred her own plans to reform indefinite leave to remain.

"This is a slap in the face to British taxpayers who will have to subsidise low-skilled, low wage migrants."

Speaking earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham denied Mahmood had been forced to ditch the plans because Rayner viewed them as "un-British", saying the reforms would need to "strike the right balance".

Asked whether he was "Team Shabana" or "Team Angela," he told LBC: "I'm both of them, I'm Team Angela and Shabana.

"But it just reflects that there's a consultation, there's different not just opinions from politicians, but obviously there's a range of views that have gone into that consultation, so we're in the process now of looking at that."

News.title: Slipknot fans threaten boycott after Marilyn Manson announced as support act for UK show
News.content:
Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.

The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.

Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.

Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.

Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.

While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".

Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.

One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."

Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.

However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".

News.title: Aldi boss says some of rivals' loyalty discounts 'dupe' customers
News.content:
Aldi's UK boss has accused rival supermarket chains of duping customers in some cases with loyalty discounts that start with "unrealistically high prices" and then drop.

Chief executive Giles Hurley said discounts are helpful "when they're real and when they show realistic reductions", but hit out at what he said were unrealistic reductions which "dupe customers".

Aldi is the only major supermarket chain that doesn't operate a loyalty scheme, which are used by millions of shoppers.

The UK's official competition watchdog investigated supermarkets' loyalty pricing schemes in 2024 and concluded shoppers "almost always make a genuine saving".

Former Asda buyer and retail consultant Ged Futter told the BBC Hurley's comments were a "a distraction from the fact is that Aldi is under pressure in the UK".

He said Aldi was "on a meteoric rise until about two years ago" but that it is "now growing behind the main supermarket pack".

"The price gap isn't as clear as it once was," he added.

Hurley, who has made similar comments on discount schemes in the past, was speaking as Aldi reported a 5% increase in sales to Â£19bn for 2025 from 2024.

However, operating profits had fallen slightly over the same period, which the retailer said was due to higher staff pay as well as investments in infrastructure and prices.

Hurley said the business was attracting new customers despite fierce competition across the sector.

"We are the only retailer where the price of your weekly shop is actually cheaper this summer than last summer," said Hurley

He said the business was focussed on "everyday low prices, not short-lived offers that disappear the following week".

"Promotions can supplement every day low prices when they're meaningful, when they're real and when they show realistic reductions.

"However, when promotions start with unrealistically high prices â and come down to prices which aren't that competitive and dupe customers â we would view that as loyalty that isn't supportive, that isn't transparent and doesn't help customers plan and budget."

Aldi said it had spent Â£340m this year on cutting prices. The German-owned chain also announced plans to open 40 new stores next year as part of a Â£900m investment programme and expand long-term agreements with British suppliers.

Hurley said recent droughts and global events had highlighted vulnerabilities in food supply chains, arguing that boosting domestic production should be a national strategic priority, helping to reduce the UK's exposure to shocks that can push up food prices.

News.title: Russian foreign minister questions 'what will become of UK' and future of 'the Celts'
News.content:
Russia's foreign minister has questioned the future of the UK, suggesting it looks uncertain with "the Celts" looking to hold independence referendums.

Sergey Lavrov made the comments at a youth conference where he said he did "not know what will become of the country called Great Britain", according to The Times, external.

The comments come weeks after the first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland declared "Westminster's time is coming to an end" and signed an agreement to say it had no right to "block democracy".

In response to Lavrov's comments, Plaid Cymru said Wales' constitutional future was "a matter for the people of Wales", and "not for the Kremlin to endorse, oppose or exploit".

In the conference, Lavrov also suggested the west had too much influence in the UN Security Council, external - the five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the UK, and the US.

According to The Times, he said: "The Celts â Wales, Ireland, Scotland â are now seeking to hold referenda.

"We do not advocate the expulsion of any of the permanent members of the security council. Although, of course, the scale of the British Empire, when it first took its seat in the UN security council at the organisation's founding, has, naturally, diminished to the utmost degree."

News.title: UK diesel price hits all-time high, the RAC says
News.content:
The RAC data is based on the average price of diesel at a range of supermarkets, motorway service stations and independent retailers.

The Chancellor said on Monday that the the "place" and "time" for the government to deal with questions around rising petrol and diesel prices and fuel duty is next month's Budget.

John Healey told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm acutely concerned and conscious about how hard it is for families. I see that at the pumps myself.

"We can't remove the cost of living pressures, we can't remove the prices that people are having to pay, but where we can we will act and we will give people just a bit of breathing space, and the same goes for the cost to business."

Simon Williams, the RAC's head of policy, said record diesel prices "spell pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans".

"Undoubtedly these increased costs will be passed on to consumers," he said. Williams said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days".

The price of Brent crude, a benchmark for global oil used to make petrol, diesel and other fuel products, rose over the weekend and is now hovering at around $108 per barrel. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has also implemented an export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply.

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

News.title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
News.content:
Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.

These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones as well as to track criminals.

Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.

We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.

Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.

The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.

The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.

News.title: Lithium-ion battery caused fire that killed mum and 3 children
News.content:
A house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of 22 September.

Following an investigation with Merseyside Police, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said the fire was caused by an electrical event linked to a lithium-ion battery, which are used in e-bikes and e-scooters.

Kev Johnson, of MFRS, said: "This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire."

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property, at 03:45 BST.

MFRS said four people "showing no signs of life" had been found in an upstairs bedroom.

A man was taken to hospital suffering from burns.

News.title: Angela Scanlon takes over Sara Cox's drivetime slot on Radio 2
News.content:
Angela Scanlon is to take over BBC Radio 2's drivetime show after Sara Cox moved to the breakfast slot.

The Irish personality said it was "properly exciting" to be hosting the station's 16:00-19:00 show every weekday from November.

She said: "Millions of people, all having completely different days, piling into the same conversation for a few hours - what a strange and lovely thing!"

Scanlon, who hosted a Sunday early morning programme on the station from 2018 to 2021, was among a number of people who filled in after Cox vacated the drivetime slot in May, including Joel Dommett, Jason Manford, Ellie Taylor, Alex Jones and Gary Davies.

Scanlon is also known for The One Show, This Morning, Your Home Made Perfect, The Apprentice: Unfinished Business, and for taking part in Strictly Come Dancing in 2023.

News.title: Mahmood to reopen scheme to resettle refugees in the UK
News.content:
Shabana Mahmood has announced the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK, as she hopes that offering "safe and legal" routes will deter small boat crossings.

The home secretary said the UK wants to "live up to our international obligations" by helping those who are fleeing war and persecution, but the process must be "capped and controlled".

The Home Office said the UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will reopen immediately and expects that around 25% of arrivals will be Afghan women and girls and Palestinians.

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Mahmood was making a "desperate attempt to appease" people within Labour who have been critical of her asylum reforms.

Hundreds of people are expected to arrive under the UKRS, which stopped taking new applicants in December 2024, and three new sponsorship routes.

The latter will involve communities, universities and companies hosting refugees from next year.

The Home Office expects arrivals to increase to the "low thousands" as levels of illegal migration fall.

A cap will be set for each year although details of the number have yet to be provided.

People arriving in Britain under the safe and legal routes will be be put on a five-year path to permanent settlement.

Mahmood told the Labour Party conference on Monday that "fairness" is behind her approach, limits are needed and communities must be "ready and able to welcome those who come here".

She also said: "That is what we can do, this is who we can be, as we restore control to our borders, bear down on small boat crossings and unlock the inherent generosity of this country."

More than 18,500 people have crossed the Channel in small boats this year compared to more than 32,000 than the same period in 2025.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "not obligated to take in more migrants", adding if his party was in power then those arriving under Labour's schemes would "not be able to stay".

He said: "If Labour are so sure the public wants their open borders policies, they'd call a general election to get a mandate."

In expressing his criticism, Farage also referenced a report in The Sunday Times, external about a former bodyguard to the leader of Hamas securing asylum and citizenship in the UK before "plotting" an attack against Jewish people in Europe.

The newspaper reported the man moved to the UK more than a decade ago and now faces extradition to Germany.

Jon Featonby, chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, welcomed the government's new proposals but said it came after a "drastic reduction in safe routes over the last year".

He said: "Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people smugglers' business model, but they only work if they operate at scale.

"The government has to show ambition and commitment, and that means thousands of places, not hundreds.

"Alongside any new schemes, the government must also reopen refugee family reunion without delay."

News.title: Orange Order parade dispute continues after main players hold talks
News.content:
The main parties involved in a parading dispute in Northern Ireland are still in a stalemate, following a day of political talks and heated exchanges at Stormont.

Members of the Orange Order are still waiting to begin their permitted parade, which was due to take place on Sunday morning, and walk down the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown.

Protesters blocked the road at the weekend and after meeting the Northern Ireland secretary, a representative of the road's residents said the Orange Order should focus on a different route.

The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, was due to go ahead for the first time in 30 years after legal challenges.

Since 1998, the Orange Order had been banned from completing its Drumcree march - and until this year had been repeatedly refused permission to finish the route by the Parades Commission, which was set up to adjudicate disputes.

The Orange Order is a Protestant pro-British organisation, while the area where it wants to walk - specifically along the Garvaghy Road - is largely Catholic and predominantly inhabited by pro-Irish nationalists.

News.title: Bulger killer's parole hearing to be held in private
News.content:
Child killer Jon Venables will have his latest parole bid heard in private despite a plea from his victim's mother for it to be public, the Parole Board has decided.

Venables tortured and murdered two-year-old James Bulger in 1993.

The 44-year-old will have his case heard by parole chiefs at an oral hearing more than two years after his last appeal.

James's mother Denise Fergus had demanded that the hearing be held in public to help combat "misinformation" about the case which had a "retraumatising impact" on her.

Parole Board hearings are usually held in private but they can be made public "in the interests of justice".

Various media organisations also applied for a public hearing.

In reaching its decision, the Parole Board said a public hearing would make it "very difficult for Jon Venables to give evidence" because he could be "being listened to by people who are seeking to get information so that they can kill him".

In 2023, the Parole Board rejected the bid and found he still posed a danger to children and could go on to offend again.

Thousands of young disabled people will be given state-funded jobs in the government’s latest bid to tackle the rising youth unemployment crisis.

Beginning next April, the initiative will see 18 to 24 year olds who receive health or disability benefits offered a guaranteed job if they remain out of employment for three months after their initial assessment.

It marks an expansion to the government’s Jobs Guarantee scheme, that ensures any young person out of work will receive a similar offer after 18 months on Universal Credit.

While the placements offered on the programme are voluntary, those who undertaken them will be paid for their work.

Tesco has become the latest major employer to confirm its inclusion in the scheme, joining several other retailers.

Businesses which previously announced placements through the scheme include Lidl, Boots and Waitrose owner, John Lewis. The government says it hopes to help 90,000 young people into work by 2029 through the scheme.

Work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said that Labour is ‘putting long-term sick and disabled people at the front of the queue’ ( Getty )

Work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said: “I’ve seen how the Jobs Guarantee is already changing lives and now we are putting long-term sick and disabled people at the front of the queue from April next year.

“For many young people, this will be the first chance they’ve had of a real paid job, and the dignity and self-respect that comes with that.”

Figures released last month show that the number of young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) continues to hover around the one million mark, recording a slight fall between April and June.

Earlier this year, Alan Milburn warned that Britain could see 1.25 million Neets by the early 2030s without urgent government intervention.

The former Labour health secretary is leading a government-commissioned review into youth economic inactivity, with the government set to take further action based on its recommendations.

Responding to the Jobs Guarantee announcement, Harriet Edwards, director of influencing at the national disability charity Sense, said: “We welcome investment that gives more young disabled people the opportunity to get into work. Too many who want to work are still locked out by barriers, including a lack of appropriate support, inaccessible workplaces and negative attitudes.”

However, shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said Labour has not made clear how it will fund the plan.

She added: “Almost every disabled person I speak to – young or old – tells me they want to work. With 300,000 fewer jobs under Labour, that’s become even harder.

“Labour could have tackled that problem head on by cutting the burdens on businesses. Instead, they are bringing back a Conservative post-pandemic scheme. Andy Burnham clearly has no new ideas.”

A £6 pumpkin spice latte might be your autumn treat, but put the same money towards driving and how far will it take you? According to home charger company Ohme, the answer ranges from just over 30 miles in a petrol car to 300 miles in an electric one.

The trick is what you pay when you plug in. Those 300 miles depend on charging an electric car at home on a cheap smart energy tariff. Plug the same car in at the standard electricity rate and that £6 would cover around 90 miles instead, according to the company’s calculations.

The comparison comes as petrol and diesel prices reach a new high, and ahead of a rise in the standard electricity rate to 26.32p per kilowatt hour on 1 October. Ohme’s cheaper example uses an 8p/kWh rate through a smart tariff such as Intelligent Octopus Go, showing how much the price you pay for electricity changes the cost of each journey.

open image in gallery Charging an EV at home on a smart tariff can save you £s as petrol prices soar ( Ohme )

The electric car figures work out at four miles for every kilowatt hour of electricity. At the cheaper rate, that means each mile costs 2p, compared with 6.58p on the standard tariff and roughly 19p for the petrol car in Ohme’s comparison.

Over a year, the gap between petrol and electricity becomes rather bigger than the cost of a coffee. Ohme calculates that someone driving 6,800 miles a year would spend £1,314.10 on petrol, compared with £447.44 charging an EV at the new standard rate. That’s a difference of £866.66, even without the cheaper charging deal.

Using the 8p/kWh smart tariff brings the annual electricity bill for those miles down to £136, or about £11.33 a month. That’s £1,178.10 less than the petrol example and £311.44 less than charging the same EV at the standard rate.

Ohme chief executive David Watson said, “With pump prices rising once again and more pressures on the cost of living, the latest rise in electricity prices is a great time for drivers to look at switching to an EV.”

The company’s smart chargers allow drivers to charge at cheaper, off-peak times. Their role is to take advantage of lower electricity prices, rather than make the car itself more efficient, so it’s the combination of the charging rate and how much electricity the car uses that delivers the saving.

The coffee budget stays the same; how far it takes you depends on what you drive and what you pay to power it. In Ohme’s example, choosing the cheaper charging tariff more than triples the miles your £6 will buy.

British culture – including fictional creations such as Peppa Pig and Mr Bean – represent a key deciding factor for international students choosing where to study, new research indicates.

According to a survey by the British Council, more than four in five (83%) foreign students attending UK universities said British culture played an important role when selecting an overseas destination.

The survey of 2,500 UK-based students originating from five countries revealed that 59% regarded fictional British figures as a major or strong influence behind their choice to study in the UK.

Of those swayed by fictional British characters, Harry Potter was selected by 22%, followed by Mr Bean (21%), James Bond (21%) and the pre-school animated character Peppa Pig (19%).

Administered by Censuswide in April and May, the study polled 500 UK-based students aged between 18 and 25 from each of the five leading sender nations to the UK: the US, China, India, Pakistan and Nigeria.

open image in gallery Rowan Atkinson as Mr Bean (Yui Mok/PA) ( PA Archive )

British music was cited as a major or strong influence by more than three in five (62%) respondents deciding to undertake their education in the UK.

Among those influenced by music from the UK, Ed Sheeran (18%), Dua Lipa (17%), Coldplay (16%) and Harry Styles (16%) emerged as the most popular selections.

Furthermore, nearly three in five (58%) of all surveyed students stated that British cultural icons were a strong or major influence on their choice to study in the UK.

Among those affected by British cultural icons, Queen Elizabeth II (18%), Princess Diana (16%), Sir David Beckham and King Charles III (16%) were selected most frequently.

Catriona McCarthy, the British Council’s interim director for education, said: "The UK is renowned for our world-class degree programmes and global reputation of our higher education institutions.

"It is clear from this survey, however, that UK culture is also a huge draw for international students.

"At a time of increased competition, it is crucial that the UK does everything it can to maintain its position as a global leader in higher education, drawing on all aspects of our higher education proposition and a culturally vibrant UK in order to attract the best students from around the world."

Donald Trump presented Americans with an improbable choice on Monday: Higher gas prices or nuclear annihilation.

The president spoke to reporters at the White House during an announcement of a new $15bn steel plant set to be built in Iowa, a lifeline for Republicans in that and other Midwestern states. But his most interesting remarks centered, as usual, around the six-plus-month-long war in Iran, which has now sapped the American economy to a painful degree and driven gas prices to new highs right as Trump and his party are due to face voters in the midterms.

He tried to paint a picture of necessary hardship for Americans with those remarks, but polls show his similar warnings have largely fallen on deaf ears. Asked by a reporter whether motorists should expect higher gas prices to persist through October, Trump replied that the real “turmoil” Americans should be worried about is a nuclear attack.

“If you want to see turmoil, and a travesty, let them take out a city with a nuclear weapon,” the president warned. “I'm not only talking about Israel and big parts of the Middle East, but let them hit us with a nuclear weapon.”

In practically the same breath, however, Trump claimed that the threat of Iran’s nuclear program had already been taken out — presumably, by the initial U.S. strikes earlier this year, or by the “obliteration” he previously promised that U.S. forces had unleashed in the summer of 2025.

open image in gallery Donald Trump warned that the alternative to fighting the war in Iran and facing high gas prices was a nuclear attack on Monday ( AP )

open image in gallery Gas and diesel prices remain near Covid-era highs as the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continue to bog down energy shipments ( AFP/Getty )

And therein lies the central issue for the president and his team as they face a deepening skepticism towards the war shared by average Americans. Nearly three in four U.S. adults say they do not believe Trump has a plan for ending the war, and majorities also disbelieve Trump’s stated (and contradictory) position for launching the war in the first place: the imminent threat supposedly posed by Iran’s nuclear program. A Quinnipiac poll as far back as March found that more than half of Americans did not believe the administration then. The White House’s numbers on Iran have only worsened since then.

The president and his team have offered no proof in congressional hearings or other settings that, since the strikes in February, any Iranian nuclear facilities were being reconstituted. Tulsi Gabbard, Trump’s former director of national intelligence, testified under oath to the contrary in March. The administration’s entire premise for the war rests on a wholly unproven assertion that, unlike the controversial explanation for the invasion of Iraq during the Bush era, the Trump machine isn’t even bothering to address.

So why does the president, master of moving on from controversy, keep raising it?

Trump gave a vague answer to another foreign policy question during Monday’s press availability as he insisted that he knew whether the suspects arrested at a British airbase used to support the American war effort against Iran were connected to the Iranian government in any way, but couldn’t tell us. The president instead insisted that he wouldn’t have supported the suspects being released on bail, as the five suspects arrested on terror and explosive offenses at RAF Fairford were on Monday.

"We know everything about them,” the president claimed. At a gaggle with reporters on the tarmac Sunday evening, Trump seemed to nod when asked if the suspects were migrants, though U.K. police have said that all five men are actually British nationals, living in London. Iran’s embassy denied involvement.

open image in gallery Trump told reporters on Sunday evening that the suspects in the RAF Fairford attack were migrants, which turned out to be untrue ( Reuters )

The president entered office in 2025 seeking to make foreign policy the forefront of his second-term agenda. Largely delegating domestic policy to the likes of Elon Musk and Stephen Miller, Trump focused on efforts to establish his global leadership credentials, including dispatching deputies in efforts to orchestrate (or simply glom on to) peacemaking efforts around the world. At the same time, he launched an aggressive military campaign against small vessels alleged by the U.S. military to be facilitating drug smuggling in the Caribbean, and launched a wave of U.S. strikes against several key Iranian nuclear installations.

Those efforts culminated in a failed bid to obtain the Nobel Peace Prize, an award he has long coveted since it was given to Barack Obama shortly after Obama became president. The 44th president’s efforts to begin extracting the U.S. from Iraq, a more than decade-long endeavor, as well as his efforts to restart diplomacy with the Muslim world were cited as reasons for Obama’s selection as the 2008 peace prize winner. Trump largely ceased talking about his war-ending efforts after losing the 2025 peace prize, and what was once supposed to be a weeks-long military assault against Iran is now a conflict with no end in sight more than half a year on.

Trump may simply be trying to resuscitate that image now. While Republicans still largely say they approve of his overall job performance, on issue-based polling he has suffered significantly — and on Iran worst of all. Only about half of Republicans in a CNN/SRSS poll last week said that Trump’s actions have helped America’s standing in the world, and only 55 percent of Republicans (Trump’s own voters!) say they currently believe the war was “worth it”. That is not, putting it simply, a group of people who believe they were facing an imminent nuclear attack.

With the midterms approaching, Democrats are likely hoping that the president’s message on Iran remains unfocused and unconvincing, even to Republicans. More and more of his party’s frontline members are breaking rank as a result and are calling for Trump to find a way to resolve the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, causing gas prices to recover, by November.

For many Republicans, that hope may be their only way to electoral survival in the midterms, which are just 36 days away.

A “life changing” new therapy for an extremely rare medical condition which causes patients to grow a second skeleton has been proven successful in a key clinical trial.

Relatives of people living with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) say that they have “desperately waited” years for a medicine to “stop the disease in its tracks”.

FOP is a genetic disorder which causes the human body to generate extra bones where they ought not to grow.

That can include within muscles, tendons, ligaments and other connective tissue.

The bone growth typically occurs after flare-ups, which may be provoked by minor injuries or sickness.

The condition is life-limiting as it results in progressive immobility, along with difficulties speaking, swallowing and breathing.

open image in gallery A multi-country clinical trial has returned positive results for those with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

However, the new “disease-modifying” treatment has now been shown to cut new bone growth by over 90 per cent, decrease flare-ups and potentially provide renewed hope for surgical options in the future.

FOP ranks among the world's rarest medical conditions, impacting just one in every million people.

Data provided by the charity FOP Friends indicates that there are 70 patients across the UK, with only 900 recorded cases found worldwide.

The charity said that “treatments can only change lives if patients can access them” as it called on health officials to approve the drug garetosmab for NHS use.

The new treatment, also known as Pasatru and made by Regeneron, is an antibody that blocks a protein called activin A, which has been found to be critical in the development of new abnormal growth development in people with FOP.

Because the disease is so rare, the clinical trial took place in 16 countries and regions, including the UK.

It involved 63 adults with FOP with an average age of 27 who were split into three groups: one group received a dummy drug, or placebo, another was given a low dose of garetosmab and the other received a higher dose.

After just over a year of treatment, the total number of new abnormal bone growths was significantly lower among the groups who received the treatment.

open image in gallery FOP causes bones to grow where they should not ( Getty/iStock )

People who had the placebo had an average of 19 new ‘lesions’ while people who received the treatment had just one or two.

Those taking the higher dose also saw a reduction in flare-ups, researchers found.

Writing in The Lancet, the authors said: “The current treatment landscape for FOP is marked by unmet need.

“However, the findings from this study provide strong evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of garetosmab in adults with FOP.”

They went on: “Given its efficacy in preventing the formation of new heterotopic bone lesions, reducing flare-ups, and reducing the total volume of new heterotopic bone lesions, garetosmab has the potential to become an efficacious disease-modifying treatment for FOP, with a generally well-tolerated safety profile.

“By dramatically reducing the process of heterotopic ossification, long term preservation of mobility and function is anticipated, as further ankyloses of joints will potentially not occur with garetosmab treatment.

“Moreover, the ability of garetosmab to prevent new bone formation in FOP might allow its use as a basis to reconsider surgical remobilisation efforts, which could allow for the significant return of function for many people with FOP suffering from immobilised joints, and which has so far been avoided due to the induction of exuberant aberrant bone formation by surgical intervention.”

open image in gallery FOP affects only about 70 people in the UK ( Getty/iStock )

Chris Bedford-Gay, FOP Friends founder and trustee, said that the community “has desperately waited for a way to stop FOP in its tracks”.

He said: “For many years, our community has hoped for the day there would be a treatment for FOP, a way to stop the devastating, irreversible condition impacting our lives.

“Now, over 15 years since we joined the battle when our eldest son, Oliver, was diagnosed just after his first birthday, we finally have not one, but two potential treatments heading to the UK.”

The US medicines regulator has approved garetosmab and another treatment called zilurgisertib.

Mr Bedford-Gay said this “is the moment a life-changing treatment comes that bit closer”, adding: “For patients, parents and carers who have watched helplessly as FOP steals mobility and independence piece by piece, this news proves that our fight, the years of fundraising, advocating and participating in clinical trials, has not been in vain.

“However, for our community here in the UK, celebration is mixed with anxiety – treatments can only change lives if patients can access them.

“As part of FOP Friends, and as a dad to a child with FOP, my focus now shifts to the UK regulatory pathway.

“We must argue the case for all FOP patients in the UK to have access to these treatments, ensuring we do not have to wait a single day longer than necessary for this life-altering medicine.

“Our job now, as a community, is to persuade the UK regulatory authorities that these new treatments are safe, effective and life-changing for FOP patients, their families and beyond.

“Soon we will have a weapon against FOP. But for now, our fight must continue.”

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2007 after Middle East tensions pushed oil prices above $108.

Yields on 10-year gilts, which determine the price the treasury pays to borrow money, rose above 5.43pc on Monday, before edging back to 5.42pc.

These are levels not seen in almost two decades, underlining the challenge facing John Healey as he prepares for next month’s Budget.

The Chancellor is coming under pressure to slash spending or raise taxes to bring Britain’s borrowing costs under control, against a backdrop of growing debt and rising inflation.

The surge in 10-year gilt yields pushes them above the 19-year high of 5.41pc recorded earlier this month, threatening to put a dent in Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom – a self-imposed guardrail to guide public spending.

Economists said high costs reflect the scale of Britain’s near-£3tn national debt and the rise in inflation facing the country.

“The uncomfortable truth for the PM and his Chancellor, John Healey ... is that the wide spread of gilt yields over peers is fair, in our view, given the UK’s dire fiscal position and the inflationary pressures stemming from high energy prices,” said Elliott Jordan-Doak, at Pantheon Macroeconomics.

“Gilt yields will fall if energy prices drop, but investors will continue to be driven by the economics and the Government’s willingness to take tough fiscal decisions, both of which point to yields staying high.”

UK borrowing costs are growing amid a wider bond market sell-off after Donald Trump rejected a peace deal with Iran over the weekend, pushing oil prices higher.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 3pc to just over $108 a barrel on Monday, adding to global inflation pressures. Bond traders reacted by demanding higher yields from governments to lend them money.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose to above 5.24pc, the highest level since 2007.

News.title: Taylor Swift becomes most-awarded artist in MTV history
News.content:
Taylor Swift broke records at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) on Sunday, becoming the most-awarded artist in VMA history.

The pop star, 36, was previously tied with Beyoncé for the title, with 30 VMAs each. However, Swift took home three awards at the ceremony, bringing her career total to an unmatched 33.

The Fate of Ophelia, ⁠Swift’s first single from her record-breaking The Life of a Showgirl album, claimed the top trophy – Video of the Year – and she dedicated the honour to the late country music legend Dolly Parton.

During her speech, Swift praised Parton as “the ultimate showgirl” who told stories that were “so vivid and so rich”.

“I think that we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time,” she said.

Parton, an award-winning country singer, died in August at the age of 80.

Swift also received the inaugural Artist Director Honors, a new award meant to recognise artists “whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling”.

The 36-year-old has written and directed 18 videos of her roughly 60 videos during her career. The ‌most recent, for ‌her new single Patient Zero, debuted during ⁠the ceremony.

News.title: Five reasons why Australia’s win over Boks was an all-time classic
News.content:
If the Wallabies play like this in their own backyard at their own World Cup next year, boy we are in for a treat. After years in the doldrums, this five-try victory over South Africa was the latest reminder of their transformation under the stewardship of Les Kiss.

Their gritty performance in Perth – the city where Australia will open rugby’s showpiece in 12 months’ time – was caveated by the fact they were facing a second-string Boks side. But there can be no denying they are on an upward trajectory, even if their discipline dramatically deserted them late on.

In a helter-skelter denouement, Australia played the majority of the final 10 minutes of the match with 11 men on the pitch as South Africa threatened to mount a late comeback. Tom Wright’s eye-catching intercept try looked to have secured a match-winning moment, but it was scratched off after Hunter Paisami joined Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan and Joseph Sua’ali’i in the bin.

Ox Nche’s 80th-minute score made it a four-point game with time left for the restart, but Australia had enough fight to secure a dramatic victory largely built on execution and patience.

Five tries by the hour mark, including a Len Ikitau first-half double, ultimately gave South Africa a mountain to climb. The Wallabies’ field coverage and industriousness in defence was far superior to that of the four-time world champions, while Max Jorgensen and Sua’ali’i were pillars of excellence out wide.

After clinching a 3-1 win over New Zealand in their historic “Greatest Rivalry” series, Rassie Erasmus had the luxury of resting several of his A-listers for this one-off Test in Western Australia. The changes ultimately had an adverse effect, with the visitors faulty at the set-piece and lacking their usual snarl and bite. They found themselves playing catch-up in a chaotic game that Australia, despite their discipline creaking in the dying moments, deserved to win.

Here, Telegraph Sport explores five reasons why this was one of the craziest Test matches in recent memory.

Wallabies outmuscle Boks over 60 emphatic minutes

The Wallabies front up impressively to earn a seven-point lead at the break after a quickfire Len Ikitau double cancels out tries from Johan Grobbelaar and Edwill van der Merwe, before Ben Donaldson finishes a sublime attacking set from the hosts.

News.title: England show ODI depth in thrashing of Sri Lanka
News.content:
England’s international summer comes to an end at the Oval with a series decider against Sri Lanka. After England won the first game in Durham, Sri Lanka bounced back to take a 16-run win at Headingley on Thursday to set up this winner-takes-all match today. Sri Lanka put up a much better fight in the second one-day international than they have throughout the rest of their white-ball tour. The tourists posted 321 for six, with their captain Kusal Mendis leading the way with 121 off 100 balls, his seventh ODI century.

England’s reply got off to the best possible start, with both openers Tom Banton and Ben Duckett hitting fifties. It appeared to be going well for England, with Jos Buttler and Will Jacks also registering half centuries, but Buttler’s hamstring injury in addition to the regular loss of wickets meant Sri Lanka were able to claim victory to take us to a series decider in London today.

“I am so happy winning and getting the hundred,” Mendis said. “The overall performance was very good. We started really well and the middle order batted really well. Nothing special, basic cricket and I was very happy with 320, we wanted more than 300 on this pitch. [Dunith] Wellalage bowled really well, the whole team, after the powerplay. The guys gave 100 per cent. Today [Thursday] is finished and now we have to focus on the next game and do the basics right.”

When Buttler retired hurt in the 38th over of England’s run chase, the hosts were 254 for four and were in a great position to chase the total down and claim a series victory. From the 37th over onwards, England were only able to score one four and one six.

“It was an outstanding game,” England captain Harry Brook said. “You can look back and dwell on some many different areas but that is not what this team does, we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the Oval. We put up a really good fight with the ball. To restrict them to 320 and have the chance to chase that down was a hell of an effort.

“The lads got the chase off to a flyer. You could not really ask for much more. We probably stalled in that middle period and lost a few too many wickets, but the fight we showed was great. We have got a great opportunity now to try and win this series, and a great opportunity for 12 months’ time. In pressure situations, like the one that awaits us at the Oval, it will be great to see where we are as a team.”

Buttler has been ruled out of this match due to a hamstring injury and has been replaced in the squad by Dan Lawrence, who had been playing for Surrey in the final round of the County Championship.

Play from the Oval will get under way at 10.30am.

News.title: Saracens storm Leicester to launch new Venter era in style
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Gallagher Prem meeting as Leicester Tigers host Saracens at Welford Road.

Last season, Leicester reached the play-off semi-finals in Geoff Parling’s first full season at the club, before losing to arch-rivals Northampton Saints, who went on to win their third title in the competition.

In a new era for Leicester as they plot a route back to the very top, Aaron Wainwright and Mako Vunipola make their Prem debuts.

Leicester head coach Geoff Parling is brimming with excitement ahead of this tasty match and has talked about his side’s preparation for the new season.

“Firstly we are looking to evolve our game, we’re not looking to rip it up and completely restart,” he said. This team is built on being competitive and winning, we’ve got to be in the mix every year. For me it’s all about being consistently near the top and then getting in those big games and having the ability to perform in them.”

“I’m well aware that there’s lots of elements from the season and different circumstances but the main thing is that the league is designed to have a top four that go into the play-offs so the top four is the aim.”

Saracens finished one place below Leicester in the previous campaign and missed out on the play-offs after a 32-12 final round loss to Exeter Chiefs.

Boss Joe Shaw has handed debuts to Tomos Williams and Alfie Barbeary, and he’s raring to go ahead of this fixture.

“We’ve had a great pre-season, but we’re itching to get stuck into the league campaign now,” he said. “We have a really competitive squad who are driving standards and good habits across the pitch. We are confident in the squad we have put together and are excited to see what they can achieve this campaign.”

Kick-off is at 15:00.

News.title: England throw it away with defending unworthy of a top nation
News.content:
Tuchel does not plan to address the issue with his players ahead of the remaining Nations League games against Czech Republic and Croatia.

Asked if the City verdict had been a cause of discussion ahead of the Spain game, Tuchel replied: “Not for me, but I can imagine maybe for the Man City players. I won’t comment on it as it’s an ongoing case.

“I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking about Spain and the team and meetings. The players have more time than me. So I can imagine they talk about it. It’s good they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”

Kane added: “There was a discussion, but when we’re with England, we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week.”

Tuchel also refused to point the finger of blame at Guéhi, O’Reilly or Kane, who missed a penalty, for England’s defeat despite admitting his team got off to the worst possible start by conceding a goal after two minutes.

“We will focus on the positives, but also highlight the stuff we can do better,” Tuchel said. “Not even speaking about individual mistakes because this is normal. It just happens. It should not happen, and for sure not in this amount. But there is no sense in showing the individual mistakes or telling them ‘please don’t make mistakes’. That is normal, but we can do things better. We can defend the third goal better. But we will focus on the positives. There is a lot to take away from the game.

“We wanted to be the team desperately to beat them [Spain] and we think we had them. We still think we had them at half-time. That was the way the team showed up after half-time. So we will focus on that, but the reality is we lost and the reality is we need to prove it again.”

News.title: Red Roses triumph over New Zealand in chaotic late scenes – how it unfolded
News.content:
Just when it looked like the Red Roses’ lustre was beginning to fade, up stepped Zoe Harrison.

In one of the most dramatic finishes to an England match in recent memory, the fly-half gobbled up Amy Du Plessis’s pass to glide over the whitewash and secure a pulsating win over New Zealand.

Ever the epitome of calmness, Harrison was undeterred by the fact she had just missed what would have been a match-winning penalty from 42 metres out with the score locked at 19-19.

But after their arm-wrestle with Canada last weekend in Exeter, which finished 26-26, there was simply no way the Red Roses were going to settle for a draw for a second week running.

A year to the day since they were crowned world champions in their own back yard, England’s status as the most dominant side in the women’s game was all but confirmed by this never-say-die victory over the Black Ferns.

News.title: Russell holds his nerve to see off Verstappen and win Azerbaijan GP
News.content:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend went the way many believed the 2026 season would play out. George Russell strolled to victory from pole, though with a little late jeopardy, whilst Kimi Antonelli’s crash in qualifying meant he had to fight his way through the field to finish fifth. That, after all, was the order of things last season.

Yet the past few days in Baku are an inversion of the season’s storyline. It is Antonelli who has been the faster driver, heading for a maiden world title at the second time of asking. Russell has been the troubled one. This was only the Briton’s third victory of the season and his first since Austria in late June. Antonelli has racked up eight wins and, before this weekend in Baku, a well-deserved 81-point lead over Russell.

Russell’s dominant and impressive run from pole to the chequered flag on Saturday is both a reminder of what he is capable of and also what might have been, had he been able to find this type of form earlier and more often. The reality, though, is that he needs to replicate this for the rest of the season to even be in with a sniff, barring a catastrophic meltdown from Antonelli. Still, Russell looked elated to have ended his barren run.

The finish was a little more tense than Russell deserved, having established a healthy lead in the first half of the race. Two late safety cars eradicated his advantage and helped put Max Verstappen’s Red Bull on his gearbox. In the end, he triumphed by just under 0.2sec and, as Antonelli finished fifth – with some help from two safety-car inducing crashes – he made up 15 points on his Mercedes team-mate. Isack Hadjar completed the podium for Red Bull after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.

Sports.title: Man City charges LIVE: Punishment latest as 115 charges verdict decided
Sports.content:
Danny Mills believes Manchester City should be punished for as long as they are found to be cheated. The former Manchester City defender reckons his former team should be handed a points deduction over multiple seasons

"People are talking about relegating them to the EFL - we know that they're two separate competitions, two separate bodies," he said on talkSPORT

"I just heard from a fan, 'It would be great for the EFL'. No it wouldn't. City would bounce straight back immediately, which means instead of two spots available for (automatic) promotion (from the Championship), there would only be one.

"You're only going to play Manchester City twice that season, so you're not going to make huge revenue. You've only got 20,000 people in your stadium, one sell-out is not going to change your whole season in any way, shape or form.

"You go to City, you're not going to get any money there anyway because it's all home gate receipts.

"I was listening over the last few days and I think, once everything has settled, realistically the only way going forward to do this is to maybe look at every season that they allegedly cheated.

"Every season they have cheated, give them a massive points deduction for every season going forward.

"So if they cheated for nine years, give them a 20-point deduction for the next nine years and see how that goes, see where they get to in that.

"There is no fair and just system, because it's going so far back retrospectively, and it's going to be very, very difficult because other clubs are going to then complain that they lost out and got relegated, how do you work that out?"

Sports.title: Rio Ferdinand takes firm stance over Man Utd and JJ Gabriel - 'Can't be bullied by a young kid!'
Sports.content:
Rio Ferdinand takes firm stance over Man Utd and JJ Gabriel - 'Can't be bullied by a young kid!'

JJ Gabriel has informed Manchester United that he wants to leave, with several European giants keen to sign him, and Rio Ferdinand has given his old club some advice

View 2 Images Rio Ferdinand has a clear message for his old club (Image: Rio Ferdinand Presents)

Rio Ferdinand has told Manchester United not to be "bullied" by JJ Gabriel after he asked to be released by the club.

‌



The 15-year-old star's future at United has been the subject of intense speculation recently after it emerged that he was unhappy. Gabriel is yet to make his first-team debut for United and has grown frustrated by the lack of opportunities, despite his age.

‌



He is not happy to just be starring for United's under-21s and his family believe Gabriel's development would be better served elsewhere. Gabriel has been courted by Barcelona, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain, while United's Premier League rivals are also interested, if his exit can be arranged.

‌



Ferdinand visited United's squad during their pre-season in Ireland and was hugely impressed by Gabriel's ability. But the former United defender has urged his old club not to bend over backwards because it would set a dangerous precedent.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



"I just feel that Man United can't be seen to be bullied by a young kid who is 15 years old, no matter how good he is," Ferdinand said on his YouTube channel.

"So whatever the outcome is, Man United have to remain strong in this until the end because whatever the decision or whatever way this plays out, there will be kids coming after this who will be using it as a reference point and you can't be seen to be weak in this situation as a football club.

"But I'm not going to sit here and hammer on the kid or pick apart what's going on because I don't have the facts around how they've got to this situation, this end point, that JJ Gabriel and his family are demanding to leave."

‌



View 2 Images JJ Gabriel wants out of Manchester United (Image: Manchester United/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Two of Ferdinand's children, Lorenz and Tate, are pursuing professional careers in the Brighton academy and he was asked if he sympathised with Gabriel's family.

"As a parent I'm the same," he admitted. "I want to know what you think of my son and how you see him and how long it will take. But I know that nothing is guaranteed in this game because there are too many things that can alter your path, be it injuries, form, timing and confidence etc."

Article continues below

Gabriel turns 16 on October 6 and can then be legally represented by an agent. But currently, he would only be allowed to find a new club at the end of the season, unless United agree to deregister him.

It's a messy situation, but one thing isn't in doubt for Ferdinand. "What a talent this kid is," he said. "It’s crazy. I don’t know where this kid’s ceiling is. I’ve seen him play, I’ve seen him train, I’ve listened to people who have coached him for a number of years and there’s no doubt this kid is going to the top."

Sports.title: Joe Hart opens up on Man City guilty verdict with clear message - 'I know what we did'
Sports.content:
Joe Hart opens up on Man City guilty verdict with clear message - 'I know what we did'

Manchester City players have rarely spoken about the Manchester City charges verdict since reports emerged on Friday, with Joe Hart now becoming one of the first

View 2 Images Joe Hart has spoken out about Manchester City's guilty verdict (Image: BBC)

Joe Hart does not think that Manchester City will be found guilty of their Premier League charges because of how much their former goalkeeper trusts chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak. In response to Friday's reporting, the Abu Dhabi Executive Council member insisted: "Our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."

‌



Hart, 39, played a part in City's first two Premier League-winning teams. He played 348 times in 12 years at the club.

‌



Barely any former City players have reacted publicly to the reports. Hart became one of the first, but spoke very carefully.

‌



Erling Haaland gives manager what he wants after Man City 115 charges verdict made public READ MORE :

Why Premier League have not made a statement on Man City 114 charges bombshell READ MORE :

Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live during The Monday Night Club, he said: "I've heard everyone else go down every single rabbit hole, every single wormhole, every single discussion. My honest opinion is I've got no reason not to trust Khaldoon [Al Mubarak]. What he said is enough for me.

"I loved how he spoke. I loved the letter because that was from someone who cared about the club."

Al Mubarak said in part: "The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the Club's innocence is just as strong as when this began."

‌



"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position.

View 2 Images Khaldoon Al Mubarak wrote an open letter to Manchester City supporters over the weekend (Image: Getty)

"But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it mean I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."

Hart continued on the radio programme: "If Man City are found guilty, which I don't think they are because of what Khaldoon said, then there are conversations to be had, but right now I'm very confident and very, very calm.

"I'm very proud of what I've achieved and what I did with Manchester City and what we achieved as a team. And that doesn't change, that doesn't change until you tell me."

‌



The player-turned-pundit later concluded by saying matter-of-factly: "I did what I did. I lined up 11 v 11 and had it out on the pitch. I won some games, lost some games, drew some games, and I shook hands, and I walked off.

"I know what I did, I know what we did, and I know how it happened. It didn't feel like we were scheming or plotting."

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel backs England to overcome defensive frailties as he drops selection hint
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel backs England to overcome defensive frailties as he drops selection hint

Thomas Tuchel's side face Czech Republic in Prague on Tuesday night looking to re-establish their rock solid defence following a night of mishaps in the defeat by Spain

View 4 Images Thomas Tuchel has backed his error-prone defence to turn it around (Image: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

Thomas Tuchel admits England have become a “danger to themselves” when it comes to defending.

‌



Tuchel oversaw a perfect World Cup qualifying campaign as they were water tight at the back and did not concede a single goal. But the three goals conceded against Spain at Wembley means they have now shipped 13 goals in their last six games.

‌



They have kept just four clean sheets in 13 games in 2026 and, tellingly, in each of the last five times they have conceded three or more goals Jordan Pickford has not been in goal.

‌



That run dates back to Aaron Ramsdale, Dean Henderson (twice), Nick Pope and now James Trafford, who obviously shipped three goals against Spain at Wembley on Saturday. Leeds keeper Trafford will be between the posts again in Prague against the Czech Republic as he continues his job share with Pickford.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



But Tuchel made it crystal clear that England’s defending is actually trying to cut out individual errors as on Saturday it was Marc Guehi and Nico O’Reilly who were guilty of uncharacteristic mistakes. England boss Tuchel said: “We suffered clearly from individual mistakes when we had the ball, especially in the deep build-up.

“Of course, that is something we cannot repeat, especially not at this kind of level. We have to take care about this. We have to be technically absolutely clinical also under pressure.

“We need to improve these things but strangely enough, when we had the ball we were the biggest danger to ourselves around the box because we just had too many individual mistakes. Purely in defending, I have no concerns and trust that we can do it.

‌



“I don't see a pattern. It was individual mistakes. I didn't see a pattern in defending. I think we defended very well in a block when we were organised, but we had just big individual mistakes. But I could not see any defensive pattern that would concern me.”

View 4 Images James Trafford will keep his place in goal (Image: Carl Recine/Getty Images)

Maybe it is not the time to make too many changes - and Tuchel made it clear he will back his defenders - and bringing in Trent Alexander-Arnold would seem like something of a risk because of his attacking instincts.

‌



Tuchel was not giving anything away on that front, but says he is relishing to see the keeper job share and also said that Alexander-Arnold is proving his desire to play for England.

Tuchel said: “We use the Nations League to see where we are with the other goalkeepers. It is in this camp it’s Traff and Pickers and we absolutely know what he gives us and how he performs under pressure. He did nothing wrong.

“There was no reason from performances to open up this position for competition. I think it's necessary with every other player that we are aware of ‘what if’.

‌



View 4 Images Marc Guehi's mistake allowed Lamine Yamal to make it 1-0 to Spain (Image: Carl Recine/Getty Images)

“If a player that starts a season well, like Traff at Leeds, has the chance to prove it and to play in our style and to do the build-up and patterns and defensive patterns in the way we want to do it. We just need to see it at some point.

“I will not tell you about other changes. We wait and then we see. But I will not change now because someone made an individual mistake, and they've been good for us through all the other matches.

‌



“Trent has been good, he had a very good training week and the excellent training in Wembley after the match, where he showed that he absolutely wants to play and wants to be with us. We're good. Today was a good training session. Everything is fine. He's ready to go.”

View 4 Images Czech Republic beat England 2-1 in October 2019 (Image: Denis Doyle/UEFA via Getty Images)

Back in 2019, England lost to the Czech Republic in Prague and that ended their 43-game unbeaten run in qualifying. That must serve as a warning to this England team as they try to finish in the top two to qualify to progress in the Nations League.

‌



Even Jurgen Klopp is finding international management tougher than it looked after Germany lost to Greece and that is a feeling that Tuchel is familiar with.

Tuchel added: “Everyone told me. Everyone told me that it is tough to form a team and everyone comes with different ideas and the focus was to bring them together, play properly as a team and implement patterns of play and we are a step further.

“We had a tournament together, we had this experience together. We digested it. We had a result that some think was not enough, some think it was a good result, whatever we had a result and we continue and this helps us. It is a process. So, it is another proof that to do it in international football you do it in four or five days what you do in four or five weeks at a club.”

Sports.title: Thomas Tuchel makes Jude Bellingham feelings crystal clear after Spain show
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel makes Jude Bellingham feelings crystal clear after Spain show

Thomas Tuchel has lauded Jude Bellingham after the England midfielder produced another fine display in the recent 3-2 defeat against Spain at Wembley

View 2 Images Jude Bellingham shone in England's 3-2 defeat to Spain

Thomas Tuchel says Jude Bellingham has become England’s Duracell bunny.

‌



Bellingham, 23, has been in brilliant form for England and Tuchel says the Real Madrid superstar has found a new level. The Three Lions midfielder enjoyed a sensational World Cup, where he helped lead England to a third placed finish in the United States.

‌



But Tuchel says that while Bellingham has always delivered in big moments, now he is staying strong and playing at his best level for the whole 90 minutes just as he did against Spain at Wembley last Saturday.

‌



England boss Tuchel said: “I liked his performance a lot the other day because it was very consistent throughout the 90-plus minutes. He was always involved.

‌



“Jude can play in these high intensive patterns and then needs time to recharge the batteries and maybe goes again and has these moments and minutes when he plays at the highest intensity and then he needs to recharge.

“Now, he played at a highest level but was always involved. He had played economically and was always a difference maker, always available.

“A little bit of a new position for him where he can overload both sides and that suits him very well but it was a very mature, very very good performance.”

‌



Bellingham has silenced all of the doubters and is now England’s key man with Harry Kane as they look to bounce back from Spain against the Czech Republic.

View 2 Images Thomas Tuchel has praised Bellingham

It is a big shift for the way that Tuchel views Bellingham as gone are the doubts and snipes to be replaced with just glowing praise and the England manager highlighting his dedication to being a part of the squad.

‌



Tuchel added: “He looks like a real member of the squad on and off the pitch. That is the key in itself that players want to come and want to really play and don't only say it but prove the point.

“We provide an environment and atmosphere where they can actually feel free and express themselves and be the best visions of themselves. It is a give and go. We need to provide that and the player needs to have the hunger and the excitement to show up.”

Sports.title: Man City chief declares Premier League charges battle far from over in bombshell statement
Sports.content:
Man City chief declares Premier League charges battle far from over in bombshell statement

Manchester City's CEO has addressed the recent reports claiming that the former Premier League champions have been found guilty of almost all the 115 charges brought against them

View 2 Images Ferran Soriano (R) and Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (Image: Getty Images)

Ferran Soriano, the Manchester City chief executive officer, is said to have stressed that the club's fight with the Premier League over the 115 charges brought against them is far from over during a European Football Clubs board meeting.

‌



Football was rocked last week by reports that City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges against them, though the former Premier League champions are expected to appeal the verdict. Formal confirmation has yet to arrive but City's chairman, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, released a statement over the weekend reiterating that the club were confident of clearing their name.

‌



And Soriano, speaking at a meeting which was also attended by senior figures from other Premier League clubs, adopted a similar stance of defiance during an impromptu address on Monday.

‌



Per The Athletic, Soriano wanted to address the reports and made it clear that the club would continue to fight against the charges.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



“It has taken eight years to reach this point and it will still take much more time,” he is understood to have said.

Soriano declined to comment further when he was asked to do so by reporters in Copenhagen after the meeting.

His comments echo similar sentiments to that of Al Mubarak, who released a statement over the weekend in the wake of the reports which claimed City have “irrefutable evidence” to help fight their case.

‌



“I have been part of this Club for 18 years. I have had the privilege to stand with you in the Etihad, at Wembley, and in Istanbul,” City's chairman wrote in a message which also referenced previous statements made by the club.

View 2 Images Manchester City could be handed a significant point deduction

“This Club matters to me, and you have shown and told me – time and time again - how much Manchester City matters to you. This is why I am writing to you today. Following Friday’s media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I.

‌



“Here’s what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the Club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began. There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position.

“But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies. Every word matters and holds true.”
