The rare trip, if confirmed, comes exactly one month before Israel’s October 27 election and against the backdrop of heightened political controversy in Israel over reporting by Haaretz and The New York Times alleging that Bin Zayed had warned Netanyahu of a major Hamas operation days before the October 7, 2023, attack.

The Atlantic separately reported that Egypt’s intelligence chief Abbas Kamel flew to Israel on September 26, 2023, to warn that Gaza would “blow up.” And on Sunday, The Wall Street Journal reported that there were at least three Egyptian warnings conveyed to Israel about Gaza, the last one in a phone call to Netanyahu, just days before the attack.

Netanyahu’s office has repeatedly denied receiving any warning and has dismissed the reports as fabricated lies aimed at damaging him electorally. But his rivals have used the allegations to make accountability for the failure to prevent the October 7, 2023, attack a central campaign issue.

People walk past a television channel  featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, and his main rival, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of Israel’s general election, in Ramat Gan, Israel, on Wednesday. Oded Balilty/AP

After initial reports of a warning from Bin Zayed, the UAE’s Foreign Ministry said earlier this month that it “does not comment on media stories or speculation regarding conversations between government leaders,” but it did not deny the call. “When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities,” the statement said.

At the time, an Israeli source familiar with the matter said Netanyahu’s office tried to get the UAE to deny the report, but the UAE only agreed to issue a statement about intelligence sharing.

Netanyahu’s Likud party subsequently issued a statement, posted on the prime minister’s X account, alleging “blatant foreign interference” in Israel’s elections by UAE-based Palestinian politician Mohammed Dahlan. The party provided no evidence for the claim.

Netanyahu’s rivals, meanwhile, have seized on the reported warning to renew their attacks on his handling of the events preceding October 7.

Gadi Eizenkot, currently polling as the prime minister’s main challenger in Israel’s upcoming elections, said Saturday that the revelation about the warning “leaves no room for doubt: Netanyahu led, with blindness, arrogance and irresponsibility, the State of Israel to the greatest disaster in its history.”

In May, Netanyahu’s office said the prime minister had secretly visited the UAE in March, during the early days of the Iran war, calling it a “historic breakthrough.” The UAE foreign ministry, however, denied his claim at the time as “completely unfounded.”

During the war, Israel is also said to have deployed an Iron Dome missile defense system to the UAE and Israeli officials have said security cooperation between the two countries reached unprecedented levels.

Netanyahu has never made a publicly acknowledged official visit to the UAE.

World.title: AI agents promise to do everything for you. There may be a big wrinkle in that plan
World.content:
Meta wants its new Muse AI agent to be the gateway to users’ digital lives. But that all depends on whether popular apps and services are willing to give it the keys.

Agents go a step beyond how most people have used AI up to this point. Instead of simply answering questions, organizing emails and creating images, they can take multistep actions on the internet. They can compare prices, shop, book reservations and fill out forms, if the companies that sell things and take reservations allow them.

That change may spark a new battle over the future of internet services. Amazon recently blocked Muse’s AI agent from accessing its store, and some experts say the move could foreshadow a dilemma for online businesses.

If more people use AI agents for daily tasks, businesses may need to make a critical choice: Partner with companies like Meta and risk their own platforms possibly becoming irrelevant. Or potentially miss out on reaching billions of customers through what may be the future of how people get things done.

Shares of Airbnb, Expedia, and Trip Advisor fell around 5% last week after Meta announced new updates for its Muse agent.

Meta’s Muse makes waves

The idea of AI agents isn’t new; OpenAI, Google, Apple and Amazon, along with Meta, have been working towards this future for years and have gradually rolled out new agent-like features.

But Muse caught on almost immediately, shooting to the top of the free app chart on Apple’s App Store 10 days after its September 8 debut. Meta owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp, and its pervasive internet presence — along with the app’s relatively easy interface — largely drove the AI agent’s success.

Meta launched an app for its AI agent, Muse, on September 8. The app rose to the top of the free app chart on Apple’s App Store 10 days after its debut. Samuel Boivin/NURPHO/AP

Compared to other tech giants, Meta has done a better job at showing Muse’s capabilities to consumers, according to Francisco Jeronimo, an analyst with technology market research firm International Data Corporation.

“Others have not been so vocal about using the agents to be able to shop as Meta has been with Muse, and I think that’s the main difference,” he said.

Meta has partnered with Walmart, GameStop, Sephora, Expedia, OpenTable and Shopify to incorporate their services into the Muse app. But e-commerce juggernaut Amazon refused to play ball with Meta. Amazon blocked the agent, saying it was not given notice or a choice about whether its store should be available through Muse.

The company also cited concerns around how Amazon account data and credentials would be handled, and said agents don’t offer Amazon’s personalized recommendations.

“We think it’s fairly straightforward that third-party applications that offer to make purchases on behalf of customers from other businesses should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate,” Amazon said in a statement to CNN.

Online restaurant reservations platform Resy also told CNN that it “does not currently permit unapproved third-party bots or agents” to access its service. The platform locked a user’s account following attempts by his AI agent, a separate assistant called Instinct, to book hundreds of tables per hour earlier this month.

“Unapproved automated activity can introduce risks to the platform and compromise a fair reservation experience for diners,” the company said.

CNN was able to book a reservation through Muse after providing login information, like a phone number and confirmation code. Resy integrates with ChatGPT and Claude and said it will “continue to evaluate opportunities” as AI agents progress.

Risks and rewards of agents

Amazon may be an outlier. But some experts say AI agents pose real risks that could give many online service providers some pause before allowing agents to use their platforms.

For one, there’s the potential decrease in web traffic if tasks are primarily handled on the AI agent apps. Brands could also lose the ability to learn about customer shopping habits or further entice users into additional purchases with in-app promotions or product recommendations.

“You browse Amazon for that thing that you’re looking for, but then you also see other things that you know you may end up buying,” said Mandeep Singh, a senior industry analyst for Bloomberg Intelligence.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event September 23. Jeff Chiu/AP

Additionally, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Wednesday that the company eventually plans to charge a commission for transactions made through Muse. This means other companies may lose a cut of their sales.

And it’s not just shopping and reservation apps that may be impacted. AI agents are generally good at tasks that require research, like comparing insurance policies or mobile carrier plans. This could potentially make it easier for users to switch plans to land a better deal.

But the upside could also be huge. Muse has already been downloaded more than 2.5 million times, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, giving businesses visibility to millions of people around the world. That could make Muse especially appealing to smaller and mid-sized brands, like those who work with Shopify.

That was part of the appeal for travel platform Expedia, which chose to allow AI agents because it wants “to show up wherever travelers are searching,” Kathryn Heinz, Expedia’s vice president of enterprise alliances and AI, said in a comment to CNN. She added that about two-thirds of Expedia’s traffic comes through its own platforms.

And some might see it as a move to future-proof their business.

“I think long term, that’s exactly what we will see: the AI platforms to become the layer and the main interface for most of us when we are when we are shopping,” International Data Corporation’s Jeronimo said.

World.title: Inside the Trump campaign strategy to reverse Republicans’ dwindling hopes of winning the midterms
World.content:
The midterms mood among Donald Trump’s inner circle has soured as GOP candidates openly break with the president and his approval ratings hit an all-time low, prompting a largely unspoken but age-old question: How does an unpopular president best help his party keep control of Congress?

Trump advisers have privately acknowledged that there’s little expectation he can win over large numbers of independents and swing voters, which was part of his path to victory in critical states in 2024. And while they’re more concerned about losing control of the House, Republicans’ previous confidence that they can hold onto the Senate is dwindling by the day.

“It’s obviously going to be f***ing rough,” one Trump adviser told CNN, adding that they believe the best-case scenario is achieving what Democrats did in 2022, when under former President Joe Biden they narrowly lost control of the House but kept the Senate.

Still, Trump’s team is planning an aggressive campaign schedule for Trump and Vice President JD Vance in October in both battleground and deep-red states alike, multiple officials told CNN — as advisers believe their only hope at holding ground is increasing turnout, and the president can help with that.

“The system is built around what areas we need to goose turnout 2-3 points,” one operative told CNN.

In recent weeks, Trump’s senior advisers, including chief of staff Susie Wiles, put together a calendar that has Trump on the campaign trail for most days in October, though two administration officials said that not all stops had been confirmed. He is planning trips to Alabama and Oklahoma next week, but a GOP official said those were “outliers” in the travel strategy, which would focus more on battleground districts.

“He’ll be playing hard in Florida, Texas, Michigan and Ohio — he’ll be on the road just about every day in October campaigning. We’re leaving it all on the table,” the official added. However, even in more purple states, the plan is for Trump to go to more conservative areas, according to another official.

Advisers also hope the Trump-Vance campaigning will help raise money as Republican groups — including Trump’s MAGA Inc. PAC — have begun hemorrhaging cash across the country. This week, the Senate Leadership Fund increased its spending in Texas to $100 million to support GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton in a state they haven’t lost in decades, exposing the party’s fresh worries about the Senate.

And while one Republican operative said that the enormous sum was moving the needle in their direction “some,” it wasn’t clear it would be enough to reverse the strong political headwinds largely created by the president himself.

Asked if there was anything Republicans could do to change the tide, the operative replied: “Go back in time and never start the war with Iran.”

Running away from Trump

Republicans in both purple territories and even some red districts have broken from Trump on issues ranging from the Iran War to the economy to immigration. Republican Mike Rogers, the Michigan Senate candidate in one of the most closely watched races this cycle, lamented in a recent ad that “Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down.”

“The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly,” Rogers said. “When it does, energy costs will plummet, but Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen.”

That sentiment was echoed by the GOP’s Senate candidates in Iowa and Ohio. Other Republican lawmakers have voted to limit Trump’s war powers. House lawmakers in Florida and Texas have also criticized the administration on immigration. Several others have removed Trump references from campaign websites.

The GOP official involved in strategy brushed off concerns about candidates distancing from the president, saying “they need to run the races they need to run, and we’re obviously encouraging them to do what they need to do.”

In a sign of how potentially polarizing the president and his MAGA brand are right now, much of the money being spent by Trump’s PAC is coming through two newly formed groups with far less politically aligned names: No Going Back PAC Inc. and Safety & Affordability PAC Inc.

However, Trump’s political team still believes that his ability to drive turnout is one of Republicans’ greatest assets come November. While some Republicans have quietly expressed concerns about candidates in sensitive races appearing alongside Trump, one official brushed off the notion.

“The cake is already baked. There’s no getting away from Trump for these guys. So we have to lean into it,” the official said. “The left is going to attack [Republican candidates] as being close to Trump no matter what, so why not get the benefit out of it, which is max turnout.”

Trump’s midterms catch-22

Multiple sources working on midterm strategy told CNN that Trump’s political operation was working off that central belief — that they could still win with enough turnout. In order to minimize the percent of “persuadable” voters that are needed, their thinking goes, it’s critical to get as many base voters to the polls as possible.

“It’s all a turnout game,” a GOP campaign official said. “From day one, the campaign committees and the president’s political operation have been sharing data to make sure we’re hammering the exact people we need to turn out.”

A voter cast a ballot on the first day of early voting in Minnesota on September 18 in Minneapolis. Ellen Schmidt/AP

Sources noted that while this was not the traditional way to look at a midterm when a president’s approval ratings are so low, Trump has always been a different political animal who defies typical expectations.

But his advisers also privately acknowledge a major problem with that strategy: Trump isn’t just an incredible driver of enthusiasm for his own supporters; he’s also a strong driver of Democratic turnout.

“The issue with putting his name on the ballot is it could ultimately serve as a bigger driving force for Democratic voters who hate him,” the campaign official said.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that Trump has “built one of the most robust coalitions in political history” and “the President understands how to communicate with them.”

“President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” Ingle added.

Deploying Vance

The White House and the president’s political apparatus view Vance as a crucial surrogate, and one that tends to stay far more on message compared to the president. But the campaign doesn’t exactly view him as an ace card to deploy in truly competitive territories — he’s still viewed as an extension of Trump. Both men are seen as potentially doing more damage than good in certain swing districts, sources familiar with the discussions tell CNN.

The decision of where and when to send both men is driven directly by the massive data operation that the president’s political team has amassed, one that was fortified during Trump’s 2024 campaign and is now also being used by the Republican National Committee and the GOP’s House and Senate campaign arms. James Blair, who left the White House to take charge of the political operation ahead of the midterms, has been weighing in on the calendars.

Vance, who has met directly with GOP lawmakers and candidates on the ballot in November to help them workshop messaging, has also been tasked with raising so-called “hard money” for the Republican National Committee.

“JD’s primary responsibility has been fundraising,” one source told CNN, nodding to Vance’s role as the RNC’s finance chair. The source described that as an urgent necessity, particularly given the Supreme Court’s ruling earlier this month allowing political party committees, like the RNC, to get discounted television ad rates ahead of the midterm elections.

Vance isn’t the only surrogate the White House has deployed — senior staffers have also worked directly with Wiles to pick campaign stops and priorities for members of Trump’s Cabinet. In fact, Trump’s political team has tracked and ranked Cabinet officials’ campaign involvement, with higher points for traveling to swing districts and subtractions for overseas trips.

The rankings have been shared with officials in group settings in hopes it would incentivize more campaign involvement, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. During a summer meeting at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, Blair credited Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler as leading the pack, with Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling in second, sources present at the meeting said.

World.title: Huthi missiles threaten civil aviation over Red Sea, warns Yemen’s Information Minister
World.content:
Yemeni Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani warned civil aviation authorities and international airlines of the Huthi group’s use of Iranian air defense weapons that have been converted into cruise missiles.

This threat could extend to international flight paths in southern Red Sea, he stressed, coinciding with escalating confrontations on the ground and the Yemeni leadership’s declaration of “general mobilization and national call to arms” against the group.

He said that the gravity of the alarming development revealed by the Yemeni army lies not only in the nature of the weapons used but also in their launch sites, particularly as they are being directed from Huthi-controlled areas toward international air corridors.

The minister recalled the 2020 downing of Ukrainian flight PS752 in Tehran—which claimed 176 lives—and called upon the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), aviation safety authorities, and airlines to incorporate this new development into their risk assessments for regional flight paths and to take action before an “aviation disaster” occurs.

The Yemeni Armed Forces had previously announced the detection of Huthi use of Iranian air defense weapons—reportedly converted into cruise missiles—launched from al-Hudaydah Governorate toward international flight paths in the southern Red Sea.

The Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili said that the Huthis employed these weapons using “innovative techniques and tactics,” noting that the missile is capable of loitering for up to 25 minutes and utilizes heat-seeking technology to target heat sources.

He added that these weapons, according to Yemeni army intelligence, lack the ability to distinguish between military and civilian targets; consequently, launching them along international flight paths poses a threat to civilian aircraft and passengers, as well as to planes operated by the United Nations and humanitarian and relief organizations.

Nuzaili called on the ICAO and the International Air Transport Association IATA to take the necessary measures to address potential risks.

These warnings come amidst escalating military tensions, following the announcement by the Coalition to Support Legitimacy that it had intercepted and destroyed two drones launched by the Houthis toward the Riyadh area, as well as a ballistic missile aimed at Khamis Mushait, in Saudi Arabia, according to Coalition spokesman Brigadier General Turki Al-Maliki.

The Huthis announced that a bridge in al-Makhadir district of Ibb Governorate had been struck by Saudi airstrikes.

The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states called on the international community to adopt a firm stance to put an end to the repeated terrorist attacks by the Huthis against Saudi Arabia.

General mobilization

In a speech marking the 64th anniversary of the September 26, 1962 Revolution, Rashad al-Alimi, Chairman of the Presidential Leadership Council, called for “general mobilization and a national call to arms.”

He urged Yemenis to rally behind the armed forces and security services and to join their ranks through official channels, with the aim of “restoring state institutions and extending sovereignty over all Yemeni territory, all the way to Sana’a.”

Alimi announced an opening for a safe return to the fold of the Republic and constitutional legitimacy, pledging a comprehensive amnesty—in accordance with constitutional and legal procedures—for anyone who abandons the Huthis and ceases fighting or working on their behalf.

He also promised to regularize the status of military and security personnel and preserve their legally acquired employment rights.

World.title: Sisi moves to delegate certain Presidential powers to Defense Minister – here’s what that means
World.content:
The former Director of the National Defense College, Mohamed al-Ghabbary explained President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s decision to delegate certain Presidential powers —as stipulated in the General Mobilization Law—to the Minister of Defense and Military Production.

During a phone-in to the program “Ala Massoulity” (On My Responsibility) on the Sada al-Balad channel, Ghabbary said that the decision is a routine legal and administrative measure that recurs whenever a new Minister of Defense assumes office.

The Official Gazette published the presidential decree, issued on September 22, delegating the Minister of Defense and Military Production to exercise the powers stipulated in Articles 9, 12, and 24 of Law #87 of 1960 for a period of one year, with the decision to take effect on November.

Routine Procedure

Ghabbary noted that the delegation is not a new decision linked to an emergency situation, but rather a routine procedure that repeats with the change of the Minister of Defense.

He explained that the President, in his capacity as head of the National Defense Council, delegates specific powers to the Minister of Defense in accordance with legal provisions.

Ghabbary added that the Minister of Defense undertakes this task alongside his primary duties, given that the administrative aspect of implementing mobilization measures is linked to the entity he heads.

He stressed that the decision does not signal a change in the state of general mobilization, explaining that a mobilization plan is already in place, and that the call-up of reservists or the reinforcement of units is linked to training exercises and operations conducted by the armed forces.

What is general mobilization?

Ghabbary explained that military organization relies on both active-duty and reserve forces, and that mobilization is the mechanism used to bring the armed forces up to the required strength.

He noted that an army’s peacetime force typically ranges between 50-70 percent, depending on the specific country and its arrangements, whereas mobilization serves to bring that force up to the required level—a process applicable to both peacetime and wartime scenarios.

Peacetime mobilization is linked to continuous training, he said, as certain units require their personnel force to be fully staffed while conducting exercises and training maneuvers.

Not a Declaration of War

Linking the authorization decision to regional conditions has raised concerns, he said, noting that he had received inquiries from people both inside and outside Egypt asking if the decision meant the country was heading toward war.

A state of war is preceded by other measures, including the declaration of a state of emergency and the implementation of a strategic state initiative, he explained.

Ghabbary affirmed that the current decision constitutes neither a declaration of war nor a declaration of a state of emergency, explaining that it is a routine legal procedure.

Citizens have the right to ask such questions and that it is the role of specialists to clarify the nature and rationale of the decision, he affirmed.

Civilian Resources

The former head of the Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS), Abu Bakr al-Gendy, explained that the general mobilization system is not limited to the armed forces and their personnel.

It also encompasses an inventory of the state’s civilian resources, allowing them to be utilized in accordance with specific needs and governing regulations, he said.

Gendy said that the events of 2011—accompanied by unrest, chaos, and the disruption of certain transport services—demonstrated the practical importance of this system. At the time, the state was able to leverage available resources to respond rapidly, he said.

Gendy cited the transport of wheat supplies to various governorates—following disruptions to transport networks—as a prime example; the armed forces intervened using their own transport assets, successfully moving and distributing the wheat within a short timeframe.

He added that a decision was issued at the time to deploy transport vehicles to move quantities of wheat from areas such as Alexandria and Suez to other governorates, thereby facilitating the delivery of supplies to citizens within a short timeframe.

Wheat and food supplies were transported across governorates and heavily secured following the events of 2011. he noted.

Gendy emphasized that the successful handling of those circumstances was linked to the existence of a database and a prior inventory of civilian capabilities; this enabled the state to act swiftly without having to start from scratch to assess resources during the crisis.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Liberia: Lawyers for the former Vice President Say Arrest, Detention, Prison and Search Breached Constitution as Bail Fight Heads to Appeal
World.content:
MONROVIA – When the Monrovia City Court issued a writ on August 25, 2026, commanding police to “arrest the living bodies” of Jewel Howard-Taylor, it set in motion one of the most consequential criminal cases against a former senior official in Liberia’s recent history.

By Rodney D. Sieh

A month later, the former Vice President sits under house arrest, her bail application denied, her phones and computers seized, and her lawyers argue that nearly every step the State has taken against her has run afoul of the Constitution.



In a formal statement, her legal team lists what it calls a “cumulative constitutional injury”: ten separate points at which, they contend, Mrs. Howard-Taylor’s liberty was taken or restricted without full regard to the safeguards in Article 21 of the 1986 Constitution.

The allegations against her remain unproven, and so do her lawyers’ claims. Both will ultimately be tested in court.

WHAT THE STATE ALLEGES

The writ of arrest, obtained by FrontPageAfrica, lays out the government’s case in stark terms.

According to the writ, businessman Sheik Bashiru Kante brought two foreign nationals, Taras Zadereiko, alias “Tony,” and Mihovil Vrovac, alias “Michael,” to Liberia in 2021, where they allegedly conspired to import and export cocaine through Liberia to Europe.

The State claims the group set out to recruit top government officials to protect the scheme, and that in 2022 Kante introduced the two men to Mrs. Howard-Taylor, then Vice President.

The writ alleges that in early 2022 she met the men at her Sophie residence in Congo Town, and that they invited her to Dubai to meet Croatian national Nikola Ivancic, whom the government describes as a drug kingpin and ringleader of the cartel. There, prosecutors claim, a meeting was held about using Liberia as a transit point for cocaine, and she agreed.

The State further alleges she received US$45,000 from Ivancic in Dubai “for shopping,” later requested and received US$75,000 from the cartel through Kante, and subsequently received a further US$15,000.

She is charged under the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act of 2023, the New Penal Law and the AML-CFT Act of 2021, with offenses including importation and exportation of controlled drugs, illicit trafficking, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation and criminal solicitation.

THE DEFENSE’S TEN COUNTS

Her lawyers do not address the merits of those allegations in their statement. Instead, they focus on process, and they list ten grievances:

1. Arrest without presentation of a writ of arrest

2. No demonstrated completed investigation to justify the initial deprivation of liberty

3. Incarceration beyond 48 hours

4. Failure to formally charge and present her before a court within 48 hours

5. Absence of an indictment at the relevant stage

6. Incarceration at the Monrovia Central Prison while unconvicted

7. Treatment inconsistent with the distinction between an accused and a convicted prisoner

8. House arrest and substantial restrictions on movement

9. Continued pretrial deprivation of liberty

10. Denial of bail despite the passage of several years since the alleged conduct

“An accusation is not a conviction,” the statement declares.

THE 48-HOUR RULE

At the center of the defense argument is Article 21 of the Constitution, which requires that anyone arrested be formally charged and presented before a court of competent jurisdiction within 48 hours.

The legal team contends the records show Mrs. Howard-Taylor was held beyond that window before the required judicial process was completed. If that chronology holds up, it would be among the most straightforward constitutional questions in the case: the 48-hour rule is not discretionary.

The lawyers are careful to concede the State’s right to investigate. “The issue is not whether the State has authority to investigate alleged criminal conduct. It does,” the statement says. “The issue is whether that authority was exercised within the constitutional limits.”

‘WHILE UNDERGOING INVESTIGATION’

The defense’s second count, that no completed investigation justified her detention, finds an unexpected echo in the government’s own paperwork.

A court interim order dated September 22, 2026, signed on the directive of Judge Ousman F. Feika of Criminal Court “C,” describes Mrs. Howard-Taylor as “currently being detained while undergoing investigation by National Joint Security authorities.”

That language, a month after the arrest writ was issued, suggests the investigation was still underway while she was held. The lawyers argue that an ongoing investigation does not by itself justify continued detention, particularly under a Constitution that expressly bars preventive detention.

FROM CENTRAL PRISON TO HOUSE ARREST

The former Vice President’s journey from arrest to the Monrovia Central Prison and then to house arrest forms another pillar of the defense case.

Her lawyers argue the Constitution protects accused persons from being treated as convicted prisoners, and that housing an unconvicted former Vice President at the country’s main penitentiary raises questions about both the legal basis for her confinement and the conditions she faced.

The later move to house arrest, they argue, is itself a restriction on constitutionally protected freedom of movement, one that must rest on a clear court order and a lawful basis.

THE SEARCH: ‘ALL TELEPHONES, MOBILE PHONES’

Perhaps the most concrete dispute concerns the search of her home.

The September 22 interim order directed the Sheriff of Criminal Court “C” to “immediately move into” her residence, conduct a “comprehensive inspection,” and seize “all telephones, mobile phones, communication gadgets and/or devices” found on the premises or in her possession, then produce an inventory.

The order was served on one of her lawyers at 6:27 p.m. that Tuesday.

According to the defense, officers removed a desktop computer, a printer, an internet connection device, and several mobile phones reportedly belonging to other people, along with other electronics.

The breadth of the order is likely to be contested. It covers every device “found in the premises,” not only those belonging to the accused. The Constitution requires search warrants to specifically identify the place to be searched and the objects sought. Whether an order to seize every phone in a house, regardless of owner, meets that standard is a question the courts may be asked to settle.

“What was the legal basis for taking property belonging to persons other than the accused?” the lawyers ask.

THE BAIL BATTLE

The bail question may prove decisive. Article 21 of the Constitution provides that accused persons shall be bailable on recognizance or sufficient sureties, except for capital offenses or grave offenses as defined by law, and prohibits excessive bail.

Mrs. Howard-Taylor’s bail application was denied at trial level. Her lawyers have excepted to the ruling and are pursuing an appeal.

‘EACH OFFENSE STANDS ON ITS OWN STATUTE’

The defense’s sharpest bail argument centers on the money laundering count.

Attorney Gbawou Kowou, a prominent Liberian lawyer, criminal justice professor and former law enforcement official who represents the former Vice President, argues that money laundering under Section 15.2.1 of the AML/CFT Act of 2021 is not classified as a capital, grave or non-bailable offense. The statute, he notes, expressly makes money laundering a first-degree felony without designating it as grave or non-bailable.

In his view, the presence of drug charges in the same writ should not automatically make the separate money laundering allegation non-bailable. “The bailability of each offense should be determined according to the specific statute creating and classifying that offense,” Kowou said.

Unless the government can point to a specific provision of law making money laundering itself a grave or non-bailable offense, the defense will argue that the count remains subject to the constitutional and statutory right to bail.

The argument puts the burden squarely on the State. It forces prosecutors to show, statute by statute, the legal basis for denying bail, rather than relying on the overall gravity of the case.

THE STATE’S LIKELY ANSWER

The government is expected to rest on the drug counts. The 2023 amendment to the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act was widely reported to have made major drug trafficking offenses non-bailable. If that holds for the drug charges in the writ, prosecutors may argue that a bailable money laundering count does not entitle her to release while non-bailable charges remain.

That tension is likely to be at the heart of the appeal. Can a single non-bailable count keep an accused in detention even when other counts in the same writ are bailable?

THE 2023 LAW AND 2021 CONDUCT

The defense has a further line of attack against the State’s reliance on the 2023 Act. Most of the conduct alleged in the writ dates to 2021 and 2022, before that law took effect. Article 21 prohibits ex post facto laws, which penalize conduct more harshly than the law did when it occurred.

If the courts find the 2023 non-bailable provisions cannot reach conduct from 2021 and 2022, the State’s main basis for denying bail could fall away. That would leave the money laundering question, in Kowou’s framing, as the clearest test of whether the law is being applied count by count.

BIGGER THAN ONE DEFENDANT

The legal team frames the case as a test of the justice system itself.

“No citizen is above the law,” the statement reads. “But neither is the State above the law.”

They argue that constitutional protections matter most when they are claimed by people who are politically controversial or unpopular, and that the question should be answered by the record and the courts, not by political loyalty.

The statement closes with a question that will hang over the case as it moves through the courts: “Is Liberia a nation governed by laws — or a nation governed by men?”

World.title: Liberia: Ten Years On, Liberia’s Ebola Survivors Still Fighting the Aftermath
World.content:
Summary:

A decade after Liberia was declared Ebola-free, survivors and families still carry emotional, economic, and social scars, from loss, disrupted education, and unmet support.

Grandparents are raising orphaned children, while survivors and health workers say the trauma and health effects have not fully disappeared.

Public health experts say Liberia must support survivors, protect frontline workers and apply the lessons of 2014 as Ebola-related threats continue.

By Nukanah Kollie with New Narratives

SUAKOKO, Bong County — All was calm at Phebe Hospital on a recent afternoon. White buildings sat behind freshly cut grass. Ambulances stood nearby. The former Ebola Treatment Unit looked like an ordinary hospital ward.



More than a decade ago, it was part of an hourly battle between life and death. Klebu Pewu was a nurse here. As family and workmates got sick and died around her she tried to keep going. But the virus finally caught her. She was lucky. More than half of the healthcare workers infected died.

Ten years on, she says she avoids talking about it: “Too much sorrow and pain to me.”

Pewu’s grief is not unique, and it is not over. Families across the country still carry the financial, physical, and emotional costs of what remains to this day, the world’s worst Ebola outbreak. Orphaned children have struggle to stay in school. Survivors report lingering health problems, while others say promised support never came. Experts say their unfinished recovery raises questions about how Liberia cared for people who survived its worst health crisis and whether the country fully applied the lessons of 2014.

Bong County was hard hit by the devastating outbreak that is thought to have started in April 2014 when a small child contracted it from a bat killed for bush meat in neighboring Guinea. It quickly engulfed the region paralyzing Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia for more than a year and spreading to Mali, Nigeria, Senegal, Spain and the United States. By the end there were 18,603 confirmed cases and 6,915 dead.

At the peak, Liberia recorded 300 to 400 new cases a week and drew an overwhelming international response for an uncontrolled outbreak that caused alarm throughout the world. The United States deployed nearly 3,000 troops to help build treatment units, train health workers and expand laboratory testing. Eventually 10,675 cases were reported in Liberia with nearly 5,000 dead, the highest toll for any country. In Bong County, researchers recorded 607 suspected, probable, or confirmed cases with a 53.5 percent death rate .

Healthcare workers took the brunt of it. Nationally, 378 health workers contracted Ebola, and 192 died, a fatality rate above 50 percent, according to a study . Liberia already had one of the world’s lowest doctor-to-patient ratios, so every loss further strained the health system.

A health care worker and a family devastated by Ebola live with lingering fear and trauma

Pewu’s family was among the hardest hit in the Bong village of Sinyea Town. Their experience tells the cruel nature of the disease that passes from family member to family member as they try to care for loved ones, and then, even as they bury them. Ebola entered the family early in the outbreak in June 2014 through her sister-in-law, who contracted it while caring for a sick relative at Phebe Hospital. At this stage few in the country understood the scale of what the country was facing.

Klubo Pewu, a nurse at Phebe Hospital, lost family members during the 2014 Ebola outbreak.

After returning home, her sister-in-law’s husband, Pewu’s brother Matthew, and their 25 years old son Abraham, also became infected. The sister-in-law soon died. About a week later her son followed. This early in the outbreak the danger from dead bodies was not well established. There was no burial team. Pewu’s brother helped bury the bodies. About a week after the burial, he began showing symptoms.

Bong County had no treatment unit. It did not open until mid-September. Health workers disinfected the family home and brought him back inside to wait. He died the next day.

Pewu was a nurse at Phebe Hospital where staff worked mostly without appropriate protective equipment. As colleagues fell sick and died, she became frightened.

“I was very angry when I go to work. I was just crying,” she recalls.

She tried to protect herself with a sweater, double dresses and socks. But as more health workers died, she decided to quit.

But it was too late. Pewu came down with severe body pain. Fearing for herself and her two children, ages 11 and 3, she refused to go to a treatment facility after hearing stories of people dying there. She stayed away from others and her household next door, for 21 days, enduring body pain, red eyes, vomiting and diarrhea, and trying to keep herself hydrated. By the time health workers came to check on her, she says, she had recovered.

Pewu still keeps an old phone loaded with recordings from that period. She has never listened to them. “I kept that phone because I knew one day we had to share this story with the children,” she says. “They must know exactly what we went through.”

Health care workers and burial teams suffered stigma and isolation

As the virus spread, relatives were barred from touching the dead because handling infected bodies could spread the virus. Burial teams took over; leaving families unable to perform funeral rites. Bodies were burned instead of buried to ensure the virus was killed.

It was a difficult time. Many families resisted. It was not until religious leaders, especially imams, came forward to tell families that God would forgive them for not observing religious practices, and to allow the bodies to be burned, that communities accepted the directive.

Ambulances arriving to collect sick health workers only deepened the fear. In some communities, the sight of hospital vehicles came to mean the hospitals themselves were spreading the virus, not fighting it. Health workers who served at the Bong County Ebola Treatment Unit say that suspicion isolated many of the people working the front line of the response, at the moment they were needed most.

Comfort Harris Kollie, 66, was a scrub nurse at Phebe Hospital during the outbreak. She returned to work in September 2014 and continued working as Ebola spread through the hospital and surrounding communities.

She believes she contracted the virus on the Phebe Hospital bus, recalling that she had sat where an infected passenger had previously sat. The bus driver later became infected and died.

Like other health workers at the time, Kollie says she went to work without adequate protective equipment, relying instead on sweaters and extra layers of her own clothing. She watched colleagues from different wards fall sick and die, and the losses made the danger feel increasingly real each time she returned to the hospital.

She was eventually infected herself and spent about 10 days at an Ebola treatment unit in Bong before recovering. Surviving brought its own fear that she might have carried the virus home. She stayed away from her family for three months after returning home.

She returned to work at Phebe Hospital and continued caring for patients until she retired in 2017. But her experience did not end with her recovery. Ten years on, she still lives with the physical effects. Her eyesight and balance have never recovered fully.

Survivors and families face ongoing health problems and other hardships

In her 50s, Pauline Gbeeyan sits with a pink headscarf wrapped tightly around her head, tears welling in her eyes when she recalled her battle with Ebola.

Gbeeyan’s daughter, Kou, worked at Phebe Hospital where she contracted the disease and died after being taken to an Ebola treatment facility in July 2014. Kou had been the family’s breadwinner and left behind two children who now depend on their grandmother.

Pauline Gbeeyan is raising two grandchildren orphaned by Ebola.

Gbeeyan has spent the years since fighting for their education. One granddaughter completed 12th grade but they have not been able to afford to pay for the other. Churches and a Liberian community group in Minnesota provide occasional food and cash, but Gbeeyan says the help is never steady.

“I’m still fighting for them,” she says.

She is asking government for scholarships so children who lost parents to Ebola can continue through college.

Many impacted by the outbreak continue to deal with the aftermath. Dr. Mosoka P. Fallah, a founding member of Liberia’s National Public Health Institute and a key figure in the 2014 response, is now working on Ebola vaccine research in Central Africa says most survivors may be doing well, but a smaller group still struggles and needs continued support such as vocational training to help rebuild livelihoods when a breadwinner dies.“They lost everything,” he says. “They put their broken pieces together. They try to rebuild their lives.”

Abraham B.Jabateh and his son Mohammed Jabateh, both survived Ebola. Forty Members of their family did not. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/New Narratives.

Experts warn Liberia is not prepared for another outbreak especially with aid cuts

Dr. Fallah also warns that Liberia’s weak response last time has not been fixed in the years since. Laboratory capacity was limited, and treatment units were slow to open. He says one of the deepest lessons was that outbreaks are won or lost at community level. Government leadership, a free press, international partners, and a response decentralized to the counties all mattered.

Dr. Fallah is now working on the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo which has now claimed the second highest number of victims after the 2014 West Africa outbreak. Global health experts blame major cuts to the World Health Organization and the United States Center for Disease Control for the inability to bring the outbreak under control. Dr. Fallah warns Liberia and the region cannot afford to lower their guard as Ebola-related threats continue to emerge.

Joseph S. Wiah, the National Public Health Institute of Liberia’s communication officer, contacted via WhatsApp, said the institute holds no records on Ebola survivor support, assistance, or programs for survivors and orphaned children and does not consider it their responsibility. Augustus Sayweh Walker, director of communications at the health ministry, referred all questions to the National Public Health Institute.

Ebolas’s survivors now say they share a hope that lessons will be learned so that the country does not go through the unnecessary trauma and loss of the last outbreak. But as time goes on and memories fade, the lack of knowledge and preparation does not give them confidence.

This story is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” Reporting Project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The donor had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Why Liberia’s New Maritime Pact With India Matters Far Beyond the Water
World.content:
Liberia and India launched the Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers at the UN General Assembly in New York on Friday.

The pairing unites the world’s largest ship registry by gross tonnage with one of its largest sources of seafarers.

Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti tied the initiative directly to Liberia’s revenue, coastal communities and economic interests.

The group has no terms of reference yet, and whether it delivers practical protection for crews remains the key test.

By Rodney D Sieh

New York – Somewhere tonight, on a tanker crossing the Red Sea or a bulk carrier waiting off a Gulf port, there is a sailor who has not seen his family in months. The ship he works on may be owned in Greece, managed in Singapore and crewed from Mumbai. But there is a good chance the flag flying from its stern is Liberia’s.

That quiet fact sits at the heart of a new diplomatic partnership launched Friday in New York. On the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Liberia’s Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti and India’s External Affairs Minister Dr. S. Jaishankar unveiled the Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, known by the shorthand GoF on S4.



On paper it is another UN coalition. In practice, it is a meeting of two countries whose stakes in global shipping are enormous but very different: one owns the flag, the other supplies the hands.

A Natural, If Unusual, Partnership

Liberia has for years run the world’s largest shipping registry by gross tonnage, a remarkable standing for a small West African nation still rebuilding after war. India, for its part, is one of the biggest sources of the people who actually sail those ships.

That makes the two countries natural allies at a time when the sea has become more dangerous. When a Liberian-flagged vessel is attacked, the crew on board is very often from South Asia. When Indian seafarers are stranded or harmed, the flag state is frequently Liberia. The new group formalizes a relationship that already existed on thousands of decks.

Nyanti called the launch a landmark diplomatic and maritime achievement. She reminded delegates that the global economy moves on the oceans, with more than 80 percent of the goods that sustain economies worldwide carried by sea.

The Danger on the Water

Jaishankar was blunt about why the group is needed now. He pointed to recent attacks on commercial ships in the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Black Sea, noting that such incidents have cost innocent lives, including those of Indian seafarers. Attacks on civilian shipping that disrupt trade and endanger lives, he said, are unacceptable.

For Liberia, those headlines are not abstract. Several Liberian-flagged vessels have been among the ships struck in Red Sea attacks in recent years, putting the country’s flag in the middle of conflicts it has no part in.

Beyond the missiles and pirates, Jaishankar described a quieter set of hardships: sailors confined aboard ships for months, crew changes and repatriation delayed, long separation from families and the psychological strain that follows. Nearly two million seafarers keep the world’s merchant fleets moving, he said, and they deserve stronger international protection.

Three Pillars, and a Promise Not to Duplicate

Nyanti laid out what the group is meant to stand on: safety of shipping, security of maritime transport and protection of seafarers.

On safety, she stressed strict technical standards, vessel compliance and environmental stewardship. On security, she spoke of protecting commercial sea lanes from piracy, armed attacks, regional instability and emerging asymmetric threats. On seafarers, she named crew abandonment, fair labor standards, rapid medical help and protection for crews passing through conflict zones.

She was also careful to say what the group is not. It is meant to be action-oriented and to complement, not duplicate, the work of the International Maritime Organization and the International Labour Organization. That is an important signal in a UN system already crowded with overlapping bodies.

India has brought ideas of its own. Jaishankar recalled New Delhi’s proposal at the recent BRICS Summit for a Seafarers Emergency Support Network that would link maritime authorities and embassies to handle distress alerts, medical help, family communication and evacuations. India also co-hosted, with Greece and the Philippines, a UN Arria Formula meeting on the protection of seafarers in November 2025.

What Is in It for Liberia

The most telling part of Nyanti’s remarks may have been the least nautical. She said Liberia will work with the Liberia Maritime Authority and international partners to secure safe corridors for goods, while safeguarding Liberia’s economic interests, domestic revenue generation, coastal communities and people.

That line speaks to an old tension at home. The maritime registry is one of Liberia’s most important sources of foreign revenue, yet many Liberians have long questioned how much of that global prestige reaches ordinary citizens. By placing revenue and coastal communities alongside sailors’ safety, the government is signaling that it wants maritime diplomacy to deliver at home, too.

There is also a reputational calculation. A flag that is seen as unsafe, or indifferent to the crews who serve under it, risks losing business to competitors. Being seen to lead on seafarer welfare strengthens the Liberian brand on the high seas.

The Hard Part Comes Next

For now, the group is a promise. India and Liberia say they will work with members to draft its modalities and terms of reference through a consultative process. There is no secretariat, no budget and no timetable yet.

The real test will be whether the coalition can do anything a stranded or endangered sailor would notice: speed up an evacuation, force action on an abandoned crew, or make a dangerous shipping lane even slightly safer. Diplomatic groups of friends often begin with strong speeches and fade into quiet annual meetings.

What makes this one worth watching is the combination at its core. A flag without crews has little moral weight; crews without a flag have little legal standing. Together, Liberia and India can speak for both the ship and the people on it.

For the sailor on the Red Sea tonight, that is still only words. Whether it becomes more will depend on what Monrovia and New Delhi do after the cameras leave New York.

World.title: Liberia, Where the Diaspora Story Began, Takes Center Stage in Sharpton–Boakai Meeting
World.content:
NEW YORK – When the Reverend Al Sharpton sat down with President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly last week, the meeting fit a pattern older than the Republic of Liberia itself: Black Americans and Africans meeting to ask what they owe one another.

By Rodney D Sieh

Sharpton, the civil rights activist and founder of the National Action Network, described the encounter on Instagram as a “meaningful meeting” with the Liberian leader. The two, he wrote, discussed Africa having “a strong seat at the table,” strengthening the relationship between Africa and the diaspora, and the responsibility “to help build, invest in, and uplift the Motherland.” He called President Boakai and his staff “gracious and welcoming” and said Liberia “has an important voice on the global stage.”



Sharpton had earlier greeted the President at a high-level gathering on African cultural heritage. Ghana hosted that side event in New York on Wednesday, September 23, to review progress on reparatory justice and the restitution of cultural heritage, co-hosted with Germany and France, with UNESCO Director-General Khaled El-Enany among those expected to take part. ￼ ￼

Boakai’s heritage pitch

At that event, President Boakai proposed a Liberia–Ghana Cultural Heritage and Historical Recovery Cooperation Framework, under which institutions from both countries would digitize historical records, train archivists and museum professionals, research and preserve historic sites, and develop exhibitions and educational programs. He argued that “Restitution should ultimately be about more than the physical return of objects,” and suggested the two countries appoint a small technical working group to identify immediate areas of cooperation, leading eventually to a formal agreement. ￼

The President was in New York for the 81st UNGA, where he delivered Liberia’s national address on September 24 under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All.” ￼

A nation born of the diaspora

Few countries embody the diaspora story as directly as Liberia. Beginning in 1822, the American Colonization Society settled freed and freeborn Black Americans on the Grain Coast, and in 1847 Liberia declared independence as Africa’s first republic. The settlers’ arrival was not a simple homecoming: the divide between Americo-Liberians and indigenous Liberians shaped the country’s politics for more than a century and remains part of its unfinished reckoning.

Liberia also became a laboratory for Pan-African thought. Edward Wilmot Blyden, the Caribbean-born scholar who made Liberia his home, argued in the 19th century that Africans and their descendants shared a common destiny. In the 1920s, Marcus Garvey’s Universal Negro Improvement Association looked to Liberia for its back-to-Africa ambitions, while W.E.B. Du Bois traveled to Monrovia in 1924 as a U.S. envoy to the inauguration of President Charles D.B. King.

After independence swept the continent, President William V.S. Tubman helped shape the Organization of African Unity, founded in 1963. Its successor, the African Union, has since recognized the diaspora as the continent’s “sixth region,” and Ghana’s 2019 “Year of Return” drew thousands of African Americans to the continent.

Unfinished business at home and abroad

The conversation in New York comes at a sensitive moment for Liberians in America. Not every reaction to Sharpton’s post was celebratory: one commenter asked whether the meeting addressed Liberians who had lost protected immigration status.

That status has a long history. Since March 1991, certain Liberians have been eligible for either Temporary Protected Status or Deferred Enforced Departure (DED), allowing them to remain in the United States. In 2019, Congress passed the Liberian Refugee Immigration Fairness provision, opening a path to permanent residency for Liberians continuously present in the U.S. since November 2014. President Biden later extended DED through June 30, 2026, but according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, DED for Liberia expired on June 30, 2026. Neither Sharpton’s post nor available statements indicate whether the issue came up. ￼

From words to action

Sharpton closed his post by calling this “a moment for partnership, progress, and action.” For Liberia, which was built by people crossing the Atlantic in the opposite direction from their ancestors, the test will be whether such meetings produce more than photographs, whether in heritage cooperation, investment or protection for Liberians living in America.

World.title: What Liberia Could Gain From Its Diaspora’s Skills, Not Just Its Money
World.content:
MONROVIA – For most Liberians, the diaspora has a familiar face: the money transfer queue on Randall Street, the phone call before school fees are due, the barrel shipped home before Christmas.

By Rodney D Sieh, [email protected]

A new report suggests that picture captures only part of what Liberians abroad have to offer.



In hospitals, classrooms and social service agencies across Minnesota, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Maryland and Texas, tens of thousands of Liberian Americans go to work each day in the fields Liberia struggles hardest to staff. According to the report, nearly 20,000 of them work in education, health care and social assistance alone.

“The report moves this conversation from assumptions to evidence,” said Axel Addy, the former Commerce and Industry Minister whose firm, Ecocap Investment Group, commissioned the study.

Counting the Community

The report, Liberian Americans: An Economic Profile, was published this month by Liberia Diaspora Exchange (LDx). It arrives as the government hosts the second edition of the Liberia Diaspora Annual Conference.

Data and analysis come from Professor Bruce P. Corrie of Concordia University-St. Paul in Minnesota, home to the largest Liberian community in the United States. The study draws on U.S. Census Bureau survey estimates for 2017 to 2021.

Its central estimate is that 86,657 Liberian Americans live in 28,881 households across the United States. Together those households earn about US$2.2 billion a year, and the median household earns US$61,453.

Liberians have long talked about the diaspora in rough terms: “plenty people in America,” “the ones sending money.” The report replaces those impressions with figures, each checked against published Census tables and each carrying a margin of error.

Degrees, Not Just Dollars

The most striking numbers are about education.

Among Liberian Americans aged 25 and older, 91 percent have finished high school. About 34 percent, or roughly 17,600 people, hold a bachelor’s degree or higher. Some 6,200 hold a master’s, professional, or doctorate.

Their work follows that training. Of 45,372 employed Liberian Americans, 43 percent work in education, health care and social assistance. Among women alone, more than 12,300 work in health care and social assistance.

The authors note that this workforce matches the Human Capital Development pillar of the government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, which covers education, health and skills training.

For a country where university departments run short of qualified lecturers and hospitals short of specialists, the implication is plain. Much of the expertise Liberia hopes to build is already Liberian. It simply lives elsewhere.

A Settled People

The profile also shows a community that has put down roots.

About 65 percent of Liberian Americans were born abroad, and 58 percent of those have become U.S. citizens. Another 35 percent were born in the United States, a generation raised on stories of home rather than memories of it.

One in three households owns its home. Corrie estimates their residential property is worth about US$2.3 billion, though the report stresses this is a derived estimate, not a Census total.

Prosperity is uneven. About 27 percent of households earn under US$35,000 a year, while 40 percent earn US$75,000 or more. Minnesota, the largest community with 13,545 people, has the lowest per capita income among the leading states at US$20,244. Maryland’s smaller community of 4,936 has the highest at US$39,136.

That spread matters for how Liberia approaches its diaspora. The report is careful to say that many households have the capacity to save or invest, and many do not. Not every Liberian American is a potential investor. Far more may be potential teachers.

Beyond the Money Transfer

Money still matters enormously. World Bank figures cited in the report show personal remittances to Liberia from all countries rose from about US$346 million in 2019 to about US$1.02 billion in 2024, equal to 21.3 percent of GDP.

But remittances largely flow household to household. They pay fees and rent, and they cushion hard times. They rarely build institutions.

The report argues that skills can do what cash alone cannot, if there is a system to carry them.

That system does not yet exist in any organized form. Diaspora doctors and professors visit home often, and some give a lecture or spend a day at a clinic. Those efforts are mostly informal, arranged through personal contacts, and gone when the visitor flies back.

Building the Bridge

LDx proposes to change that through a Diaspora Knowledge Transfer Programme:

• Ministries, universities, hospitals and TVET institutions would request lectures, training or mentoring.

• LDx would vet visiting diaspora professionals and match them to those requests.

• The host institution would approve each session and its honorarium.

• Sessions would be recorded with the speaker’s consent and stored online, so a single lecture could keep teaching long after the visitor leaves.

A first test is already under way on paper. The University of Liberia and LDx signed a memorandum of understanding this year for a 12-month pilot that includes diaspora guest lectures and mentorship.

LDx was established by Ecocap with support from the USAID-funded Liberia Economic Policy Dialogue Activity, implemented by Nathan Associates. Addy said the initiative “seeks to build a structured bridge for two-way social and business engagement, connecting Liberia with the talent, time and resources of its diaspora.”

He said he believes in “the power of Liberia’s Diaspora Engagement Policy to build a structured and productive relationship between Liberia and its citizens abroad.” He also commended the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of State for advancing the policy, and congratulated the government on the diaspora conference.

Old Walls Still Standing

Goodwill alone will not be enough. The report revisits barriers the government itself named in its 2016 Diaspora Engagement Policy, and many will sound familiar to anyone who has tried to come home and do business:

• Mistrust between Liberians at home and abroad

• Disputes over land and inheritance

• Investment rules with capital thresholds too high for most diaspora savers

• Embassies unable to give clear answers on residency, entry or business registration

• Lingering uncertainty over what rights the diaspora actually holds

The report recommends publishing clear guidance through foreign missions, focusing outreach on the five largest state communities, and tracking results with simple indicators: sessions delivered, trainees reached, investments made.

The authors also acknowledge the limits of their own data. It covers only the United States and only the period 2017 to 2021, and it cannot measure who wants to invest, return or teach.

From Assumptions to Evidence

What the data can do is end the guessing.

For decades, Liberia has spoken of its diaspora as a resource without being able to say precisely what that resource is. Now, for its largest diaspora community at least, the country has a count, an income, an education profile and a map.

The next queue on Randall Street will still be there. The question the report leaves with policymakers is whether, alongside it, Liberia can build a second channel: one that brings home not only what its people abroad earn, but what they know.

Addy urged Liberians at home and abroad to read the full report on the LDx Community Exchange platform at https://liberian-diaspora-exchange.mn.co/.

World.title: Finance Minister Ngafuan Makes Case For Liberia At Annual Diaspora Conference
World.content:
Washington, D.C – Liberia has had one of the darkest past – a long range of civil war that stretched all the way to 14 years; however, Finance and Development Planning Minister, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan has presented a case to convince diaspora Liberians and investors why the country remains one of the best destinations for investment.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Held under the theme: “Making an Investment Case for Liberia – Betting on Liberia, which is being held in Washington, D.C in the United States of America (USA), is a key event that strengthens the bond between Liberians abroad and their homeland.



The theme before us is direct: Making an Investment Case for Liberia—Betting on Liberia.

So let me begin with an equally direct question: if you are deciding where to place your capital, your technology, your networks and your trust, why should you bet on Liberia?

Because Liberia offers a rare combination: growing stability and unfinished opportunity; improving institutions and first-mover advantage; abundant resources and a government determined to convert them into jobs and shared prosperity.

Dark Days Gone

Driving through the ugly past, Minister Ngafuan says the dark days that saw the shells of bullets in different street corners, destruction of major infrastructure, economic collapse and rule of law displaced are over, and Liberia is on the path of tangibles.

Since the cessation of political brouhaha some 23 years ago, the MFDP Minister points out that Liberia has been moving strong and placed in the global headlines most often for good reasons – has sustained peace for more than two decades, conducted competitive elections, transferred presidential power peacefully, rebuilt democratic institutions; and earned the confidence to serve today as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council.

“A nation once defined in global headlines by conflict is now helping to deliberate on peace and security for the world. That is not only diplomatic progress. It is evidence of national recovery, institutional credibility and political risk moving in the right direction,” Mr. Ngafuan told the gathering of dominant Liberians and investors.

Advancing With Purpose

Accordingly, the Minister used the platform to inform the world that Liberia is no longer merely a country emerging from crisis, rather it is a country advancing with purpose.

Why Bet On Liberia?

The MFDP boss craved the world’s attention to bet on Liberia as the country continues to restore macroeconomic credibility and strengthening fiscal discipline.

“Our economy grew by about 5.1 percent in 2025. The latest assessment by the International Monetary Fund projects growth of approximately 5.5 percent in 2026, driven especially by mining, construction and manufacturing. Inflation averaged about 4.5 percent during the first half of this year, despite turbulence in the global economy, and the Liberian dollar has remained broadly stable.”

He said that fiscal performance is also improving, referencing the International Monetary Fund (IMF) that projects the primary fiscal surplus, excluding grants, at approximately 2.4 percent of GDP in 2026.

He cited the passage of the national budgets before the beginning of the fiscal year in two consecutive years as reason for Budget execution rate improvement. This means that spending entities who meet all the commitment and procurement control requirements of government are more assured today of receiving their budgeted funds as compared to the past.

“Those figures may sound technical. Their meaning is not: when government makes a commitment to a school, clinic, road, contractor or community, there is now certainty that it will move from paper to reality. They mean we are working to pay civil servants on time; to pay vendors and contractors on time; to service our lawful debts; and to honor legitimate government contracts and obligations.”

“Payment discipline is not a favor from government. It is part of the infrastructure of trust. When government pays on time, firms can pay workers, banks can lend with greater confidence, projects can remain on schedule and the entire economy functions better,” he furthered.

Crossing The One Billion Mark

For the very first time in the nation’s history, domestic revenue collections exceeded one billion United States dollars in a single year.

That achievement, Minister Ngafuan reported, belongs to every Liberian; both at home and abroad, who continue to contribute to the ‘common future.’

“We have moved from roughly US$612 million in domestic revenue in 2023, to about US$699 million in 2024, to about US$848 million in 2025 – and now beyond the billion-dollar mark by mid-September 2026.”

All Problems Not Solved Yet

In a clearer economic tone, Ngafuan explained to the gathering that collecting one billion dollars does not mean Liberia has no more problems, noting that even five billion dollars in revenue cannot solve all the country’s problems.

“Rasing one billion in revenue from January 1 to September 14 of this year does not mean every road is paved, every school is repaired, or every hospital is fully equipped. Revenue is not the same as uncommitted cash. Revenue fund salaries, education, healthcare, security, infrastructure, county development, debt service and many other national obligations.”

But while this does not absolutely solve all the problems, he points out that the billion-dollar threshold is not a finish line, but a proof of capacity and a summon to greater responsibility.

“It tells our citizens that Liberia can increasingly finance its development; it tells our partners that we will do our share; and it tells investors that the state is becoming more capable of honoring obligations and providing the public goods enterprise needs. That is what we mean by development sovereignty.”

‘A Clear National Plan’

The Minister encourages Liberians and nations of the world to invest in Liberia based on a responsible stewardship anchored in a clear national plan.

He cited the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development – Agriculture, Roads, Rule of Law, Education, Sanitation and Health, and Tourism as a framework for changing the economy and improving lives.

“We do not want growth that exists only in a statistical table. We want growth that creates jobs; expands agriculture and industry; improves power, roads and digital connectivity; strengthens the rule of law; and reaches all fifteen counties. Liberia today looks, in many places, like a construction site. That is because the work of rebuilding and connecting our country is under way.”

Highlights Of Key Development

Along the western corridor, Minister Ngafuan reported that work has begun on a 255-kilometer road network that includes the St. Paul Bridge–Klay–Bo Waterside route and the Voinjama–Kolahun– Foya -Mendikorma corridor, an infrastructure that strengthen Liberia’s links with sisterly nation Sierra Leone.

Also across the Cavalla River, he revealed ongoing construction works of a new bridge to connect Liberia and Côte d’Ivoire, with completion targeted for March 2028. This would end the sometimes deadly adventure of crossing the river in ferry or canoes, as the Minister maintains that a modern bridge will facilitate movement of people and trade.”

“We have procured earth-moving equipment to help keep roads passable year-round in all fifteen counties. We are advancing an overpass to ease congestion in Monrovia, and constructing and renovating schools and hospitals, including C. H. Rennie Hospital in Margibi, three schools in the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS), and facilities at the University of Liberia,” the Minister emphasized on development projects and initiatives.

At the same time, the Minister told the diaspora conference that the government is currently expanding electricity access from about 32 percent in 2024 toward 40 percent today, adding that more communities are seeing reliable public power, some for the first time since the civil war.

“Buchanan has been energized. Voinjama and other areas are seeing progress. The Liberia Electricity Corporation is connecting more homes and businesses in Montserrado and beyond.”

In the agriculture sector, disclosed that tractors are arriving to support food production.

He tells the conference that construction of the Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zone in Buchanan is under way, and at completion, it will create a platform to process rice, cocoa, oil palm, fisheries and other products closer to source.

“Our aim is straightforward: Liberia must not remain a country that exports raw potential and imports finished prosperity. We must add value at home.”

Building The Systems

The third reason to bet on Liberia, Minister Ngafuan indicated, is that government is building the systems that make investment easier, faster and more profitable.

“For too long, too much of the Liberian economy has effectively shut down at five o’clock. A business owner may need two phones and two mobile-money accounts because the systems do not speak to one another.”

He asserted that the old narrative is changing, pointing to the launch of the Inclusive Instant Payment System, connecting Lonestar Cell MTN and Orange Money as the first phase of the National Electronic Payment Switch.

In its first three months, the system processed more than 1.5 million transactions, worth over L$1.4 billion and US$9 million.

When the full National Electronic Payment Switch comes online, targeted for March 2027, he explained that commercial banks, mobile-money platforms, government-payment channels and other financial institutions will be interoperable.

“For a market woman in Ganta, it means receiving money instantly. For government, it means easier tax collection, fewer leakages and a traceable audit trail. For an investor, it means paying suppliers and employees in seconds instead of days, with lower risk and greater transparency.”

“We are moving from a cash-heavy economy to a connected economy—from an economy that slows after business hours to a true 24-hour economy.”

Furthermore, the MFDP Minister narrated that government is also strengthening the environment for public-private partnerships, stressing that the 2026 Public Procurement and Concessions Act provides an improved legal foundation for PPPs, concessions management and electronic government procurement.

National Ownership

With several reason to bet on Liberia for investment, one of several put forward by the Finance Minister is owing to the fact that international cooperation is backed by national ownership.

According to him, the country’s partnership with the IMF under the Extended Credit Facility supports macroeconomic stability and reform; hence, the governance diagnostic helps in identifying institutional weaknesses honestly and address them.

“Cooperation with the World Bank, African Development Bank, European Union, Millennium Challenge Corporation, the UN and other partners brings financing, technical knowledge and independent validation.”

However, he reckoned that partnership must not become dependency, noting that the strongest international cooperation begins when a country has a plan, mobilizes its own resources, improves its systems and invites partners to reinforce and not replace national effort.

“That is the approach we are taking. We are strengthening anti-corruption institutions, expanding competitive electronic procurement, improving asset-declaration compliance, digitizing public services and making it easier to register and operate a business,” he added.
