World.title: US visa clash exposes Sudan’s forgotten war as foreign powers compete for strategic foothold
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

UNITED NATIONS — Sudan’s military leader is openly defying a U.S.-backed ceasefire push after Washington withheld his visa to attend the U.N. General Assembly, exposing a widening rift over a war that has become not only one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters, but also a regional struggle for influence stretching to the Red Sea.

Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of Sudan’s armed forces and de facto leader, had been expected in New York during UNGA before the Trump administration withheld his visa amid a dispute over a proposed 90-day humanitarian truce. Days later, Burhan struck a defiant tone from Khartoum.

"We will keep our heads high. We will not accept bargaining, sell ourselves cheaply to anyone or bow to anyone," Burhan said Saturday, according to Anadolu Agency. "We do not need a visa to any country or anyone’s permission."

WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR?

The State Department has accused both Burhan’s Sudanese Armed Forces, or SAF, and the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, of failing to make serious commitments to an immediate truce.

"Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said Sept. 22, adding that the conduct of both leaders renders them "ineligible to govern the country."

The State Department said both sides had instead intensified combat operations and drone strikes that killed civilians and said Washington had repeatedly asked them to accept a humanitarian truce "without preconditions" and commit to an inclusive political dialogue leading to civilian government.

But a senior advisor to Burhan disputed Washington’s account in an on-camera interview with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of UNGA.

SUDAN'S FORGOTTEN WAR LEAVES MILLIONS HUNGRY AS GLOBAL ATTENTION REMAINS ELSEWHERE

Dr. Amjad Farid Al-Tayyib, the foreign affairs advisor to Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council, said Sudan never rejected the American ceasefire proposal and instead submitted technical comments on it.

"We never rejected this proposal," Farid said. "The Sudanese government wants war with no one."

Farid said a negotiating team had intended to accompany Burhan and accused Washington of undermining the very diplomatic process it was seeking to advance by preventing the delegation from traveling.

The State Department declined to comment on Burhan’s specific visa case, citing its policy of not discussing individual visa decisions. A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital on background that Washington is instead focused on a broader diplomatic framework with Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through the Quad, linking a humanitarian truce and sustained aid access to a permanent ceasefire, civilian transition and reconstruction.

"We are working with our partners to encourage the parties to agree to the humanitarian truce and guarantee humanitarian access, and to also ensure external military or financial support to the warring parties is cut off," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that the Quad supports the Quintet-led civilian political track and rejects parallel diplomatic processes that could fragment negotiations.

The United Nations also challenged Washington over the visa decision. "We immediately raised with the U.S. authorities the issue regarding the denial of visa to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of the Sudan, who was scheduled to address the General Assembly this week," U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric told Fox News Digital.

PUTIN USING AFRICA AS ‘PURSE’ FOR UKRAINE WAR WHILE US FACES ‘INTELLIGENCE BLACK HOLE’: COMMANDER

Cameron Hudson, a former director for African affairs on the National Security Council who also served as chief of staff to successive U.S. presidential special envoys for Sudan, said his understanding was that Washington had asked the Sudanese to send a delegation both to the U.N. and to Washington for talks on a ceasefire.

He said the Sudanese were preparing to do so before Washington, in his understanding, made Burhan’s visa contingent on signing the ceasefire agreement before traveling.

"It doesn’t fully make sense why the United States took this decision at the last minute," Hudson told Fox News Digital.

Farid said the central dispute is whether the RSF would be required to withdraw from civilian areas it controls. He argued that freezing current lines of control risks turning a temporary ceasefire into a de facto partition of Sudan.

The dispute comes against the backdrop of a brutal civil war that erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti.

Both sides have been accused of serious violations, but Hudson told Fox News Digital that treating their records as interchangeable obscures an important distinction.

"The RSF is committing war crimes on a scale and with an intention that the army does not," Hudson said.

Hudson said SAF has struck civilian targets and committed war crimes, including through drone attacks, but said the RSF’s record goes significantly further.

"They have committed mass rape, mass killing, torture, sexual enslavement," Hudson said, arguing that Western descriptions of "both sides" can create the impression that the two forces are committing the same crimes "on the same scale or with the same intention."

U.N. investigators have also drawn distinctions while documenting abuses by both forces.

AS WORLD FIXATES ON OTHER WARS, SUDAN SEES 12 MILLION FORCIBLY DISPLACED IN DEVASTATING CONFLICT

A U.N. fact-finding mission reported in September 2025 that both SAF and RSF were responsible for direct, large-scale attacks against civilians and the destruction of critical civilian infrastructure. But it found that the RSF, particularly during its siege of El Fasher and surrounding areas, committed crimes against humanity including murder, torture, enslavement, rape, sexual slavery, forced displacement and persecution on ethnic, gender and political grounds.

A separate U.N. Human Rights Office report released in February documented more than 6,000 killings during the first three days of the RSF’s final offensive on El Fasher and found that the violations could amount to war crimes and possible crimes against humanity.

Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a ‘false equivalence’ between Sudan’s military and the RSF.

"The U.N. is not staying neutral," he told Fox News Digital, arguing that international institutions have documented RSF atrocities without taking sufficient action against the group or those supporting it.

Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a false equivalence between Sudan’s military and the RSF.

U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric rejected the allegation that the organization was equating the two sides. "This is not about equating two sides," Dujarric told Fox News Digital. "We focus on the facts, the violations that have been documented, and above all, the devastating toll this war has taken on civilians since 15 April 2023."

Dujarric said both the RSF and SAF have used explosive weapons in densely populated areas and that the U.N. Human Rights Office has documented attacks affecting schools, hospitals, markets and religious sites.

He pointed specifically to what he described as "particularly grave violations" by the RSF and affiliated forces in Darfur, including mass killings, sexual violence, torture, abductions and forced displacement, while noting that serious abuses have also been documented in SAF-controlled areas, including arbitrary detention, torture, ill-treatment and summary executions.

The war, meanwhile, increasingly extends beyond Sudan’s borders.

Foreign backing has become a central feature of the conflict. A July 2026 UK government assessment, drawing on U.N. and other reporting, said the RSF had benefited from support networks involving the UAE and neighboring countries, while SAF had received backing from states including Egypt, Iran, Pakistan and Turkey. The UAE has repeatedly denied providing military support to the RSF.

Fox News Digital reached out to the UAE Embassy in Washington and the UAE mission to the U.N. but did not receive a response in time for publication.

BAB EL-MANDEB STRAIT FACES GROWING THREAT AS HOUTHI ATTACKS RAISE FEARS OF A SECOND HORMUZ

Hudson said the RSF’s foreign relationships are only part of a much larger regional competition.

He said Egypt, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Qatar have supported the army to varying degrees, while outside powers pursue their own strategic interests in Sudan.

That competition increasingly centers on Sudan’s Red Sea coastline. "There is a regional battle of influence among neighboring states and regional states who want to be able to control Sudan’s Red Sea coastline," Hudson said, pointing to potential military, port and economic access.

"Superimposed on top of the conflict inside Sudan is a regional proxy conflict for influence in Sudan and in the wider Horn of Africa, Red Sea region," he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also said foreign powers are central to prolonging the war. "What’s happening in Sudan would not be happening were it not for external actors supporting one side or the other," Rubio told reporters during UNGA week, describing U.S. efforts to secure even limited humanitarian agreements as "very frustrating."

Rubio said the parties have repeatedly agreed to commitments only to abandon them when one side believes it is gaining the upper hand. "There are external actors. I’m not going to single them out. You know who they are," Rubio said. "That war and that conflict and that crisis would not be happening were it not for the active participation of external actors that are feeding one side of that conflict or another."

He said meaningful progress would depend on those states pressuring their respective partners in Sudan.

"Until those external actors are prepared to use influence and pressure their respective proxies to live up to the commitments that they’re making, we’re not going to make progress," Rubio said.

WORLD'S HUMANITARIAN SYSTEM BUCKLING, 'NO LONGER FIT FOR PURPOSE,' US-BASED RESEARCHERS SAY

Sudan’s strategic value goes beyond geography. The country has significant gold, agricultural and livestock resources and sits at the crossroads of Africa and the Middle East. The World Bank has described Sudan as rich in fertile land, water and minerals, while noting its substantial gold production and agricultural potential.

Sudan also controls critical infrastructure used to transport South Sudanese crude oil to the Red Sea. A World Bank assessment says South Sudan’s oil has historically traveled through pipelines across Sudan to Port Sudan, its key export route.

Hudson said that broader regional competition helps explain why Washington has struggled to force Sudan’s outside backers to pull away.

"The United States is not going to use the limited political capital that it has with Saudi Arabia or Egypt or Turkey or UAE to get them to control their support to one side or the other in this conflict," he said.

Hudson also questioned Washington’s diplomatic strategy, arguing that pressure on Burhan has not been matched by sufficient direct engagement inside Sudan.

He said Massad Boulos, President Donald Trump’s senior advisor for Arab and African affairs, has never traveled to Sudan while attempting to mediate the conflict.

"He’s trying to mediate peace in a country that he’s never been to," Hudson said, arguing that Washington needs more "personal diplomacy" and less reliance on public statements and social media.

"If we want these people to sign a ceasefire deal, then they have to trust us," Hudson said. "And right now we’ve given them no reason to do so."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The U.N. acknowledged that international efforts have so far failed to stop the fighting. "Unfortunately, we are not seeing the war abating," Dujarric said, reiterating the U.N. position that "there is no military solution to the conflict," and noting Washington’s diplomatic role as the US and African Union co-chaired a Sept. 23 meeting bringing together the Quad and Quintet diplomatic groupings.

"The immediate priority is to stop the killing and secure a cessation of hostilities, while creating the conditions for a credible political process," he said.

World.title: Once again, no one knows when Josh Simmons will return — perhaps including the Chiefs
World.content:
Kansas City Chiefs left tackle Josh Simmons is mysteriously absent from the team — again.

Simmons holds one of the most important jobs in football. He is paid to protect the blindside of Patrick Mahomes, the central figure of the NFL’s defining dynasty and one of the most valuable assets in American sports.

Yet Simmons has played in just eight of 20 games since the Chiefs drafted him two seasons ago.

Khali Benson, an undrafted rookie right tackle who played exclusively on the right side in college, has filled in for Simmons this season. The Chiefs are 3-0, but Benson showed clear limitations on Sunday against the Dolphins. The team’s own highlights package of the victory is marred by defenders beating him almost immediately off the line of scrimmage.

The Chiefs offense misses Simmons' stability. And yet, there is still no information regarding when he might return, or whether he will return at all this season.

How does that happen in a league where highly paid insiders compete to deliver minute-by-minute injury updates on even the most obscure players in the NFL?

To understand how, we have to return to the 2025 pre-draft process.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In October 2024, Simmons suffered a season-ending patellar tendon injury at Ohio State. After the season, reports indicated that he was well ahead of schedule in his recovery. The Chiefs selected him 32nd overall. A week after the draft, Simmons was active for rookie minicamp.

According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, the national reporter most connected to the Chiefs, the injury did not cause Simmons to fall to the final pick of the first round. The concern was something less clinical and more ominous: his character.

"Several teams agree: Josh Simmons had best tape of any OT last year. And they aren't very concerned with recovery on the torn patella tendon. More of the concern is maturity/character. But he's going to the ideal, veteran-laden place," Fowler posted on X on April 24, 2025.

It remains unclear what those "character concerns" were. But they had to be substantial for nearly every team in the league to pass on a left tackle with elite tape who had already been cleared for contact by draft night.

For the first month of last season, it appeared the Chiefs had taken advantage of the rest of the league’s hesitation. Simmons looked like the long-term answer to Kansas City’s chronic left tackle problem.

That reading no longer holds.

On Oct. 6, 2025, two hours before the Chiefs’ Monday Night Football game against the Jacksonville Jaguars, the team abruptly listed Simmons as questionable due to an "illness." He ultimately played and played well.

The episode would have disappeared into the weekly churn of NFL oddities if not for what happened days later.

After a full week of practice, Simmons did not show up for his pregame responsibilities the following Sunday against the Lions. It was reported that players and members of the staff were unsure of his whereabouts. After the game, head coach Andy Reid suggested he knew where Simmons was.

Reid and the Chiefs offered almost no explanation afterward. The silence continued throughout much of Simmons’ four-game absence, which the team described only as a personal/family issue.

Reporters provided no real clarity over the past year about what happened or why members of the organization were apparently unaware of Simmons’ absence until close to game time.

Last month, Sports Illustrated’s Matt Verderame provided the first substantive report on the matter, saying Simmons left the team without approval the Saturday before the Lions game and that there was a period of time in which the "team didn't know where he was."

That is also the version of the story OutKick has heard but have been unable to independantly verify. The team will not confirm, deny, or comment on the matter. OutKick emailed Chiefs general manager Brett Veach and Simmons’ agent Drew Rosenhaus before Verderame’s report to ask whether those details were accurate. Neither responded.

Which brings us back to the present.

After a full training camp, Simmons missed his first practice of the season on Aug. 18. Verderame reported afterward that Simmons was "fine."

"On Chiefs LT Josh Simmons missing practice with a back injury, I’m told 'he’s fine.' Don’t sense any concern about the second-year star," Verderame posted on X.

It is now Sept. 28. Simmons has not practiced since. He has missed the first three games of the season. Though the team says he has been in the building, he's clearly not "fine."

However, we have already established that Verdemran's sources with the team are strong. There is reason to believe that the team did consider Simmons' injury minor at the time.

Something changed.

On Monday, Reid offered a vague, almost eerie update.

"I’ll tell you what," Reid told Chiefs Digest reporter Matt Derrick. "I will let you guys know when Josh [Simmons] is coming back. I’ll be the first to tell you. So we’ll just see how that all works out."

The contrast with Reid’s other injury updates is difficult to ignore. Asked about safety Chamarris Connor, who, like Simmons, is the only other starter to miss the team’s first three games, Reid sounded far more direct.

"Yeah, so he practiced last week, and he’ll get going this week, too," Reid said. "So there’s a good chance he’ll be out there. We’ll just see how the week goes, but it looks like it’ll be a pretty decent chance."

Now consider the reporting around other injured Chiefs players. When rookie Mansoor Delane injured his shoulder in Week 1, Adam Schefter, Ian Rapoport, and Tom Pelissero quickly reported that the injury was minor and continued providing updates throughout the week.

ESPN, Fox, NFL Network, NBC and Amazon devote weekly pregame segments to injury news. They inform viewers about the availability of backup linebackers and rotational defensive backs. Yet we cannot find a single example of them discussing the status of the player tasked with protecting Patrick Mahomes.

Over the past month, there has been one national report about Simmons. It came from Fowler, who, fittingly, described the injury as "mysterious."

We keep coming back to that word.

At minimum, we can establish this: the NFL’s top reporters either do not know the story behind Simmons’ absence or are choosing not to pursue it publicly.

Likewise, the Chiefs either do not know when Simmons will return or are deliberately withholding information they routinely provide about other players.

That is unusual, to use a term.

Simmons’ absence has naturally invited speculation about whether it is connected to last year’s disappearance from the team.

Yahoo NFL analyst Hayden Winks is among those asking.

"So Josh Simmons is going to miss more time than what he would've on IR, which could mean he's missing longer than the Chiefs expected based on this back injury. There's also a history of him just not being around. There could be a lot more to this story than what's public," he posted Monday.

Price Carter is one of the top Chiefs film analysts. He detailed the unusualness of the Simmons saga to OutKick:

"It would be difficult to describe the Josh Simmons injury timeline as normal. What started out as a routine back injury, described by several reporters as a 'minor issue' that he could 'play if it was game week' has now lingered on for the better part of two months. With no timeline for return, and no corresponding roster move the local media is only left with the information they are given by the team. Andy Reid is notorious for not saying much at the podium and the team only provides a very brief look at practice to the media. Reporters state that Simmons is with the team but that is all the news that there is."

That speculation is warranted. Simmons is not an anonymous private employee. He is the left tackle for the Kansas City Chiefs. And by offering so little clarity, his own team has invited the public to fill in the blanks.

Perhaps there is a deeper explanation for Simmons’ absence. Maybe the pre-draft character concerns are connected to last year’s absence and this year’s. There is precedent for NFL teams describing a personal matter as an injury in an effort to protect a player. The Bills did this with Ed Oliver in the face of tragedy.

Still, the Chiefs have made the matter worse by saying nothing while keeping Simmons on the active roster. They could have placed him on injured reserve and said they would re-evaluate him later in the season. They could have placed him on the non-football injury list and said he was out until further notice while asking the public to respect his privacy.

For whatever reason, the Kansas City Chiefs do not want to provide the details about Josh Simmons.

Already, there is speculation that Simmons does not want to play or does not love football. At this juncture, how can that not be among the possibilities that come to mind?

World.title: Stocks fall, bond yields surge and oil fluctuates as war keeps markets on edge
World.content:
Stocks fell Monday alongside a jump in bond yields and erratic oil trading as geopolitical upheaval remained front and center for traders.

The S&P 500 ended lower by 0.7% and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.9% as oil prices rose, pushing Brent crude oil back above $106 per barrel.

Earlier in the day, Brent rose beyond $108, but the jump moderated after reports said mediators planned to meet with U.S. and Iranian officials separately to discuss the stalemate between the two sides over the war with Iran. Iran’s semiofficial ISNA news agency downplayed the significance of the meetings, saying that Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, would attend talks with mediators but that no U.S. representatives would be present.

Other reports throughout the day that said President Donald Trump was open to offering Iran economic concessions to reboot talks and reach a deal also took some of the heat off oil prices. NBC News has not confirmed those reports.

Over the weekend, Trump said he had rejected a recent proposal from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which critical energy supplies flowed before the war.

“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine,” Trump told reporters in Washington. “I like making a deal too, but ... that deal would not be acceptable.”

Monday’s rocky oil trading has been a familiar feature of this year’s turbulent markets.

Bond yields also surged to fresh multiyear highs.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose as high as 5.27%, its highest since mid-June 2007. A wide swath of other Treasurys also continued to trade above 5%, and the yield on the 30-year bond hit its highest level since May 2004.

The 2-year Treasury, which is often viewed as a signal of where the market expects central bank rates to go, reached its highest level since 2024.

Market watchers’ anxiety has grown alongside the rise in bond yields.

“The significant increase in oil prices so far this year hasn’t knocked the wind out of the global economy’s sails,” longtime market analyst Ed Yardeni wrote Saturday. “The question is whether rapidly rising interest rates will do so.”

“Unfortunately, these higher rates also exacerbate the outlook for large government deficits worldwide,” wrote Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research.

Still, stocks have largely remained resilient in the face of rising inflation from higher oil prices and bond yields that keep shooting higher.

Part of the reason “is that financial conditions have changed little” since January, analysts at Goldman Sachs said. They added that “the substantial rise in interest rates has been nearly offset by the effects of higher equity prices.”

But the equity market’s rise this year has been driven primarily by just a few sectors, which troubles some analysts.

For the year so far, the S&P 500 has risen a little more than 12%. But a look under the hood reveals a different story. The information technology sector has gained 27% this year, and the energy sector has added 38%.

The healthcare, industrials and materials sectors are up 10%. But the real estate, consumer staples and communication services sectors have all gained less than 7%. The utilities, financial and consumer discretionary sectors have all contracted.

On top of higher oil prices, rising bond yields and geopolitical headlines that could swing stocks in either direction at a moment’s notice, the end of the month features prominent central bank meetings, including meetings at the Federal Reserve, where rates could rise further.

World.title: Ahead of rare execution, lone woman on Tennessee’s death row says ‘I am at peace’
World.content:
Pike doesn’t dispute her role in the grisly killing. But details about her upbringing, marked by years of sexual and physical abuse and neglect, were not shared with the jury that sentenced her to death. Her lawyers believe that if such evidence of abuse were presented at a trial now, a death sentence would not be guaranteed.

They have asked the Supreme Court to halt Pike’s execution, saying that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder stemming from being molested and raped beginning when she was a toddler. Being held down and strapped to a gurney, they wrote, will likely create “severe mental suffering and superadded psychological terror under Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol.”

The state hasn’t denied that Pike has suffered from abuse. But in a response filed Monday, the attorney general’s office said a judge already concluded last month that it was “speculative whether Pike would suffer” greater mental harm from how the lethal injection protocol is carried out.

The Supreme Court is Pike’s remaining chance for a reprieve after Lee said he was upholding her death sentence “after deliberate consideration.”

Pike’s lawyers said Monday they were “saddened and heartbroken.”

Another woman, Gaile Owens, was on Tennessee’s death row with Pike until 2010, when Gov. Phil Bredesen changed her sentence to life in prison.

A letter written by Pike before learning she was denied clemency from Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee. via Rev. Mikey Noechel

In her letter, Pike wrote that people have seen a “limited public persona that has been the only narrative” about her. Her lawyers had tried to convince Lee that she was a product of a tumultuous childhood.

“Stepping into the chaos of Christa’s life that led her to that moment will not justify her actions that night,” one of her lawyers, Randall Spivey, said of when she committed her crime. “But the chaos will show you that Christa was broken, not evil.”

Different sentences

Pike’s lawyers also point to her age and how it led to such a different outcome in her case.

While she faced a death sentence because of her first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder conviction in Slemmer’s death, another conspirator was spared: Pike’s boyfriend, who was 17 at the time. Tadaryl Shipp received a life sentence because he was a juvenile and remains eligible for parole. Shipp testified at his post-conviction hearing that he was the one who carved a pentagram into Slemmer’s chest.

The third accomplice — Shadolla Peterson, then 18 — served as a lookout in the crime and received probation in exchange for her cooperation.

Colleen Slemmer. May Martinez via News Sentinel / USA TODAY Network via Reuters file

Pike told police she “wasn’t even thinking” when she assaulted Slemmer and that she had been jealous believing the victim was trying to steal Shipp’s attention. Pike’s lawyers say that her age would have been more of a factor today, given how scientific research has evolved in understanding that young people’s brains are still developing well beyond their teen years.

In addition, her lawyers say that her legal representatives at the time could have accepted a deal from prosecutors who were offering a life sentence without parole in return for a guilty plea.

Pike sobbed as the judge told her she would die by electrocution, then the only form of execution in Tennessee before the state moved to lethal injection as its primary method.

Christa Pike looks at her mother after the jury read the guilty verdict in Knox County Criminal Court on March 29, 1996. Byron Small. / Knoxville News Sentinel / USA TODAY Network via Reuters file

She pleaded through tears: “Can I please hug my mom?”

Pike entered prison, where she was placed into solitary confinement for up to 23 hours a day and prescribed Prozac to treat her obsessive-compulsive disorder. Early on, she struggled to express remorse.

“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in her clemency petition.

Lingering trauma

Three years ago, Bethany Brand, a psychologist specializing in trauma, was asked by Pike’s lawyers to assess whether she suffers from psychological disorders and consider if any contributed to the crime.

She sat with Pike at her Nashville prison and reviewed police reports, past medical examinations and other files in her case detailing physical and sexual abuse. Brand learned that Pike’s parents were not stable figures in her life. Her mother’s boyfriends and other men had molested her from a young age, the files said. She did poorly in school, living with other family members in West Virginia and North Carolina. At 17 — one year before she would take part in Slemmer’s murder — Pike reported to North Carolina police that she was walking to the store when a man threw her to the ground and raped her. No one was ever arrested.

Christa Pike. Tennessee Dept. of Correction via AP file

In her final report, Brand wrote that the adults in Pike’s life failed her. Doctors only diagnosed a bipolar disorder a few years after she was already in prison.

The level of trauma Pike was subjected to “is almost impossible to grasp because it is so severe,” Brand wrote.

She told NBC News that medications in prison have helped Pike tremendously and that she now has “empathy and great regret” for what she did. But, she added, Pike’s case is a lesson of the need for greater awareness surrounding women’s mental health and recognizing trauma and untreated mental illness.

“In Christa’s case, nobody was trying to get her help,” Brand said.

May Martinez is unconvinced that the person responsible for mutilating her daughter’s body and leaving her nude from the waist up could change.

Martinez recalled how, after the investigation ended, she did not realize all of her daughter’s body parts weren’t buried with her remains, as some had been retained as trial evidence. She had to pick up Slemmer’s skull from the courthouse, and remembers that the medical examiner’s office mailed her other parts later. (The office said it rarely retains human remains as it had 30 years ago because of better technology, enhanced photography and lab work.)

World.title: How an American teacher’s $5,000 donation helped turn a Chinese desert into a lush forest
World.content:
HONG KONG — Ronald Sakolsky never thought his money would go this far.

What was once a vast, dry desert in northern China has transformed into a lush, green forest of 50,000 full-grown trees, thanks in part to a $5,000 donation he made more than a quarter-century ago to a local farmer and “sand-control worker” named Yin Yuzhen.

Sakolsky, 69, a retired teacher from Pennsylvania, was amazed to see the transformation in China’s Inner Mongolia region last month when he visited for the first time in 26 years.

“Seeing it with my own eyes, that was the biggest surprise,” he told Chinese state media. “I saw pictures, I was told all about it, but until you see it is when you realize that it’s real.”

Sakolsky and Yin’s reunion last month has been held up by Chinese authorities as an example of how China and the United States, the world’s two biggest greenhouse gas emitters, can work together on global issues such as climate change.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping, in Washington this week for a summit with President Donald Trump, mentioned Sakolsky’s story in his toast at a state dinner on Thursday, saying it “touches the hearts of many Chinese people and stands as a shining example of the friendly exchanges between our two peoples.”

Sakolsky was teaching English on exchange in China’s central Henan province in 1999 when he saw a TV news report about Yin. More than a decade earlier, the newly married Yin had started planting trees as a way to feel less isolated in her new home in the Mu Us Desert, also known as the Maowusu Desert (“bad water” in Mongolian).

Moved by her story, Sakolsky raised $5,000, which was many times Yin’s annual income, so she could plant even more. They met in person in 2000, when Yin promised Sakolsky that she and her family would take good care of the saplings.

World.title: Europe frets as the Kremlin pushes the limits of its hybrid warfare
World.content:
The Kremlin is testing Europe‘s limits.

After months of covert attacks and sabotage across the continent, leaders are warning that Moscow may be about to grow bolder as it seeks to sow chaos and intimidate allies of Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve to defend members on its eastern flank or respond to attacks that fall short of all-out war, these officials say, at a time when the U.S. is distracted by other conflicts and weighing reducing its military presence in Europe.

An assessment by the Danish Defence Intelligence Service released Thursday warned that in the coming months Moscow will further intensify its campaign of so-called hybrid warfare, “with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past.” It also assessed “a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.”

While Moscow has for years embraced tactics that straddle the threshold of war, a string of increasingly brazen incidents in recent months has alarmed U.S. allies.

‘A bit freaked out’

A key moment was the discovery of a Russian drone carrying explosives at an airport in eastern Germany near a Ukrainian aircraft last month. Berlin formally blamed Russia for what it said was a thwarted attack and imposed a diplomatic freeze, though Moscow denied involvement.

That incident appears to have changed the mindset about Russia’s growing threat in Europe, said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It just showed that Putin’s risk calculations are getting more liberal,” Arnold said. “Everyone just got a bit freaked out by that, quite frankly.”

It was followed by the unexpected visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, during which NATO was discussed.

Incidents have continued to pile up — at defense facilities in Estonia, rail networks in Poland and the power grid in Germany. Many have passed without clear attribution, only intensifying speculation.

All this against the backdrop of near-daily drone incursions into European airspace, fueling anxiety in eastern border towns.

World.title: Election denier Kurt Olsen has resigned from DOJ, sources say
World.content:
Kurt Olsen, an election denier who attempted to overturn the 2020 election results in favor of President Trump, has resigned from the Justice Department, sources familiar with his departure told CBS News on Monday.

Olsen had been assigned to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida, where he was working on the "grand conspiracy" investigation targeting Obama- and Biden-era officials, which has so far not resulted in any charges.

CBS News has asked Olsen for comment.

Last month, Joe diGenova, the prosecutor who was tapped by Attorney General Todd Blanche, also resigned amid tensions with senior Justice Department officials over how the cases were being managed and their pace.

Olsen was previously working out of the White House as a "Presidentially appointed Director of Election Security and Integrity," the FBI said. In 2020, Olsen was an attorney working with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton to urge the Supreme Court to overturn the election results.

CBS News reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

In 2022, Olsen was subpoenaed by the House Jan. 6 select committee, which was investigating the aftermath of the 2020 election. The subpoena alleged that Olsen "contacted various high-level officials at the Department of Justice" at the president's direction to discuss filing challenges to the election results. The committee said Olsen spoke multiple times with Mr. Trump on Jan. 6, 2021.

Olsen made the Fulton County election case referral to the FBI, prompting agents to execute a search warrant earlier this year. They seized dozens of boxes of ballots and other materials from the 2020 election, an FBI affidavit revealed.

Olsen has also made several other 2020 election-related referrals to the Justice Department, according to a source with direct knowledge.

CBS News has previously reported that law enforcement veterans have been expressing deep concerns that the Trump Justice Department's criminal investigation into Brennan and others is being systematically stacked with politically motivated personnel who are intent on a partisan indictment.

Olsen is one of several prosecutors in recent days to leave the team working on the grand conspiracy case, several sources said.

One of those sources, however, said that some of the attorneys who came in from out of state were working there on a temporary basis and that those assignments had come to an end.

World.title: Cornell fraternity rape investigation will be reopened, DA says
World.content:
The investigation into an alleged rape at Cornell University in 2024 will be reopened, authorities said Monday.

The move comes after a lawsuit was filed earlier this month by a woman who claimed she was drugged and raped by multiple people at a fraternity house over the course of several hours.

Investigation is being reopened

"I have been asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members. I have already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys. Once we determine the appropriate charges, the case will be prosecuted in the most objective and impartial means available – by testimony to the Tompkins County Grand Jury," Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said in a written statement.

"The Grand Jury will be able to consider the testimony of Jane Doe as well as any new evidence raised by the allegations of the civil complaint. Upon a vote by the Grand Jury to indict any or all of the individuals involved, this office will prosecute the charges zealously and to the fullest extent of the law," the statement continued.

What the lawsuit alleged happened

According to the lawsuit, Doe was 20 years old in 2024 when she said she was drugged and raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house. Doe's attorney Thomas Giuffra claimed that following an investigation into the allegations, two of the accused were expelled, and there were no arrests.

Doe said she went to visit a friend at the frat house while she was intoxicated, and alleged she was pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine.

A man then allegedly sent a message to the frat's Snapchat group chat suggesting a woman was available for sex. Doe says more men showed up after the message was out, and she was raped for hours.

Doe filed a report with the university's police department about three weeks later.

DA: lawsuit allegations don't match what was previously described

Van Houten however said that is not the version of events his office was told at the time.

"Jane Doe's sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten said in a statement Monday. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later. Furthermore, I have never been contacted by Jane Doe's attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe's attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit's allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit's allegations."

Van Houten said his office was contacted by police at Cornell University in November 2024 to review Doe's statement. He said his office was provided with a six-page document that was signed by Doe and that "the statement ... provides a different narrative and set of facts of the evens of October 19, 2024 than those alleged in the lawsuit."

Van Houten said it had nothing to do with whether or not the allegations would be difficult to prove.

"In this case, multiple prosecutors and criminal investigators reviewed Jane Doe's statement and correctly determined the alleged facts as set forth in the statement do not constitute a crime. This decision was not because the case would have been difficult to prove in court – it was because the facts as set forth in the statement objectively prevent the filing of criminal charges. To be clear, the credibility of the woman, who described the facts in excruciating detail, was never in question," Van Houten said.

Van Houten said he was not at present going to release the signed statement initially provided to his office. He provided a summary, however.

The Ithaca Police Department told CBS News New York the alleged incident was never reported to them, adding they are disturbed by the allegations.

Jane Doe's attorney responds

Giuffra released a new statement after the DA's office said it would reopen the investigation.

"In the days following the assault, she was traumatized, numb and unable to function or accept the horror of what had happened. She was in self preservation mode," Giuffra said.

Giuffra said she reported the incident to Cornell Police. Giuffra said Doe never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her initial complaint.

"It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted," he said. "I would have expected at the very least that she would have been interviewed several times and evidence collected by law enforcement and a case developed. This is the normal sequence for serious crime investigations."

"The defensive posture I have gleaned from the DA's statements leads me to believe that they recognize that there were failures and they are trying to excuse them. While I do not care for the attempt to blame Ms. Doe for these failures, we appreciate and support any efforts prosecute the parties responsible for the assaults and will fully cooperate with the District Attorney's Office to hold these men accountable," Giuffra added.

Cornell University, Chi Phi respond to lawsuit allegations

Cornell University released a statement about the reopening of the case.

"Cornell University supports the decision of the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) to provide an opportunity for the victim's story in the 2024 Chi Phi fraternity sexual assault case to be heard by a criminal grand jury.

"Cornell also conducted a thorough Title IX investigation, which is separate from a criminal proceeding, over the course of several months. During that investigation, temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were used. After investigation, and pursuant to federal law, the matter was sent to a hearing where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days. The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence. At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.

"In addition, the involved fraternity chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false. A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."

Cornell University previously said the school had launched a task force on sexual assaults, and set up a website where students can report bias, discrimination, harassment and sexual misconduct incidents.

The Chi Phi national headquarters sent CBS News New York the following statement following the initial lawsuit.

"The sexual assault allegations involving parties at Cornell University are deeply concerning. Anyone who reports sexual violence deserves to be heard and treated with compassion, dignity, and respect.

"Chi Phi unequivocally condemns sexual violence. Our founding principles of Truth, Honor, and Personal Integrity, and our mission of Building Better Men, call on every brother to demonstrate character through his actions and respect for the dignity and safety of others. Sexual violence is fundamentally incompatible with those expectations.

"We are aware of the lawsuit concerning an alleged incident in 2024. While we cannot discuss the specific allegations during pending litigation, we take this matter seriously. Our responsibility is to approach this with care for those affected and respect for a fair legal process."
