World.title: Colombia breaks diplomatic ties with Iran
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday that it had broken diplomatic ties with Iran and designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization.

The foreign ministry made the announcements in two separate statements that were published in its website.

In the first statement, the government claimed that the decision claimed to defend “national and hemispheric security, and the fight against transnational crime.”

According to the foreign ministry, the Iranian government has “alleged ties to international terrorist groups and other narco-terrorist groups that threaten [Colombia’s] security.”

Colombia also took into account the documented human rights violations committed by the Iranian government on its territory, the verified attacks against countries not involved in the Middle East conflict, the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the authorities’ obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) efforts to verify the scope of Iran’s nuclear program. Foreign Ministry

In regards to the IRGC, the foreign ministry claimed that the Iranian armed force “poses a serious threat to international peace and security” through “covert operations beyond Iran’s borders.”

“Colombia will strengthen its control and security measures to prevent individuals associated with the IRGC from entering its territory,” said the foreign ministry in a second statement.

In his 2017 book “Watch Your Backyard,” Foreign Minister Omar Bula claimed that “Iran and Islamic extremist groups such a Hezbollah and Al Qaeda have profusely penetrated Latin America.”

As part of his foreign policy, President Abelardo de la Espriella has renewed ties with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates.

In a response, the Iranian government said that the accusations of the De la Espriella government go “against the principles of mutual respect” and damage both countries’ “interests and benefits.”

“It is clear that none of the arguments put forward by the Colombian government to justify this decision are valid or logical, and that this measure was adopted solely under the influence of the Zionist regime and the United States,” said Iran’s foreign ministry.

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: London says Argentina “lacks the ability” to take the Falklands
World.content:
London says Argentina “lacks the ability” to take the Falklands

28th Monday, September 2026 - 09:33 UTC Full article

Streeting also said “this issue was settled in 1982” and that the will of the archipelago's residents, “the overwhelming majority of whom choose to be British”, remains unchanged

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said Argentina “lacks the ability” to take the Falkland Islands and that the United Kingdom “has the ability to defend” them, in an interview with the Sunday paper The Sun on Sunday published on Saturday. Asked whether London could protect the archipelago militarily if Buenos Aires sent warships, he answered yes.

“This isn't 1982,” the minister said, dismissing the position of Argentine President Javier Milei as “the same old bogus propaganda”. In referring to Argentine claims he used a colloquial pejorative term for the country's citizens, which Spanish-language versions rendered simply as “the Argentines”.

Streeting also said “this issue was settled in 1982” and that the will of the archipelago's residents, “the overwhelming majority of whom choose to be British”, remains unchanged. That is the British government's position and it is contested by Argentina, which maintains the dispute remains open; the archipelago is still on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose, on a 92% turnout, to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

The remarks were published three days after Milei's address to the UN General Assembly, in which he called on the organisation to act over what he described as unilateral British actions and argued that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the archipelago. Some British coverage framed Streeting's words as a response to the televised address Milei delivered on September 3, so it is not established which specific intervention he was answering.

The week in New York produced opposing positions from the same podium. On Tuesday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham included the archipelago among challenges to the rule of law; that same night, Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno exercised the right of reply, saying the British occupation “dates back to 1833, when United Kingdom forces occupied the Malvinas Islands, breaching the country's territorial integrity and expelling the legitimately established Argentine authorities and population”, while reiterating Argentina's “full willingness” to resume negotiations. Milei spoke on Wednesday, and that same Wednesday the United Kingdom entered a written statement of rejection into the assembly's record.

Argentina's government has 60 administrative proceedings open, with no penalty applied, and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors over hydrocarbon exploration in waters near the archipelago. None of the allegations has been proven. No official Argentine response to Streeting's remarks has been recorded so far.

The 1982 war lasted 74 days and left 649 Argentine service personnel, 255 British and three residents of the archipelago dead.

World.title: Chile reinforcing its military presence in Magallanes Region and Antarctica
World.content:
Chile reinforcing its military presence in Magallanes Region and Antarctica

28th Monday, September 2026 - 08:09 UTC Full article

Minister Barros said defense requires planning and Chile must have the necessary capacities to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of its people.

Chile announced the reinforcement of its military capacities in the Magallanes Region, extreme south of the country with a plan that includes renewal of aircraft, modernization of armored vehicles, increased vigilance and presence in the austral territory and Antarctica, updating of military strategy based on experiences from the current war scenarios in Europe and Middle East.

The announcement was made by Defense minister Fernando Barros, at the base of Chabunco, next to Punta Arenas, together with the commanders of all services. Chabunco is headquarters and seat of the Fourth Chilean Air Force Brigade, FACH, with jurisdiction over southern Patagonia and protection of bases in Chilean Antarctica.

The announcement was done at a very sensitive moment for relations between Chile and Argentina, following repeated statements from Argentine nationalist groups during August and September, regarding alleged ‘shared sovereignty’ over the Magellan Strait, straining bilateral relations.

Minister Barros insisted that defense requires planning and Chile must have the necessary capacities to protect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and the security of its people.

Chilean Defense said that strategic planning means replacing in Punta Arenas the current F-5 fighter jets by fourth or fifth generation aircraft, the renewal of the helicopter fleet plus strategic air transport, essential for Antarctica missions, and for the Navy long range maritime patrolling with air coverage. The Army will see the refurbish of its Leopard 1 tanks and remote control modern warfare.

Some land bases will be reformed to have a permanent presence and the strategic bases in Chilean Antarctica are to have increased air and maritime connections, confirming a greater presence form the country.

Apparently Chilean Defense has been working on these plans for some time and with a 2043 horizon, but not only with a military objective, but rather with “a standing Chilean logistics responsibility regarding the Magellan Strait and Antarctica”.

All of this erupted when Argentine head of Air Force Chief of Staff Gustavo Javier Valverde made some comments regarding the Magellan Strait that generated an immediate reaction from Chile, Taking advantage of the calendar, an anniversary of the possession of the Strait by Chile in September 1843, the Chilean vice-president, members of the Senate’s blocks plus Magallanes joined in a tour de force reaffirming sole and complete Chilean sovereignty of the Magellan Strait.

Likewise in a visit to Argentina, and again in Chile, president Juan Antonio Kast said that Argentina “does not have and will never have”, sovereignty over the Magellan Strait because it has been clearly judged, and agreed, by treaties with Argentina.

And if this was not enough five F-16 from the northern FACH base of Los Condores in Iquique, next to Peru flew non-stop with an early warning aircraft AEW, and a Stratotanker KC-135 to refuel fighter jets in flight to Magallanes Region, for an air display over Punta Arenas. Apparently the F-16 will remain a couple of weeks in the extreme south of Chile.

Chile’s FACH has proven experience with the Stratotanker KC-135 since last April when the Air and Space Show in Santiago, FIDAE, it successfully refueled two F-35A Lightning from US Air Force in their journey from Florida to Chile for the show.

Summing up, according to Chilean sources the challenge for the administration of president Kast is to advance with the military modernization while keeping open, friendly cooperation channels with Argentina.

The Kast message is clear: Magallanes Region, the Strait and its projection to Antarctica are a Defense strategic planning priority for Chile, and with the funds needed or expected to be invested, allegedly having the necessary congressional support.

World.title: The Telegraph links the Chagos deal to Argentina's Falklands campaign
World.content:
The Telegraph links the Chagos deal to Argentina's Falklands campaign

28th Monday, September 2026 - 07:51 UTC Full article

The column describes Milei as having moved from economic libertarianism to nationalism and, having once celebrated Margaret Thatcher, now seeking to attract Donald Trump with oil concessions

An opinion column published on Sunday in the British newspaper The Telegraph argues that the decision to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius served as a signal of weakness that encouraged claims over other British overseas territories, among them the Falklands. The piece, by journalist Daniel Johnson, is an argument of opinion rather than a report of new facts.

According to the author, the agreement over the Indian Ocean archipelago — taken, he writes, for reasons never properly explained to Parliament — signalled to other actors that British territories might be up for grabs, “even many thousands of miles away in the South Atlantic”. He argues that Argentine President Javier Milei launched his campaign calculating that reviving the issue would boost his popularity. Milei explicitly rejected that reading on September 23, calling it “a massive stupidity” and saying the strategy had been in preparation for three years.

The column describes Milei as having moved from economic libertarianism to nationalism and, having once celebrated Margaret Thatcher, now seeking to attract Donald Trump with oil concessions. These are the author's characterisations. He also states that an Anglo-Israeli consortium is legally drilling for oil in the archipelago's waters; in fact the companies expect drilling to begin in early 2027 and first production in the first half of 2028, and the validity of the licences is precisely what is disputed between London and Buenos Aires.

On the meeting between Trump and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the author notes that it was The Telegraph that raised Chagos at the joint press conference. Trump replied that it was “a terrible deal” and said Burnham “is going to be looking at it”; the prime minister answered “yep”. The column argues that Trump offered no reassurance on the South Atlantic islands and contrasts his stance with Ronald Reagan's in 1982.

The text includes several claims without cited sources: that Burnham had assured Mauritius he would do “everything possible” to ratify the treaty, that the Royal Navy would lack the capacity to send even a flotilla in the event of a landing, that unnamed retired British diplomats are playing down the rights of the archipelago's residents, and that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has avoided framing the islands' defence in national security terms.

The cost of the Chagos agreement is measured three ways: the British government cites £3.4 billion in net present value; the Conservative opposition a nominal total of £34.7 billion; and a third measure puts it at around £10 billion. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of Falklands voters chose, on a 92% turnout, to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

The column also refers to the meeting of the leaders of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland held in Cardiff this month, saying they signed a memorandum of understanding. It notes that Burnham did not object to a new Scottish referendum if a majority supported one, though it omits that the prime minister later clarified that it remains off limits.

World.title: Britain has just received a painful reminder that nobody respects weakness
World.content:
Britain has just received a painful reminder that nobody respects weakness

28th Monday, September 2026 - 06:01 UTC Full article

Donald Trump muses about transferring part of our territory to Ireland. The EU threatens us with illegal car and steel tariffs

By Daniel Hannan (*)



As the Chagos humiliation shows, the Foreign Office’s slavish adoration of international courts has got us nowhere. What has all our imagined soft power brought us? For all our performative internationalism, we find ourselves friendless.

Donald Trump muses about transferring part of our territory to Ireland. The EU threatens us with illegal car and steel tariffs. Our airports keep being closed for “technical reasons”. China talks menacingly of retaliation over our nationalization of steel. We have somehow managed to fall out simultaneously with Israel and Iran. Argentina sanctions oil companies around the Falkland Islands. Commonwealth grifters come after us – us, the country that abolished the slave trade – with demands of repatriation.

So much for the goodwill we were supposed to have amassed through leading on climate change, grovelling before international courts, spraying around aid money and indulging the shakedown artists.

Soft power, at least as Foreign Office types understand it, is codswallop. It is the comforting story we tell ourselves because we are too weak and indebted to exercise hard power. Actual soft power, in the sense of respect for our values and institutions, was only ever a corollary of military success. British cultural influence, as measured by other nations dressing like us, adopting our sports, establishing bicameral parliaments and so on, was a product of our nineteenth-century might. To pretend that we are still influential because Chinese children read Harry Potter is pure cope.

As a British 10-year-old in South America when Leopoldo Galtieri ordered the invasion of the Falkland Islands, I remember the upsurge in anti-British feeling after a small group of Royal Marines surrendered in Port Stanley. Local media took the line that a decrepit colonial power was finally getting its comeuppance. How the tone changed when Argentina was routed. All of a sudden, the British were admired and respected. Strangers would congratulate us in the streets. Nothing succeeds like success.

That respect has not entirely died away. A recent opinion poll showed that Chileans backed British rather than Argentine sovereignty over the Falklands by 68 to 17 per cent. While Chile is an unusually Anglophile country, I have noticed several other Latin Americans voicing the same opinion – especially since the recent World Cup, which turned pretty much the entire continent against Argentina.

Javier Milei, Argentina’s president, is the same age as me. He will also recall the mood changing when he was a child. He will remember how sympathy swung to the winners. He understands, in a way that our Foreign Office soft-power-wallahs seem unable to, that prestige is a commodity, as real as lithium or Malbec.

Listen to how he phrases his revanchism. “The United Kingdom faces multiple migratory, demographic and economic crises that will not be easily solved. It is clearly on the road to decline. Argentina, by contrast, has a prosperous future, and will prevail,” he said earlier this month.

For what it’s worth, I am not immediately worried by the prospect of another Argentine invasion. I visited the Falkland Islands three years ago, and was hugely impressed by the preparedness of our garrison. Milei, a libertarian at heart, is not going to blow away his country’s welcome economic revival by launching a war.

No, my point is a different one. Argentina, not Britain, has grasped the reality of modern geopolitics. To the extent that international courts mattered, they count for little now. What matters is military power which, in turn, rests on economic growth.

That might sound obvious, but it is plainly not obvious to our foreign policy establishment, which is even now trying to ensure that Andy Burnham does not interfere with its determined attempt to hand away thr Chagos Islands and pay for the pleasure of doing so.

Over the past week, we have seen repeated briefings claim it is too late to change the deal, that the key thing is to act before our legal position becomes weaker, and that, if necessary, we should keep Mauritius on side by giving it more handouts until a future US administration lifts its veto.

All these briefings come from our standing apparat, and all beg the question. If we start, as Sir Keir Starmer and Richard Hermer did, from a near-religious veneration of international law, then we must indeed obey the rulings of Russian and Chinese judges on a United Nations tribunal. It makes no difference that disputes between current and former Commonwealth members are excluded from the court’s jurisdiction. It doesn’t matter that Mauritius, which had no interest in the Chagos archipelago, accepted a cash payment in 1965 in return for renouncing any claim. It is of no consequence that the Chagossians themselves would rather live as British subjects than become Mauritians.

To see how unusual our approach is, try to imagine any other country taking it. Picture the Americans or the Chinese rushing to hand their territory to a country that had never owned it simply because a posse of Third Worldist judges had told them to.

While our civil servants continue to promote the deal of which they are so proud, Burnham can see how dreadful it looks. You don’t need to be a fulminating reactionary in a pith helmet to see what is wrong with betraying a poor, black, dispossessed population, and handing a pristine maritime conservation area to a country with a terrible record on biodiversity.

When the deal was first proposed, this column was a lonely voice of opposition. As the understanding of what it involved spread, so did the incredulity. This week, opposition has been voiced by Labour and Lib Dem MPs, by the Left-leaning News Agency podcast and by The Independent. All ask why we should pay to give territory we already own to a country that is increasingly close to China.

Burnham talks of Starmer’s deal as something he “inherited”: he, at least, gets the politics. At the same time, Ellie Reeves, his impressive Attorney General, has quietly altered the rules to water down the obligation on government ministries to follow non-binding rulings by international tribunals, making it much harder for Matrix Chambers types to pursue Mauritius’s claim through our domestic courts – the prospect held up by supporters of the deal as a reason to rush.

No doubt Burnham is being told by his advisers that there is no alternative – the same advisers who told David Cameron that it was not feasible to land a boat on the outer atolls, where a brave colony of returned Chagossian exiles has since been established.

In fact, there is a clear alternative. Ditch the deal and resettle the islands, allowing people of Chagossian descent to cultivate their old coconut plantations and tend their forefathers’ graves. Once the archipelago has a settled population, we can defend its right to self-determination as we do in Gibraltar or the Falkland Islands.

An opportunity is coming soon. Next month, the House of Lords will vote on the British Sovereignty Protection (Chagos Islands) Bill, proposed by the independent Lord Weir of Ballyholme. Lord Weir, a barrister and former Stormont minister, wants to make it illegal to transfer ownership of the islands without the permission of Parliament and the diaspora Chagossian population. On democratic grounds, his case is unarguable, and my guess is that his bill will sail through the Lords, Labour peers being as unenthusiastic as anyone else about betraying the Chagossians a second time.

Burnham should back the bill and announce that the Government will promote Chagossian resettlement of the outer islands – something that, while not cheap, is a fraction of what Starmer was proposing to pay Mauritius. As for Mauritius itself, its interest in the territory has only ever been pecuniary. Paying it to back our claim, rather than paying it to take our land, genuinely would be a worthwhile investment and an exercise of meaningful power.

Returning to power politics vis-à-vis Mauritius would strengthen our position globally, from the Falkland Islands to the slavery reparations moochers. It would also, for what it is worth, remove a vote-losing headache from Burnham’s inbox. Don’t hang back, Prime Minister. They’ll like us when we win.

(*) Daniel Hannan is President of the Institute of Economic Affairs, and sits in the House of Lords as an independent peer. The IEA is an educational charity and free market think tank. It describes its mission as improving the understanding of the fundamental institution of a free society and expounding the role of markets in solving economic and social problemas.

World.title: Brazil reaches the election with its top court under suspicion and the candidates tied
World.content:
Brazil reaches the election with its top court under suspicion and the candidates tied

27th Sunday, September 2026 - 12:26 UTC Full article

Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if he wins, his priorities will be to grant his father an amnesty and to bring Brazil into the security alliance Trump is promoting in the region

Brazil votes next Sunday in a presidential election that arrives with the Supreme Federal Court mired in its worst institutional crisis since the return to democracy, the right's candidate formally under investigation in the same case, and the two leading contenders tied within the margin of error in every poll.

The Banco Master case, in which the bank's former owner, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested on Supreme Court orders over an alleged fraud of up to 12 billion reais, has reached both Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and several justices of the court itself. The Liberal Party candidate has been formally under investigation since July for alleged money laundering, currency evasion and corruption, focused on his contacts with Vorcaro and on the financing of “Dark Horse”, a film about his father. There is no formal indictment or conviction. In February, a Brasília judge ordered the removal of false online content claiming an arrest warrant existed against him.

The institutional dimension came later. The law firm of Justice Alexandre de Moraes's wife held a contract with the bank, and a police report revealed around a hundred messages between Vorcaro and the justice three weeks before his arrest. Justice André Mendonça, appointed by Jair Bolsonaro and responsible for a central part of the investigation, acknowledged receiving Vorcaro once and defended the lawfulness of his conduct. The court's president, Edson Fachin, ordered the case files unsealed. No irregularity has been established regarding any of the justices. Flávio Bolsonaro called at a São Paulo rally for Moraes's removal and demanded that other cases also be made public, including one involving a son of Lula.

Polling remains stable. The latest Datafolha survey, conducted last Tuesday and Wednesday among 2,002 voters with a two-point margin, gave Lula 40% and Bolsonaro 36% in the first round, and 47% to 45% in a prospective October 25 runoff. Earlier surveys by Quaest, BTG/Nexus and AtlasIntel produced different results, all within their margins. Neither man approaches the 50% plus one needed to win outright.

Jair Bolsonaro, 71, was sentenced on September 11, 2025 to 27 years and three months in prison for attempting a coup and four other offences, alongside seven allies of what the court called the plot's core group. He is barred from office and is under house arrest with an electronic tag, granted in March on humanitarian grounds after pneumonia. In May a law was enacted allowing applications for sentence reductions, which are not automatic. He designated as his successor his eldest son, a senator for Rio de Janeiro after 16 years as a city councillor, despite establishment preferences for a candidate without the family name.

Researchers quoted by the Brazilian press attribute Bolsonarismo's electoral resilience to the combination of a discourse centred on moral questions with the growth of evangelical churches in urban peripheries. “Bolsonaro did not create moral conservatism. He did not bring broad evangelical sectors into politics, nor did he create the Brazilian far right. What he did was assemble those elements very effectively around a candidacy,” says political anthropologist Mercia Alves, of the Centro Brasileiro de Análise e Planejamento. David Magalhães, of the Observatório da Extrema Direita, says suspicions surrounding the court feed the idea that the former president is “a victim of a system”.

Flávio Bolsonaro has said that, if he wins, his priorities will be to grant his father an amnesty and to bring Brazil into the security alliance Trump is promoting in the region, from which the country was left out after Lula rejected the designation of the PCC and Comando Vermelho as terrorist organisations.

World.title: De la Espriella announces the reopening of oil exploration in Colombia, including fracking
World.content:
De la Espriella announces the reopening of oil exploration in Colombia, including fracking

26th Saturday, September 2026 - 11:06 UTC Full article

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella announced on Friday that his government will “fully” reopen hydrocarbon exploration and the signing of new contracts, including hydraulic fracturing, during the swearing-in of businessman Joaquín Gutiérrez as president of Ecopetrol, the country's largest company.

“My government is fully reopening the path of exploration and the signing of new contracts, including fracking, whatever it takes, as I said during the campaign, with absolutely every criterion of environmental responsibility,” the president said, adding a call to “drop the environmental hysteria”. He criticised the policy of his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, who reduced the signing of new exploration contracts as part of an energy transition strategy: “That is not energy transition but energy dependence, which is what no policy of this government will accept. In the era of the Tiger we will have energy sovereignty.” He also backed environment ministry measures to speed up licensing procedures.

The announcement does not in itself change the existing framework. Reactivating fracking in Colombia would require reversing the cancellation of the pilot projects ordered under the previous government and navigating regulatory and judicial restrictions whose precise status the executive has not detailed. The technique faces objections over its impact on water resources and the risk of induced seismicity. No environmental or opposition voices took part in the event.

The ceremony was held at the Quinta de San Pedro Alejandrino in Santa Marta, the estate where Simón Bolívar died. Gutiérrez said his arrival opens “a new era” and that the company should “be reborn to fulfil its true mission”, with the aim of aspiring to “the places of glory among the world's leading oil companies”.

The new president also announced that Ecopetrol will have a second headquarters in Barranquilla, set out plans for a “more austere and efficient” company with higher productivity, less centralised and with a greater regional presence, and said it would be “a depoliticised Ecopetrol”. He said the company would carry out “responsible fracking”, that it would reach its highest ever value under his tenure and that his legacy would be to leave it “with reserves for decades”. He also said there would be complaints over the previous administration's management; no irregularity has been established to date.

Gutiérrez is a business administrator, takes up the post with no previous experience in the hydrocarbons sector and managed De la Espriella's presidential campaign. His appointment was announced on Thursday by Ecopetrol's board, whose members had been renewed by shareholders on September 15. The company is listed on the Colombian Stock Exchange and in New York, with the Colombian state as majority shareholder.

De la Espriella took office on August 7. In these weeks his government has aligned its foreign policy with the United States and Israel, saw Colombia kept on Washington's list of countries it deems to have failed demonstrably to combat drug trafficking — with explicit praise for the new president — and delegated the country's address to the UN General Assembly to his vice president.

World.title: Falklands Assembly responds to Argentina's campaign: “This Assembly remains calm”
World.content:
Falklands Assembly responds to Argentina's campaign: “This Assembly remains calm”

25th Friday, September 2026 - 23:26 UTC Full article

Ford thanked the British prime minister, the foreign secretary, the minister for the Overseas Territories and figures “right across the UK political spectrum” for their support

The chair of the Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly, Jack Ford, said on Thursday during a sitting of the body that there is “nothing new” in the claims made this week, and that the institution “remains calm” and steadfast in defending the right of the archipelago's residents to determine their own future.

“Claims of this kind have been made against the Falkland Islands many times over many years, and throughout all of them these Islands have continued to grow, to develop, and to thrive. We will go on doing exactly that,” said Ford, who alongside chairing the assembly holds the Corporate Services portfolio and has represented the Camp constituency since last December's general election.

The statement came after a week in which Argentine President Javier Milei called on the UN General Assembly on Wednesday to act over what he described as unilateral British actions, arguing that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the archipelago because, in his government's view, its population was implanted. The United Kingdom responded with a written statement entered into the organisation's official record.

Ford thanked the British prime minister, the foreign secretary, the minister for the Overseas Territories and figures “right across the UK political spectrum” for their support, saying Westminster had shown “unwavering commitment” to the right of self-determination and to developing the archipelago's natural resources. He cited the extension of offshore hydrocarbon production licences announced this month with British backing, calling it “a clear mark of confidence in our future”.

The central nuance of his remarks came next. “Our confidence does not rest on the support of others alone, welcome as it is. It rests on our own democratic choice, made clearly and repeatedly by the people who live here,” he said, citing the 2013 referendum, in which on a 92% turnout 99.8% voted to remain a self-governing British Overseas Territory, a result he described as “independently monitored and beyond dispute”.

Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, does not recognise the validity of licences granted by the local government and maintains that the referendum does not settle the question. It has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors, and last week sent Congress a sovereignty bill extending prohibitions to all natural resources on the continental shelf. None of the allegations has been proven.

It is the third public intervention by an assembly member in ten days. On September 17, Lewis Clifton, who holds the Emergency Services and Island Security portfolio, said the archipelago's defences are adequate; on September 21, Cheryl Roberts, responsible for Trade, Industry and Mineral Resources, announced the extension of the oil licences.

World.title: Guanajuato will host a free outdoor Mexican-French circus spectacle this weekend as Cervantino Festival approaches
World.content:
Acrobats and tightrope walkers will turn Guanajuato’s historic city center into an open-air circus Saturday night, performing high above the crowd in a free opening-day show at the 54th International Cervantino Festival.

“Vértigo” — a Mexico-France collaboration adapted from the French production “Vertige” — is scheduled for 9 p.m. Saturday in Plaza Allende, the small square beside the Cervantes Theater in the historic city of Guanajuato.

The 60-minute show will combine aerial circus, dance, live music and a site-specific visual design.

The spectacle will bring together artists from Chaillot, a Paris-based national theater, and Mexican performers. Some of the acrobats and aerial balance artists (aka highliners) are affiliated with Mexico City’s Cirko de Mente.

Created by choreographer Rachid Ouramdane, musician Christophe Chassol and highliner Nathan Paulin, “Vértigo” adapts a piece first staged last year at the Grand Palais inaugural festival in Paris.

It was conceived as a mobile work, with performers suspended high above a public space and moving along tensioned lines.

The Guanajuato version was developed with Andrea Peláez, co-founder of the Mexico City contemporary-circus company Cirko de Mente, and Mexican artists.

France is the festival’s guest country this year, as part of a program marking 200 years of diplomatic relations with Mexico. The initiative recently yielded an exchange of centuries-old Aztec documents known as codices.

France’s program will include 18 presentations spanning classical and contemporary music, theater, dance, cabaret, street art, film, opera and multidisciplinary work.

The aerial circus is free, but overall, the Cervantino Festival mixes ticketed events with free events and free-access areas. It will run from Saturday, Oct. 3 through Sunday, Oct. 18.

Featuring more than 200 performances by some 2,750 artists, the event will include headliners such as Mike Patton’s Italian-song project Mondo Cane, which will open the festival at 7 p.m. Saturday.

The lineup also includes Australia’s Bangarra Dance Theatre, the German contemporary-music ensemble Ensemble Modern, Colombian salsa band Grupo Niche and Austria’s Camerata Salzburg with Spanish violinist María Dueñas.

One highlight will be an Oct. 15 tribute to the late José Alfredo Jiménez, the Guanajuato-born ranchera songwriter who wrote enduring Mexican standards including “El Rey” and “Si nos dejan.” Tenor Arturo Chacón Cruz and Mexico City-based Mariachi Gama 1000 will perform at the event at the Alhóndiga de Granaditas esplanade.

For more information, visit the festival’s official website.

With reports from Milenio, Crónica and Almomento

World.title: Peso falls to 18 to the US dollar as oil, Fed worries weigh on both currencies
World.content:
The Mexican peso depreciated to 18 to the US dollar on Monday, a weakening of more than 1% compared to Friday and over 6% compared to its strongest position this month.

The sharp depreciation on Monday came just weeks after the return of the “super peso” was proclaimed at a time when the peso was trading at below 17 to the greenback.

A USD:MXN exchange rate of 18, as was the going rate early Monday afternoon, represents a depreciation of 6.2% for the peso compared to its strongest closing position this month — 16.89 to the greenback on Sept. 4, according to the Bank of Mexico (Banxico).

At 3 p.m. Mexico City time, the peso was trading at 17.99 to the US dollar, according to Bloomberg.

Banxico’s closing USD:MXN rate, reported daily at 2:10 p.m., was 17.94, a depreciation of 1.3% compared to the closing rate on Friday.

The newspaper El Financiero attributed the peso’s decline on Monday to a greater aversion to risk, an increase in oil prices — which rose after U.S. President Donald Trump’s rejection of an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days — and expectations of a more restrictive U.S. Federal Reserve, which raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75%-4% earlier this month.

The peso has benefited from the substantial difference between Banxico’s key interest rate (6.50%) and that of the Fed. However, that difference is now smaller than it was at the start of the month, and the gap could close further if the Fed raises its key rate again next month.

For now, the peso is back in a position it was last in almost six months ago.

In an X post on Monday afternoon, Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, wrote that the peso hadn’t traded at 18 to the dollar since March 31. In a separate post that includes a graph showing the peso trading at 18 to the dollar, she wrote: “Strong dollar or weak peso? Both.”

¿Dólar fuerte o peso débil? Ambos. pic.twitter.com/qC5YVeu0Jy — Gabriela Siller Pagaza (@GabySillerP) September 28, 2026

In another X post on Monday, Siller noted that the USD:MXN exchange rate was 18.0080 at the end of 2025.

“Everything seems to indicate that it could close around that level again [at the end of] this year,” she wrote.

With reports from El Financiero

World.title: Oregon woman, a ‘medical tourist,’ wins the right to have her Tijuana medical malpractice complaint heard
World.content:
While studies show that medical procedures in Tijuana can cost up to 75% less than in the United States, patients considering this option might want to embrace the maxim “caveat emptor.”

Although cheaper dental work, plastic surgery and bariatric surgery might sound appealing, insufficient regulation and inadequate oversight are legitimate concerns. And when patients’ lives have been endangered, the question of where to turn has not always been encouraging.

That might be changing, however.

Early this month, a district judge in Baja California ordered the Baja California Medical Arbitration Commission (CAMEBC) to consider a complaint of medical negligence filed by an Oregon woman who suffered severe complications following weight-loss surgery in 2024.

Julia Carpenter, 40, had traveled to Tijuana to undergo bariatric surgery at the Beauty and Light Medical Solutions clinic. But instead of the gastric bypass and cholecystectomy (gallbladder removal) that had been agreed to, Dr. Mauricio Gutiérrez García performed an ileoduodenal anastomosis, a different weight-loss procedure that ties together sections of the small intestine. What followed was a medical nightmare.

When Carpenter suffered complications back home, she found that the clinic had vacated its registered address. What’s more, it turned out that Dr. Gutiérrez not only had an expired license, but had disappeared.

A medical negligence complaint was filed in February 2025, but after delaying six months, CAMEBC refused to consider it, claiming it “lacked jurisdiction.”

Many efforts at redress would end right there, but Carpenter filed an appeal in court. Earlier this month, a judge ruled CAMEBC had violated Carpenter’s rights by delaying its decision and ordered the commission to hear the complaint.

The Carpenters have also filed criminal complaints against the doctor and the clinic.

CAMEBC has handled more than 1,000 patient complaints this year through August. The Carpenter case illustrates the risks of unregulated medical tourism in Tijuana, a city that accounts for 80% of plastic surgeries in Mexico.

In 2021, a doctor accused of negligent manslaughter in the death of a woman during cosmetic surgery agreed to pay the victim’s family US $194,000. It remains unclear what, if any, criminal punishment the doctor, who was not licensed to perform cosmetic surgery, suffered, but according to newspaper reports, criminal punishment is waived if a financial settlement is complied with.

On the positive side, the Tijuana government recently launched an alliance between the Tourism and Conventions Committee, the Baja Health Cluster and the Association of Recovery Centers with the goal of regulating the industry and eliminating fraudulent clinics.

With reports from El País, Info Mi Tijuana and El Imparcial

World.title: Following 2 years of losses, federal government is projected to net US $7.1B from oil in 2027
World.content:
The federal government is projected to earn net oil revenue in 2027 for the first time since 2024, even as it continues to provide monetary support to the state oil company Pemex.

According to an analysis of the proposed 2027 budget by the think tank México Evalúa, the government is projected to earn net oil revenue of 127 billion pesos (US $7.1 billion) next year.

That figure reflects projected oil revenue of 211 billion pesos in 2027, minus 84 billion pesos in planned government transfers to Pemex, to be made via the federal Energy Ministry.

Data published by México Evalúa shows that the government’s transfers to Pemex exceeded total oil revenue last year and were forecast to do so again this year based on the amount budgeted for the state oil company. Thus, the federal government is projected to record a net oil loss for a second consecutive year in 2026, although it could avoid such a loss if its transfers to Pemex end up being lower than planned.

While the projected 127 billion pesos in net oil revenue would be the government’s first net oil revenue since 2024, the figure would remain well below the amounts it received in some previous years.

In 2022, for example, the government earned net oil revenue of 551 billion pesos. That figure (expressed in “2027 prices,” per México Evalúa) was the result of 780 billion pesos in oil revenue, minus 229 billion pesos in transfers to Pemex.

According to México Evalúa, the government’s net oil revenue was 1.78 trillion pesos in 2012 — a year in which it didn’t transfer any money to Pemex — and 1.51 trillion pesos in 2013. The latter figure was the result of 1.64 trillion pesos in oil revenue, minus 123 billion pesos in transfers to Pemex. The government can use net oil revenue to fund things such as healthcare, security, infrastructure and education. Pemex used to be known as a “cash cow” for the government, but has become a financial drain in recent years.

This decade, the government has provided significant monetary support to Pemex, which had debt of US $77.5 billion at the end of the second quarter of 2026. Monetary support for the company peaked at 425 billion pesos in 2025.

However, the government’s support for the state oil company in 2027 is projected to decline by close to 70% compared to the budgeted outlay in 2026. Whether that in fact happens, allowing the federal government to earn net oil revenue in 2027, remains to be seen.

México Evalúa: Government has a ‘tradition’ of providing Pemex with more support than planned — but that could change in 2026

Jorge Cano, head of México Evalúa’s public expenditure program, told the newspaper El Economista that government transfers to Pemex have a “tradition” of being significantly higher than planned.

He said that if support for Pemex exceeds the planned level in 2027 to the same extent as in recent years, the government could again record a net loss from oil instead of the projected 127 billion pesos in net revenue.

Cano said that the government has discretion to increase support for Pemex beyond the planned amount and need only notify Congress if the allocation is adjusted by more than 5%.

While the government has exceeded its planned support for Pemex in recent years, it doesn’t appear that it will do so in 2026, based on data for the first seven months of the year. Mariana Campos, general director of México Evalúa, pointed out that the government had transferred 139 billion pesos to Pemex by the end of July, representing just 51% of the 272 billion pesos earmarked for the company.

She said that “for the first time,” the government’s monetary support for Pemex is lower than budgeted. This development, Campos said, supports the projection that the government will earn net oil revenue in 2027.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Cirque du Soleil, Day of the Dead festivities and Ukrainian ballet coming to town, but mind the sinkholes
World.content:
There is an exciting slate of cultural activities in Guadalajara in the coming month, including the 20th edition of Cirque du Soleil, the Leyenda de la Noche theme park and a Ukrainian ballet performing “Swan Lake.”

But before we dive in, let’s look at the myriad road closures around town stemming from dangerous sinkholes to help you navigate safely.

Be careful out there: It’s sinkhole season in Guadalajara

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Migue Saldaña (@miguesaldanagdl)

As the rainy season winds down in Jalisco state, this year’s storms have caused more than 3,000 sinkholes of various sizes around the city, with at least five massive ones creating havoc along major commuting corridors.

The gargantuan holes have caused accidents, lengthy traffic jams and road closures as SIAPA (the public water authority) tackles repairs, creating new headaches for area motorists.

To date, SIAPA has addressed only about half of the reported sinkholes due to limited resources.

According to Ismael Jáuregui Castañeda, head of SIAPA, most of the new sinkholes are in older neighborhoods where aging water infrastructure long past its useful life is collapsing, triggered by especially heavy rains this past summer.

Below is a rundown of key hotspots.

On Sept. 7, a massive sinkhole opened on Malecón Avenue at the intersection with Tanacatita in Tonalá, measuring 45 meters long by 12 meters wide and 8.5 meters deep. Commenting on the collapse, Jáuregui said the cause was a failure in the drainage system under the road.

SIAPA expects road repairs to last around two months due to the complexity and scale of the problem.

In separate incidents over the past month, Enrique Díaz de León Avenue collapsed in two places. The larger sinkhole spans roughly 17 meters long by 6 meters wide and 3 meters deep. This stretch of Enrique Díaz de León Avenue north of Camacho Avenue is closed while repairs are made.

Last week, yet another large sinkhole appeared on Manuel Ávila Camacho Avenue at the intersection of Jacarandas Street, just south of Zapopan Centro. A similar failure occurred last year about 100 meters from the current sinkhole, which measures 5 meters wide and 3 meters deep.

The northbound side of Camacho Avenue, heading toward the Arcos de Zapopan, is closed while SIAPA carries out repairs. If the weather cooperates, authorities expect to have the work finished by Oct. 2.

Cirque du Soleil performs in Guadalajara for two weeks in October

Cirque du Soleil returns to Guadalajara for its 20th season this month, performing its new show, “Echo,” over a two-week run.

The show features a young woman named Future and her dog, Ewai, as they embark on an exploratory journey. The set reportedly features a massive, enigmatic 23-foot cube on stage that is disassembled and rebuilt throughout the performance, symbolizing the delicate balance of our ecosystem.

Directed by Mukhtar Omar Sharif Mukhtar, “Echo” features plenty of the high-energy acrobatics and rich visuals the company is famous for, along with live music and vocal performances.

Dates: Oct. 8–25, 2026

Location: Gran Carpa Soleil, Plaza Patria, Guadalajara

Cost: Available at the on-site box office and through Ticketmaster.

Visit Leyenda de la Noche, a holiday horror theme park

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Leyendas de la noche (@leyendas_de_la_noche_)

This month, Guadalajara welcomes a new horror theme park inspired by beloved stories in Mexican pop culture.

Legends of the Night brings immersive experiences for all ages. The park will feature five themed houses, plus live shows, characters and an atmosphere designed to transport visitors into each magical setting.

While some houses deliver terror and surprises best suited to guests with nerves of steel, others promise more family-friendly fun.

Dates: Oct. 1–Nov. 2, 2026

Location: Calzada Independencia Norte 500, across from Parque Morelos in Guadalajara Center

Cost: On sale now from AKP Tickets

Make plans to enjoy Guadalajara’s Day of the Dead parade

One of the most anticipated and colorful events is back for its 20th anniversary edition in Guadalajara: the traditional Day of the Dead Parade.

This popular annual parade fills the streets with brilliant colors, traditional music, art and joyous dancing for an unforgettable day. Hundreds of participants embrace the celebration with skull-themed costumes and spooky makeup.

This year, the parade takes place Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, with the route beginning at the former Oblatos Penitentiary. It is open to the general public with participation by voluntary donation.

For more information, follow the event’s Instagram account.

Palenque de las Fiestas kicks off in Zapopan Oct. 2

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Palenque Fiestas Octubre (@palenquefiestasoct)

The Palenque de las Fiestas is a traditional concert arena and major annual music event held during Guadalajara’s famous month-long Fiestas de Octubre festival.

This year’s event, which takes place at the Benito Juárez Auditorium in northern Zapopan, includes top-tier Mexican acts performing banda, mariachi and pop music. Confirmed artists include Alejandro Fernández, Banda MS and Grupo Firme.

Below are the dates for several of the most anticipated performances:

Oct. 3–4: Jorge Medina & Josi Cuen

Oct. 9: Banda MS

Oct. 16–17: Alejandro Fernández

Oct. 25: Remmy Valenzuela

Oct. 29: Julión Álvarez

Oct. 31–Nov. 1: Grupo Firme

The full schedule can be viewed on the festival website.

For those considering attendance, this event retains some traditions — such as cockfighting — that many foreigners (as well as some locals) find offensive.

Dates: Oct. 2–Nov. 1, 2026

Location: Auditorio Benito Juárez complex in Zapopan

Cost: Available online from Mi Pase

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Polo will make landfall in Baja California Sur today. What you need to know
World.content:
Hurricane Polo is poised to make landfall this afternoon in Baja California Sur after moving across the Pacific as a major cyclone. Although it is expected to lose some strength before reaching the peninsula, authorities warn that it will remain a powerful hurricane, bringing the risk of destructive winds, torrential rains, flooding and dangerous surf.

At 9:45 a.m., Polo remained a Category 3 storm with maximum sustained winds of approximately 185 kilometers per hour and gusts of up to 220 kilometers per hour, the National Water Commission (Conagua) reported. The eye of the storm was located 140 km southwest of Santa Rosalía, moving northeastward.

Hurricane Polo is only a few hours away from possibly becoming the FIRST known Major Hurricane to make landfall on the western coast of Mexico’s Baja California peninsula. Usually, the ocean temps this far north are too lukewarm to sustain CAT 3+ intensity (which is why the… pic.twitter.com/KRGGogI4PA — Backpirch Weather (@BackpirchCrew) September 28, 2026

Forecasters expect it to make landfall in central Baja California Sur, and subsequently make a second landfall in Sonora before moving across the northwestern mainland, potentially affecting parts of Sinaloa and Chihuahua.

The state government suspended in-person school and work activities this Monday and Tuesday.

Beyond strong wind gusts, intense rainfall is expected in Baja California Sur. According to the U.S. National Hurricane Center, the state could see rainfall totals of between 100 and 200 millimeters, with isolated areas potentially receiving up to 250 millimeters.

Authorities have called on residents of affected areas to take extreme precautions, as this rainfall could trigger flash floods, surging streams, and landslides, particularly in rugged terrain, on rural roads, and in areas near watercourses.

Hurricane #Polo Advisory 32A (11 AM MST, Mon Sep 28): NOAA Hurricane Hunters Investigating Polo. Conditions Deteriorating Over Portions of Baja California as Life-Threatening Winds and Flash Floods Expected to Occur Soon. https://t.co/NyUGSIFCuo — NHC Pacific (@NHC_Pacific) September 28, 2026

Surf associated with Polo could also trigger rough seas, rip currents and potential coastal flooding. Authorities advise avoiding beaches, piers and jetties, as well as refraining from boating activities even if it does not appear to be raining or the system’s center is still far away.

The ports of Cabo San Lucas, San José del Cabo, San Carlos, Bahía Magdalena and Loreto have been closed to small craft, in addition to other maritime restrictions.

When and where is Polo expected to make landfall?

Head of the National Civil Protection Coordination Laura Velázquez said in a live broadcast during President Claudia Sheinbaum’s morning press conference that Polo is expected to make landfall in the municipality of Comondú between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. local time today. The cyclone will make a second landfall as a Category 1 hurricane on the central coast of Sonora late on Monday or early on Tuesday.

Velásquez called on residents to remain calm and to anticipate power and internet outages for a period that could extend through midnight.

Rachel intensifies into tropical storm off southeastern coast

Meanwhile, south of the country, Tropical Storm Rachel, which was moving 13 km/hr approximately 370 km south-southwest of Acapulco, Guerrero, at 8:27 this morning, is bringing winds of up to 95 kilometers per hour and heavy rains to Guerrero, Oaxaca and Michoacán.

Federal authorities activated prevention and surveillance zones for tropical storm winds from Punta San Telmo, Michoacán, to Cabo Corrientes, Jalisco. Rachel is currently traveling west-northwest and is not expected to make landfall.

With reports from La Jornada, CBS News, El Financiero and NMás

World.title: 2 UAEM prep school students killed in Cuernavaca, weeks after Spanish student’s femicide
World.content:
Just two weeks after the femicide of a Spanish exchange student in Morelos, two prep school students were shot dead in the state capital, Cuernavaca, on Saturday night.

After attending a birthday party in the Chula Vista neighborhood, a group of teenagers was reportedly gathered on the street when attackers on motorcycles approached. They fired indiscriminately into the crowd, killing two boys and seriously wounding another.

This brings to six the number of students murdered in Morelos this year, including Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, the 21-year-old Spaniard who was stabbed to death on Sept. 12.

Like Tacoronte, the other three victims — Kimberly Ramos Beltrán and Karol Gómez Toledo, killed in March, and Michelle Itzayana Fuentes, murdered in June — were all studying at the Autonomous University of the State of Morelos (UAEM).

The two boys killed on Saturday — identified as Gael and Christian, both 17 years old — were students of the UAEM-affiliated high school, the “Antonio L. Mora del Castillo” Preparatory School.

Upon hearing the gunshots, neighbors notified emergency services. Agents from the State Attorney General’s Office (FGEM) arrived soon thereafter and cordoned off the crime scene to collect ballistic evidence, while beginning an inquiry to determine the motive for the attack.

The UAEM issued a statement offering condolences to the families of the victims, decrying the violence and demanding justice, as well as greater assurances of security for the university community.

“Outrage is no longer enough,” it said. “We neither want to nor should we get used to a permanent state of mourning at the UAEM.”

On Sunday, UAEM students — joined by members of Somos (a new center-left political party) and dozens of local residents — staged a protest outside the FGEM headquarters demanding results and calling for greater transparency in the investigation of these murders, as well as unsolved disappearances of female students.

Attorney General Fernando Blumenkron Escobar responded by saying that some progress has been made, though critics say such progress has only occurred in cases where considerable public pressure has been generated, pointing to the quick arrest that occurred after Tacoronte’s murder.

The FGEM said it “will exhaust all lines of investigation” in its pursuit of justice.

With reports from El Financiero, CNN, La Jornada, Proceso and Tribuna de México

World.title: Sheinbaum announces new report on Ayotzinapa after 12th anniversary of mass kidnapping: Monday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🌀 Hurricane Polo nears Baja California Sur: Civil Protection chief Laura Velázquez said Polo, a Category 3 hurricane, is forecast to make landfall in Comondú between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m., “very probably” still at Category 3. She said that a “second impact” is forecast on the central coast of Sonora on Tuesday. She urged residents of Comondú, Mulegé and Loreto to stay in their homes or temporary shelters from 2 p.m. Monday. Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said “the three levels of government are together and ready” to respond to the hurricane.

Civil Protection chief Laura Velázquez said Polo, a Category 3 hurricane, is forecast to make landfall in Comondú between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m., “very probably” still at Category 3. She said that a “second impact” is forecast on the central coast of Sonora on Tuesday. She urged residents of Comondú, Mulegé and Loreto to stay in their homes or temporary shelters from 2 p.m. Monday. Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío said “the three levels of government are together and ready” to respond to the hurricane. 📈 1.2 million jobs created in a year: Labor Minister Marath Bolaños said the number of people in jobs reached 60.7 million at the end of August, up 1.2 million from a year earlier, while the economically active population rose 1.3 million to 62.6 million. He didn’t mention that 55% of employed people work in the informal sector, where workers typically don’t pay income tax or have access to benefits such as IMSS healthcare.

Labor Minister Marath Bolaños said the number of people in jobs reached 60.7 million at the end of August, up 1.2 million from a year earlier, while the economically active population rose 1.3 million to 62.6 million. He didn’t mention that 55% of employed people work in the informal sector, where workers typically don’t pay income tax or have access to benefits such as IMSS healthcare. 📑 New Ayotzinapa report due at 1 p.m.: Sheinbaum said Deputy Interior Minister Arturo Medina and special prosecutor Mauricio Pazarán will present new “lines of inquiry” in the 2014 case of the 43 missing students. She stressed the investigation is “not closed” and said the students’ parents have already been informed of the report’s contents.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Monday morning press conference as Hurricane Polo continued to move toward Baja California Sur ahead of its forecast landfall later on Monday.

National Civil Protection chief Laura Velázquez joined the mañanera by video link to provide an update on the hurricane, which strengthened to Category 5 level last week before weakening. The hurricane remains a dangerous storm mere hours before it is expected to slam into the Baja California Sur coast.

8 AM MST Mon Sep 28 (Advisory 32) Key Messages for Hurricane #Polo. Latest info: https://t.co/NyUGSIFCuo 8 AM MST lunes 28 de septiembre (Aviso 32) Mensajes clave sobre el huracán #Polo. Más información: https://t.co/NyUGSIFCuo pic.twitter.com/2JdqMvIH2P — NHC Pacific (@NHC_Pacific) September 28, 2026

Also of note at today’s mañanera was the presentation of new employment data and Sheinbaum’s comments on a new report on the 12-year-old investigation into the disappearance and presumed murder of 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers College. The students disappeared on Sept. 26, 2014, in Iguala, a city in the southern state of Guerrero.

Scores of people have been arrested in connection with the case, but no one has been convicted of the crime and some suspects have been released from prison. Among those who have been detained are soldiers, high-ranking members of the Mexican Army, police officers, members of the Guerreros Unidos crime gang and Jesús Murillo Karam, federal attorney general at the time of the students’ disappearance.

Just last month, former Guerrero Governor Ángel Heladio Aguirre Rivero was arrested in connection with the crime, which shocked Mexico and provoked widespread outrage during the presidency of Enrique Peña Nieto.

Hurricane Polo approaches Baja California Sur

At the start of her press conference, Sheinbaum noted that Hurricane Polo was on track to make landfall in Baja California Sur (BCS) on Monday afternoon before heading to Sonora.

Via video link from Ciudad Constitución in the BCS municipality of Comondú, Civil Protection chief Velázquez noted that Polo was a Category 3 hurricane. She said that the hurricane was forecast to make landfall in Comondú between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m., “very probably” as a Category 3 hurricane.

Velázquez said that the hurricane was forecast to make a “second impact” on the central coast of Sonora on Tuesday.

“Wind, rain and swells will continue intensifying in Baja California Sur and Sonora,” she said.

Velázquez called on residents of various communities in the municipalities of Comondú, Mulegé and Loreto to “remain attentive to all the recommendations that Civil Protection authorities make, and to remain in their homes or in temporary shelters from 2 p.m. today.”

Seated alongside Velázquez, Governor Víctor Manuel Castro Cosío thanked Sheinbaum as “federal forces” — the army, the navy and the National Guard — have been working with BCS authorities in recent days to prepare for the arrival of Hurricane Polo.

He said that the municipalities of Comondú, Loreto and Mulugé were forecast to bear the brunt of the hurricane.

“We’re here in Comondú … to take care of all the people who need support, finalizing the last details at the shelters. … We still have half a day to finalize anything that is needed here in Comondú, in Loreto and in Mulegé, where it is believed Hurricane Polo will be strongest,” Castro said.

“… We hope that this … [hurricane] causes as little damage as possible. The three levels of government are together and ready,” he said.

Mexico’s workforce increases by more than 1 million in the space of a year

Labor Minister Marath Bolaños noted that the National Employment Survey, conducted by the national statistics agency INEGI, found that Mexico’s “economically active population” — people either in jobs or looking for work — was 62.6 million people at the end of August, an increase of 1.3 million compared to a year earlier.

He also noted that the number of people in jobs was 60.7 million at the end of August, an increase of 1.2 million compared to a year earlier. In other words, 1.2 million jobs were created in Mexico in the 12 months to Aug. 31.

Bolaños didn’t note that 55% of people with jobs are employed in Mexico’s vast informal sector. Informal sector workers typically don’t pay income tax and don’t have access to employment benefits such as IMSS healthcare coverage and paid vacations.

New Ayotzinapa report to be presented on Monday

Sheinbaum noted that a new report on the disappearance and presumed murder of the 43 students in the state of Guerrero in 2014 will be presented at 1 p.m. Monday.

She said that the report — to be presented by Deputy Interior Minister Arturo Medina and Mauricio Pazarán, special prosecutor for the Ayotzinapa case — includes information on “lines of inquiry” developed from “new mechanisms” and “new investigation methodologies that hadn’t [previously] been used.”

Sheinbaum stressed that the investigation into the disappearance of the 43 students — a crime in which the Mexican Army is long thought to have been involved — is “not closed.”

She said that the parents of the students have already been informed of the contents of the new report.

The remains of just three of the students have been found and formally identified in the 12 years since they disappeared.

World.title: Colombia Kills Rebel Accused of Financing a Presidential Hopeful’s Murder
World.content:
