One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

COLOMBIA · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Colombia, about 53 million people, signed a peace deal with the FARC guerrillas in 2016. Several splinter groups never disarmed or later took up arms again.

— The background Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay, 39, a right-wing presidential hopeful, was shot at a campaign event in Bogotá on 7 June 2025 and died on 11 August. Prosecutors say the Segunda Marquetalia, a FARC splinter group, ordered the attack.

— Why now President Abelardo de la Espriella, in office since August, has put military offensives against armed groups at the centre of his government.

— What happened On Sunday 27 September 2026, an Army, police and air force operation in rural Tello, in the southern department of Huila, killed alias “Robinson Gutiérrez”. Three other group members were captured.

— Who is who Intelligence files cited by Colombian newspapers name him as Miguel Orlando Guzmán González, political and finance chief of one of the group’s regional units. The armed forces commander says he was accused of helping finance the senator’s murder.

— What it means for you The operation took place in the countryside of Huila, far from Bogotá, Medellín and the Caribbean coast. For investors, it is another sign the new government favours military pressure over talks with armed groups.

— Update, 28 September Army and armed forces communiqués confirm his death and list rifles, grenades and a grenade launcher seized. The three people captured remain unnamed.

— Still open No evidence for the financing allegation has been published, and no court has ruled on his role.

Colombian security forces have killed a guerrilla commander accused of helping to pay for the murder of a presidential hopeful. The Army has confirmed the death, which President Abelardo de la Espriella first announced as preliminary on Sunday 27 September.

The dead man, known as alias “Robinson Gutiérrez”, belonged to the Segunda Marquetalia, a splinter of the old FARC guerrilla army. Prosecutors say that group ordered the 2025 shooting of Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay in Bogotá.

What changed on 28 September

The Army and the armed forces general command confirmed on Sunday evening that alias Robinson Gutiérrez died in the operation. Their communiqués describe him as the unit’s political and financial chief, with about 35 years in armed groups.

Troops seized three rifles, two handguns, 13 grenades, 22 magazines, a grenade launcher and computer equipment, the Army says. It also accuses him of extortion, burning a vehicle and three kidnappings in Caquetá.

The Army calls him a financier of the senator’s murder. It has published no evidence, and no court has ruled on that claim.

What happened in Huila

The operation took place in the rural area of El Cadillo, in the municipality of Tello. Tello lies in Huila, a department in Colombia’s south-centre that borders the jungle region of Caquetá.

Troops from the Army’s Deployment Force Against Transnational Threats led the action, supported by the air force and the National Police. Three other members of the group were captured; their names have not been released.

De la Espriella announced it on X, saying the operation had taken place “a few minutes” earlier. “This criminal is implicated in the murder of Miguel Uribe Turbay,” he wrote. “I will not stop demanding that the whole truth about that crime be established.”

He added that the result was preliminary and that he would say more once verification was complete. The Army confirmed the death that evening.

Who Robinson Gutiérrez was

Intelligence files cited by the newspaper El Tiempo name him as Miguel Orlando Guzmán González. He was political and financial chief of the Teófilo Forero Castro unit, which operates in Huila and neighbouring Caquetá.

According to the same files, he had run the unit’s finances since 2024. The government accuses him of directing extortion and threats against farmers, recruiting minors and attacking civilians and security forces.

He faced an arrest warrant for criminal conspiracy aimed at murder and extortion. Some outlets called him a right-hand man of the group’s leader, but officials described him as a regional commander.

What officials allege about the senator’s murder

The claim is narrower than the headlines suggest. Nobody accuses him of pulling the trigger or giving the order.

General Erik Rodríguez Aparicio, the armed forces commander, said he was accused of “alleged participation in the financing” of the assassination. El Tiempo reported that his role lay in “the financing logistics”.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara went further, calling him “part of the criminal scheme that murdered Miguel Uribe”. No official has published the evidence behind either statement.

In March 2026 the Attorney General’s Office, which runs prosecutions, ordered seven group members arrested over the murder. His name was not on that list.

The group and the murder case

The Segunda Marquetalia was founded in 2019 by Luciano Marín Arango, alias Iván Márquez. He had been the FARC’s chief negotiator in the peace talks that ended in 2016, then returned to arms.

Uribe Turbay was a senator for the right-wing Centro Democrático party and grandson of former president Julio César Turbay. His mother, the journalist Diana Turbay, was killed in 1991 after being kidnapped by Pablo Escobar’s Medellín cartel.

A 15-year-old fired the shots at a rally in the Modelia district of Bogotá. He was sentenced to seven years in a youth detention centre.

Nine people have been arrested and four convicted, according to AFP. In March 2026 prosecutors said the order came from the group’s leadership, passed down through a commander known as “El Zarco Aldinever”.

Those March warrants also named Márquez himself. Investigators say the attack was planned in Venezuelan border areas, where the group’s leaders, Márquez included, have long taken refuge.

What comes next

The Army has now confirmed the death, but the three detainees are still unnamed. Whether they will be questioned about the murder is unknown.

The killing is part of a wider offensive. A week earlier, police killed a senior Caribbean armed-group commander near Santa Marta. The president has also said he signed 85 extraditions in six weeks.

On Sunday the president also reported 19 arrests and 907 kilograms of drugs seized nationwide in 24 hours. Five Clan del Golfo members were detained in Pueblo Viejo and Medellín.

On Friday night, 25 September, two explosives were thrown from a motorcycle at a security checkpoint in rural Jamundí, south of Cali. One went off, nobody was hurt, and officials provisionally blame a FARC dissident faction.

“To the narco-terrorists who attack our police in Ábrego and throw explosives in Jamundí: we are pursuing them,” De la Espriella wrote. “They will not impose terror in Colombia.”

It does not close the Uribe Turbay case. A death in a military operation is not a court finding, and the men prosecutors say gave the order are still wanted.

Nor is it the end of the Segunda Marquetalia. The group still has a leader, fighters and extortion income in Huila and Caquetá.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Miguel Uribe Turbay?

He was a 39-year-old Colombian senator for the right-wing Centro Democrático party who planned to run for president in 2026. He was shot at a rally in Bogotá on 7 June 2025 and died on 11 August 2025.

What is the Segunda Marquetalia?

It is an armed group founded in 2019 by former FARC commanders who rejected the 2016 peace deal, led by Iván Márquez. Colombian prosecutors say it ordered the attack on Uribe Turbay.

Was Robinson Gutiérrez the man who ordered the murder?

No. Officials say he allegedly helped finance it. Prosecutors say the order came from the group’s leadership, and no court has ruled on his role.

Is it safe to travel to Colombia?

The operation took place in rural Huila, away from the main tourist and business centres. Visitors should follow their government’s travel advice, which treats conflict areas in the countryside differently from the big cities.

World.title: Peru Says Troops Drove Back a Colombian Armed Group on Its Amazon Border
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Peru, a nation of about 34 million, shares a remote jungle border with Colombia. Much of it follows the Putumayo river, where Colombian armed groups tied to drug trafficking operate.

— Why it matters Peru has put its Putumayo province under a state of emergency. A joint military and police command there aims to tighten territorial control.

— What happened On Sunday 27 September the Defence Ministry said forces clashed with the Comandos de la Frontera near San Belín de Yaricaya. It said three fighters fell into a river.

— Who is involved The Comandos de la Frontera, which the ministry calls FARC dissidents formed in 2017. On Peru’s side, a joint command for the area known as CUPUMA.

— What it means for you Nothing changes for visits to Lima, Cusco or Iquitos. Anyone travelling near the Putumayo border should check official travel advice first.

— Still open When the clash took place, whether the three men in the river died, and whether any soldiers or police were hurt.

Peru’s soldiers and police clashed with a Colombian armed group on the country’s Amazon border, the Defence Ministry said on Sunday. According to the ministry, the fighters fled and three of them fell into a river.

The ministry named the group as the Comandos de la Frontera, dissidents from the FARC, Colombia’s former Marxist guerrilla army. Colombia’s El Heraldo, carrying the EFE news agency’s report, and Peru’s La República both relayed the official account.

What the Defence Ministry reported

A joint unit of soldiers and police, the Comando Unificado PUMA, carried out an operation code-named “Zancudo” (mosquito), the ministry said. After intelligence work, the unit located the group near the village of San Belín de Yaricaya, in the Teniente Manuel Clavero district.

The clash “forced the criminals to flee”, the ministry said, and three of them fell into the Yaricaya river. It said security conditions and the depth and current of the river made a search for the bodies impossible.

On the Amazon border, troops then recovered an M16 rifle with magazines, two pistols, a grenade and ammunition, according to the ministry. It also listed Colombian-style army uniforms, medicines and tools.

Who the Comandos de la Frontera are

The ministry said the group emerged in 2017 and operates along the borders of Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. It linked the group to drug trafficking and illegal mining.

La República reported that it began as an alliance of FARC dissidents and La Constru, a gang rooted in former right-wing paramilitaries. According to the paper, it controls coca-growing zones and moves cocaine towards Ecuador and Brazil.

Colombia extradited its reputed leader, alias Araña, to the United States on 25 September. The Rio Times covered that in Colombia Sends Armed-Group Boss From Peace Talks to Face US Drug Charges.

A border under pressure

El Heraldo noted that the operation followed a Peru–Colombia border commission meeting, Combifron, held in Lima from 21 to 25 September. Peru’s Joint Command of the Armed Forces said the two militaries signed agreements there to deepen border security cooperation.

Putumayo province, in the Loreto region, has been under a state of emergency that puts the armed forces in charge of order. The Defence Ministry announced a 60-day extension in June. In late July the government extended the emergency in Loreto’s border areas for a further 60 days from August, El Peruano and La República reported.

What Is Not Yet Known

The ministry did not say when the clash took place. Its statement mentions no casualties among soldiers or police.

Whether the three men who fell into the river died is unconfirmed, since no bodies were recovered. No account from residents or from the group itself had emerged by Monday.

It is also unclear whether the emergency, last extended in July, will be renewed again. Any link to the Combifron agreements is unstated.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened on Peru’s Amazon border?

The Defence Ministry said on 27 September that soldiers and police clashed with the Comandos de la Frontera near San Belín de Yaricaya, and three fighters fell into a river.

Who are the Comandos de la Frontera?

A group the ministry calls FARC dissidents formed in 2017, tied to drug trafficking on the Colombian border.

Is it safe to travel to Peru?

Nothing changes for visits to Lima, Cusco or Iquitos; anyone travelling near the Putumayo border should check official travel advice first.

What is CUPUMA?

The joint military and police command for the Putumayo area, where Peru has put the province under a state of emergency.

World.title: Dominican Republic: Police Killed at Least 37 People in September
World.content:

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic, a Caribbean nation of about 11 million people that shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti. It has no death penalty.

— Why it matters Deaths in what police call “exchanges of gunfire” have long been disputed by rights groups, who say many are executions.

— What happened Diario Libre counted at least 37 such deaths between 6 and 27 September, 23 of them between 18 and 25 September.

— Who is involved Police chief Ernesto Rodríguez García, in post since 17 August, told criminals on Sunday 27 September to surrender or stop offending.

— What it means for you The new chief’s first weeks are setting the tone of Dominican policing, and the state’s own ombudsman is already objecting.

— Still open Whether any of the September deaths will be independently investigated, and whether the government will respond.

Dominican police killings have surged this month. Diario Libre, a leading Santo Domingo daily, counted at least 37 people killed in September in incidents the National Police report as “exchanges of gunfire” with officers.

The count came a day after the new police chief warned criminals they had two paths: turn themselves in or stop offending. A leading rights group calls the deaths executions.

What the count shows

Diario Libre reported that 23 of the September deaths occurred between 18 and 25 September, the first on the sixth.

Santo Domingo province had the most deaths, with 11, followed by Santiago with six. The newspaper’s running tally since 5 January stands at 115, so September alone accounts for about a third of the year.

El Día, another national daily, reported eight such deaths in a single 24-hour stretch ending on Friday 25 September. Among them, police said, was a man they accused of shooting two officers.

The police chief’s warning

Major General Ernesto Rodríguez García took over the National Police in mid-August. He replaced Andrés Modesto Cruz Cruz, who was retired after six months in the job.

Addressing officers in the north-east on Sunday, he said offenders must choose to surrender or stop, “because otherwise we will come looking for you, no matter where you hide.” Both Diario Libre and Acento, a news site, reported the remarks.

He framed this as proportional use of force and promised to make offenders feel “the powerful arm of the state.” According to Diario Libre, police say those killed were wanted for crimes such as murder and robbery.

Ombudsman and rights groups object

The Ombudsman, Pablo Ulloa, a constitutional office that defends citizens against the state, said no one may be killed as a substitute for a court sentence. He noted the country has no death penalty.

Manuel María Mercedes, who heads the National Human Rights Commission, a non-governmental rights group, called the deaths a “massacre”, El Nuevo Diario reported. He said the group would take its complaint to international bodies.

The commission estimates about 4,500 such deaths between 2018 and 2025. That is its own figure, not an official record. Background: Dominican Republic Explained 2026 and Abinader Opens New Dominican Police Training Complex.

What Is Not Yet Known

How each of the September deaths happened. The accounts so far come from police statements, and El Día noted they still have to be tested by investigations.

Whether the government or prosecutors will open any independent review of the Dominican police killings.

The final September figure. Diario Libre’s count, last updated on Monday 28 September, runs only to 27 September.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people did Dominican police kill in September?

Diario Libre counted at least 37 deaths in what police call exchanges of gunfire between 6 and 27 September, 23 of them between 18 and 25 September.

What did the new police chief say?

Ernesto Rodríguez García, in post since 17 August, told criminals on 27 September to surrender or stop offending.

Why are the killings disputed?

Rights groups say many of the gunfights are executions, and the state’s own ombudsman is already objecting; the Dominican Republic has no death penalty.

Will the deaths be investigated?

That is open. No independent investigation of the September deaths has been announced.

Sources: Diario Libre, 28 September 2026; Diario Libre, 27 September 2026; Acento, 27 September 2026; El Nuevo Diario, 27 September 2026; El Día, 25 September 2026.

World.content:

GUATEMALA · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The country Guatemala, Central America’s most populous nation, where the Public Ministry (the national prosecution service) decides which crimes and which politicians get investigated.

— Why it matters The previous attorney general, Consuelo Porras, ran the service for eight years and was sanctioned by the United States and the European Union.

— What happened On Friday 25 September, Gabriel García Luna presented a report on his first four months in office, which began on 17 May.

— The numbers Con Criterio counts 225 removals or staff changes in an 88-page report. Prosecutors raided 13 properties in one case on 23 September.

— What it means for you The prosecution service says it will now target organised crime and corruption networks. For residents and investors, courtroom results are still to come.

— Still open No charges have been announced against Porras, and critics say officials from her era still hold key posts.

Four months into the job, Guatemala’s attorney general says he found a network loyal to his predecessor inside the prosecution service. Gabriel García Luna now confirms investigations into her, into a powerful former aide to ex-president Alejandro Giammattei, and into online “bot farms”.

He set out the findings on Friday 25 September in a report on his first four months, Infobae and Prensa Libre reported. The investigative outlet Con Criterio published its own assessment on Monday, with sharper criticism from a former anti-corruption prosecutor.

A clear-out at the top

García Luna took office on 17 May, replacing Consuelo Porras after President Bernardo Arévalo named him in early May. Porras had been sanctioned by Washington for alleged corruption, Prensa Libre noted.

Soy502 reported that he told journalists he had found “a structure” serving Porras in senior posts. “Some resigned and others were removed,” he said, without naming anyone.

According to Soy502, those gone include Rafael Curruchiche, head of the Special Prosecutor’s Office Against Impunity (FECI). That unit is now being audited before it is wound up, Infobae reported.

Porras, Martínez and the bot farms

García Luna confirmed that complaints against Porras are under investigation, Infobae and Con Criterio reported. One file, on alleged illegal adoptions during the civil war, sits with a special prosecutor.

He also said Miguel Martínez, a close associate of Giammattei, faces numerous complaints, mostly for money laundering. Prosecutors raided 13 properties linked to his family on Wednesday 23 September, Infobae reported.

La Hora and Con Criterio reported that the Public Ministry is investigating “netcenters”, anonymous account networks used to harass officials and journalists. García Luna called them “bot farms” and said some had originated inside the institution itself.

The critics’ view

Juan Francisco Sandoval, a former FECI head, told Con Criterio that “a prosecutorial career that was already destroyed cannot be protected”. He objected that a regional prosecutor who publicly praised Porras sat beside García Luna at the presentation.

Sandoval did call the plan to move staff out of idle municipal offices sensible. The report also promises fewer dismissed complaints, which Con Criterio says Porras used to dispose of up to 90 percent.

What Is Not Yet Known

The Public Ministry has not said how many complaints against Porras are active, what they allege, or whether she will be summoned. Infobae reported that no responsibilities have been established.

Guatemala’s attorney general has not said who ran the bot farms, or whether the Martínez case will lead to charges. García Luna admitted that leaks before raids were “evident” in some cases.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Guatemala’s new attorney general?

Gabriel García Luna, in office since 17 May; on 25 September he presented a report on his first four months.

What did he find in the prosecution service?

He says he found a network loyal to his predecessor Consuelo Porras; Con Criterio counts 225 removals or staff changes in his 88-page report.

Who is Consuelo Porras?

The previous attorney general, who ran the service for eight years and was sanctioned by the United States and the European Union; no charges have been announced against her.

What else is the new attorney general pursuing?

Probes into Porras, Martínez and bot farms; prosecutors raided 13 properties in one case on 23 September.

Sources: Con Criterio, 28 September 2026; Infobae, Infobae and Infobae, 25 September; Prensa Libre, 25 September; Soy502; La Hora, 25 September 2026.

World.title: Panama Election Bill Raises Donation Caps as Critics Warn of Dirty Money
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Get the brief

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

PANAMA · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country Panama uses the US dollar and elects its president, National Assembly and mayors together. The next general election is due in May 2029.

— Why it matters Bill 699 rewrites the electoral code. Lawmakers changed the Electoral Tribunal’s draft to allow bigger private donations and slower campaign reporting.

— What happened On Monday 28 September, anti-corruption campaigner Olga de Obaldía told TVN the changes lower accountability and “open the door” to organised-crime money.

— The numbers Caps for deputies of US$300,000 to US$500,000 per candidate. Parties would get 90 working days, not 30, to file certain campaign accounts.

— What it means for you Nothing changes yet. The bill still needs two full Assembly debates and the president’s signature.

— Still open Whether the full Assembly reverses the money changes in second debate, and when that debate starts.

Panama campaign finance rules are now the sharpest point of dispute in the country’s electoral reform. Transparency advocates and a former election judge say lawmakers raised donation caps while weakening the checks on that money.

The target is Bill 699, drafted by the Electoral Tribunal, Panama’s independent election authority. A National Assembly committee approved it in first debate last week by seven votes to two, after adding dozens of changes.

“Not only the amounts”

Olga de Obaldía heads the Foundation for the Development of Citizen Freedom, which belongs to the Transparency International movement. “It is not only raising the amounts, it is lowering the standard of accountability,” she told TVN on Monday.

Her biggest fear, she said, is “dirty money” from organised crime or corruption. She added that her foundation’s monitoring found candidates who have still not filed reports, and gaps between declared donations and spending.

What the committee changed

Deputies Benicio Robinson and Luis Eduardo Camacho proposed caps on private donations scaled by the number of voters. Candidates for deputy could raise US$300,000, US$400,000 or US$500,000, according to TVN and La Estrella de Panamá.

La Estrella calculated that the tiers allow up to US$17.4 million across Panama’s 43 circuits. A flat US$300,000 limit per circuit would have allowed US$12.9 million.

TVN, which obtained the approved text, reported that parties would get 90 working days after the election to file certain campaign accounts. The Tribunal’s draft allowed 30.

The Panamanian Association of Business Executives (Apede) also objects that the window to prosecute electoral crimes shrinks from the four years the Tribunal proposed to three. La Prensa reported that election-period immunity from prosecution stays in place for all party leaders.

A former judge’s warning

Guillermo Márquez Amado, an Electoral Tribunal judge from 1990 to 1996, told La Estrella there was no justification for the increase. He called it a sign of the “greed” of career politicians.

Public or private money matters less than how it is policed, he argued. He also criticised the Electoral Prosecutor’s Office, which investigates election crimes, as too passive.

The committee vote followed a business backlash reported earlier in Panama Business Chamber Urges Lawmakers to Rethink a Rushed Election Bill.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is unclear whether the full Assembly will keep the Panama campaign finance changes, including higher caps and longer reporting deadlines. TVN and La Estrella said the second debate could begin this week, but by Monday afternoon there was no report that it had started.

The Panamenista Party plans a minority report asking to send the bill back to committee, La Estrella reported. Whether the Tribunal will challenge any article in the Supreme Court is also open.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Panama’s Bill 699 change?

It rewrites the electoral code, raising deputy-candidate donation caps from US$300,000 to US$500,000 and giving parties 90 working days, not 30, to file certain campaign accounts.

Why do critics object?

Anti-corruption campaigner Olga de Obaldía told TVN on 28 September the changes lower accountability and open the door to organised-crime money.

Is the reform law yet?

No. It still needs two full Assembly debates and the president’s signature.

When is Panama’s next election?

May 2029, when the president, National Assembly and mayors are elected together.

World.content:

BOLIVIA · TRANSPORT

Key Facts — The country Bolivia is a landlocked Andean country where the state long kept fuel cheap. President Rodrigo Paz ended the diesel subsidy this month.

— Why it matters Diesel moves many of Bolivia’s buses and lorries. Decree 5716 put its price at Bs17.95 a litre (about US$1.49 at the central bank’s official rate of Bs12.05), and drivers want it repealed.

— What happened On Monday 28 September a 24-hour national vehicle pullback emptied the streets of Santa Cruz. La Paz, El Alto and Cochabamba kept largely running.

— Who is involved The national drivers’ union, led by Lucio Gómez; Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano; and Public Works Minister Mauricio Zamora, who called talks for Tuesday.

— What it means for you Monday’s stoppage hit Santa Cruz and Sucre hardest. Cochabamba’s transport cooperatives have announced their own 24-hour stoppage for Tuesday unless the government calls them to talks.

— Still open Whether Tuesday’s talks in La Paz end the dispute, and whether it merges with Evo Morales’s call for protests from 13 October.

The Bolivia transport strike over dearer diesel split the country on Monday. Santa Cruz, the largest city, was left almost without buses, while La Paz and Cochabamba largely kept moving.

The Confederación Sindical de Choferes, the national drivers’ union, called the 24-hour pullback against Decree 5716, which ended the diesel subsidy. Its leaders now take their demand for repeal to ministers on Tuesday.

Where buses stopped, and where they ran

The Cochabamba daily Los Tiempos reported that drivers in four departments joined or ratified the pullback: Santa Cruz, Chuquisaca, Potosí and Oruro. The Santa Cruz daily El Deber reported a full withdrawal in Santa Cruz.

In La Paz and El Alto, minibuses and shared taxis ran normally, the Cochabamba daily Opinión reported. There was no service, however, from La Paz to the Yungas valleys or the north.

The news agency ANF and the broadcaster Unitel reported that only Santa Cruz fully observed the Bolivia transport strike.

Defence Minister Ernesto Justiniano said the pullback was concentrated in Santa Cruz and Sucre, according to the state news agency ABI and the news site Oxígeno.

Classes moved home in Santa Cruz

Nelson Alcócer, head of Santa Cruz’s departmental education office, ordered distance classes for Monday, Unitel reported. More than 90 percent of pupils in public schools depend on public transport, the broadcaster said.

Private schools objected, but Alcócer called it mandatory. El Deber also reported distance classes.

Talks on Tuesday, and a threat from Cochabamba

Public Works Minister Mauricio Zamora has called the drivers to talks in La Paz at 9 a.m. on Tuesday 29 September. Three more ministers are due to attend, El Deber and Los Tiempos reported.

Lucio Gómez, the union’s executive secretary, told the news site Urgente.bo that it would attend and demand “directly the repeal of 5716.” El Deber quoted him promising no road blockades.

In Cochabamba, the transport cooperatives’ federation FECOTRAC announced a 24-hour strike for Tuesday if the government did not call it to talks on Monday, Unitel reported. Its president, Orlando López, warned of longer stoppages, up to an indefinite one, as ANF also reported.

Separately, former president Evo Morales has given the government until 3 October to repeal the decree, threatening protests from 13 October, Infobae reported.

Justiniano replied that nobody “is above the law”, however many people they can mobilise.

What Is Not Yet Known

Whether Tuesday’s talks bring a deal or only a pause. The drivers want full repeal, while the government points to conversion of vehicles to natural gas and credit for new ones, Oxígeno reported.

How widely Monday’s strike was observed is disputed: the government names two cities, local papers up to four departments.

It is also unknown whether Cochabamba stops on Tuesday, and whether the drivers and Morales’s supporters end up on the same streets after 3 October.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Bolivian transport drivers striking?

They want Decree 5716 repealed; it set diesel at Bs17.95 a litre after President Rodrigo Paz ended the subsidy this month.

Which cities did the strike stop?

Monday’s 24-hour pullback emptied the streets of Santa Cruz and hit Sucre; La Paz, El Alto and Cochabamba largely kept running.

What happens on Tuesday?

Public Works Minister Mauricio Zamora called talks in La Paz; Cochabamba’s transport cooperatives threaten their own 24-hour stoppage unless invited.

Who leads the drivers?

The national drivers’ union, led by Lucio Gómez.

Sources: Los Tiempos; El Deber; Opinión; ANF; ABI; Oxígeno; Unitel (schools); Unitel (Cochabamba); Urgente.bo; Infobae. All 27–28 September 2026.

World.title: Mexico to Present New Report on 43 Missing Students as Families Voice Doubt
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

MEXICO · HUMAN RIGHTS

Key Facts — The country Mexico. On 26 September 2014, 43 trainee teachers from a rural college in Ayotzinapa, Guerrero state, disappeared in the city of Iguala.

— Why it matters It is Mexico’s best-known human-rights case. Twelve years on, the remains of only three students have been identified and, according to AP, nobody has been convicted.

— What happened The government scheduled a new report for 1pm on Monday 28 September. It had been due on Friday 25 September.

— Who is involved Human-rights under-secretary Arturo Medina and special prosecutor Mauricio Pazarán are due to present it. The families were not invited.

— What it means for you A test of President Claudia Sheinbaum’s promise to solve the case. It also shapes how far Mexico’s army can be held to account.

— Still open Where the students are, and whether the army will hand over more than 800 intelligence files a court ordered released.

Mexico’s government is due to present a new Ayotzinapa report on Monday afternoon, twelve years after 43 students vanished in the southern state of Guerrero. The families say they expect little from it.

President Claudia Sheinbaum said at her morning press conference that the report would be released at 1pm, Infobae reported. She added that it will contain nothing the parents have not already been told.

What the government says it will show

The report will be presented by Arturo Medina, under-secretary for human rights at the Interior Ministry, and by special prosecutor Mauricio Pazarán. Both El Universal and Infobae confirmed the pair.

According to El Universal, Sheinbaum said it will cover searches, new arrests and new lines of inquiry. These include tracking the phones used on the night of the attack and afterwards.

Sheinbaum stressed that the investigation stays open, Infobae reported.

The most prominent recent arrest is that of Ángel Aguirre, Guerrero’s governor in 2014. El Financiero, citing federal prosecutors, reported in August that a judge ordered him to stand trial for forced disappearance and obstruction of justice, over allegedly hidden video footage.

Why the families are sceptical

“Tell us the truth, but with proof,” parents told Proceso in Iguala on Sunday. La Silla Rota quoted one father as saying the previewed findings had already been shared, “unless they surprise us.”

At Saturday’s march in Mexico City, La Razón and La Silla Rota reported, families made two demands. The army should release more than 800 intelligence files, and the independent expert group known as GIEI should return.

Amnesty International, cited by El Financiero, puts the files at 853 and says a court ordered their release. Sheinbaum replied that “the GIEI no longer exists,” Infobae reported, adding that the UN human-rights office is choosing other experts.

Background is in our profile of Claudia Sheinbaum and our report on how Mexico replaced its prosecutor general.

What Is Not Yet Known

The content of the Ayotzinapa report was not public at the time of writing. It is unclear whether it names new suspects or new search sites.

It is also unknown whether the army will hand over the disputed files. The families’ lawyer told El Financiero that the defence ministry has challenged the court order.

Which outside experts will join the case, and when, has not been announced. Sheinbaum said Medina would take further questions at Tuesday’s press conference.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Ayotzinapa?

On 26 September 2014, 43 students from the rural teacher-training college at Ayotzinapa were attacked and taken in Iguala, Guerrero. Only three have been identified from remains.

Who is presenting the new Ayotzinapa report?

Arturo Medina, the Interior Ministry’s under-secretary for human rights, and Mauricio Pazarán, the special prosecutor for the case. The families were not invited to the presentation.

What are the families demanding?

They want to know where the students are. They also want the army to release more than 800 intelligence files and the independent GIEI experts to return.

Why are the families sceptical of the new report?

They were not invited to the presentation and expect little from it, twelve years after the disappearance and with, according to AP, nobody convicted.

HONDURAS · PUBLIC CONTRACTS

Key Facts — The country Honduras, in Central America, is regularly hit by hurricanes, floods and drought, so fast public warnings can save lives.

— Why it matters A new state system that pushes emergency alerts to mobile phones was tested on Thursday 24 September. Who built it now raises questions.

— What happened On 28 September Criterio.hn reported that the 49.8 million lempira (about US$1.9 million) contract, signed on 11 September 2025, went to the ITG-HTECSA consortium.

— Who is involved Criterio.hn and Contracorriente say lead firm ITG shares shareholders with Sistemas Abiertos, a company at the centre of a social security fraud. ITG has not been convicted.

— What it means for you Phones in Honduras may sound further test alerts; iPhone tests are next. The warnings work; the dispute is over how the contract was awarded.

The new Honduras alert system sends emergency warnings to mobile phones, and Android users got a test on Thursday 24 September. On Monday the investigative outlet Criterio.hn reported who built it, and the answer revives an old scandal.

What the contract covers

Criterio.hn reviewed contract DIGER-AGEHRED-047-2025, signed on 11 September 2025 by the Directorate for Management by Results (DIGER). DIGER is the government office that runs several state digital projects.

The deal was meant to last four months. Three amendments, the last approved by Congress as Legislative Decree 125-2026, extended it to 10 July 2026, both outlets report.

The Honduras alert system sends location-based warnings through the Tigo and Claro mobile networks. Conatel, the telecoms regulator, says the 911 emergency service will test iPhones next, La Prensa reported.

The link to the social security fraud

The Honduran Social Security Institute (IHSS), the workers’ health insurer, lost around 7 billion lempiras (about US$260 million) in 2010–2015, Criterio.hn says. Sistemas Abiertos held a US$35.4 million hospital-software contract there, later raised to US$43.9 million, Contracorriente reports.

The outlet says the state audit court (TSC) ordered Sistemas Abiertos to repay US$21 million, including guarantees, for overpricing and failures. It cites the National Anti-Corruption Council (CNA), a civil-society watchdog, as finding that ITG took over Sistemas Abiertos’ business in 2016.

ITG has not been convicted in the social security case, Contracorriente notes. Criterio.hn said DIGER’s director, Elmer Ferrera, had not replied to its questions.

A contract that spans two governments

Castro’s left-wing Libre party awarded the deal. President Nasry Asfura of the National Party, in office since January, oversaw the tests (see Honduras Explained 2026: The Country, Its Politics, Its Economy and What to Watch).

Former Castro officials, including Miroslava Cerpas, who headed the board running the 911 service, claim credit for the project online, Criterio.hn reported. Former deputy human rights minister Longino Becerra said the phone companies delayed the launch because elections were near.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is unclear whether prosecutors, the audit court or Congress will examine how the consortium won tender CPI-DIGER-CF-001-2025. Contracorriente says the tender file is missing from DIGER’s transparency pages and from Honducompras, the state procurement portal.

It is also unknown how much has been paid and whether the system is fully delivered. No date has been given for the iPhone tests.

Background: Auto Draft.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Honduras’ new phone alert system?

A state system that pushes emergency alerts to mobile phones, tested on 24 September; the contract is worth 49.8 million lempira (about US$1.9 million).

What is the scandal link?

Criterio.hn and Contracorriente say lead contractor ITG shares shareholders with Sistemas Abiertos, a company at the centre of a social security fraud; ITG has not been convicted.

When was the contract signed?

On 11 September 2025, so it spans two governments.

Does the alert system work?

Yes. The warnings work and further tests are planned, including for iPhones; the dispute is over how the contract was awarded.

Sources: Criterio.hn, 28 September 2026; Contracorriente, 14 September 2026; Criterio.hn, December 2024; La Prensa; El Heraldo.
