These documents record changes that have already occurred: a 1.1°C rise in temperature, declining water resources, longer droughts, fewer frost days in the mountains, melting glaciers and a falling Caspian Sea level.

Moreover, Azerbaijan’s NDC 3.0 document, which remains in force in 2026, describes a situation very different from the one the president presented in his speech: Azerbaijan “is seriously affected by the climate crisis”.

Climate change in Azerbaijan

World.title: “Saturday march” in Tbilisi: “Abkhazia is Georgia” and solidarity with Ukraine. Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Baku outraged by Georgian Patriarchate’s “unacceptable” remarks over church in Azerbaijan’s Gakh district
World.content:
Kurmukh Church, Azerbaijan-Georgia

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry has protested against a statement by the Georgian Patriarchate regarding the restoration of a church in Azerbaijan’s Gakh district.

The Patriarchate said the Church of St George, known as the Kurmukh Church, is an important monument of Georgia’s spiritual and cultural heritage. It expressed outrage that restoration work was being carried out without coordination with Tbilisi and without official information from Baku.

The Patriarchate also said the church is located in the “historical [Georgian region of] Hereti”.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said the Patriarchate’s statement regarding the church, known in Azerbaijan as Kurmuk, amounted to a territorial claim against Azerbaijan.

What happened

In a statement published on 24 September, the Georgian Patriarchate expressed concern over ongoing work at the Kurmukh Church and the surrounding area, noting that although the church is currently located in Azerbaijan, it is an important monument of Georgia’s historical and spiritual heritage and of the Georgian Orthodox Church.

“Any interventions carried out both in the church itself, in historic Hereti, and in the surrounding area are of particular concern to the Georgian Orthodox Church. Many questions arise due to both the unclear purpose of the work and the restoration of a monument of Georgian cultural heritage without the consent of the Georgian side,” the statement said.

According to the Patriarchate, it has not received any official information from the relevant Azerbaijani state authorities about the ongoing work at the Kurmukh Church.

The church believes that the relevant Georgian state authorities should be involved in the process and determine what work is being carried out at the church, what research it is based on and who is conducting it.

The Patriarchate also called for its representatives and Georgian specialists to be included in the discussions.

“Only timely and coordinated cooperation can ensure the proper protection and preservation of this monument of Georgian spiritual and cultural heritage,” the Georgian Patriarchate said.

What Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry says

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said that the Georgian Patriarchate’s statement regarding the church, known in Azerbaijan as Kurmuk, amounted to a territorial claim against Azerbaijan.

“Azerbaijan has always respected the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Georgia. At the same time, the Georgian side’s demonstration of the same respect for the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Azerbaijan constitutes an important foundation of the strategic partnership relations established between the two countries. […]

In this regard, repetition of the the known approaches of the Armenian Church or following its path is not recommended. […] All historical, cultural and religious monuments located in the territory of Azerbaijan constitute an integral part of the national heritage of the Azerbaijani people and the Azerbaijani state,” the ministry said.

The statement also said it was “unacceptable to refer to geographical and historical toponyms located in the territory of Azerbaijan by other names.”

“It is important that religious institutions refrain from approaches that could undermine the historical bonds of friendship and good-neighbourhood that have developed between the peoples of Azerbaijan and Georgia over the centuries,” Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said.

News in Azerbaijan

News in Georgia

World.title: ‘Unresolved issues and conflicting narratives remain’ — Pashinyan on relations with Azerbaijan
World.content:
Pashinyan’s UN address

In his address to the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan spoke about the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established. At the same time, he addressed outstanding issues that the two countries still need to resolve. These include determining the fate of several thousand missing people, carrying out demining operations and securing the return of Armenians, whom Azerbaijan holds in its prisons.

Pashinyan stressed that, beyond these issues of concern to Armenian society, conflicting narratives and discourses among certain circles in Armenia and Azerbaijan also fuel pessimism. Sometimes, officials themselves voice these views.

“I think that we, meaning Armenia and Azerbaijan, have achieved more than satisfactory results. These should mean more to us than the use of conflicting narratives, whether about history, cultural monuments or anything else,” he said.

In effect, the prime minister was responding to a recent visit by diplomats to Karabakh, which Azerbaijani authorities had organised. During the visit, officials attempted to present the Armenian monasteries of Gandzasar and Dadivank as part of “ancient Albanian Christian heritage”.

The move sparked such public outrage that many politicians called on Armenia’s leadership to issue a strong official response. Tensions between Armenia and Azerbaijan rose against this backdrop. Politicians described the situation as a serious crisis that could hinder further progress in the peace process.

Against this backdrop, Pashinyan stressed that Armenia and Azerbaijan must now focus on “safeguarding peace, strengthening it and developing its institutions”.

In his address, Pashinyan also touched on other issues of current importance to Armenia, including the implementation of the Armenian-American “Trump Route” project (TRIPP), relations with the European Union and Russia, as well as the normalisation of relations between Armenia and Turkey.

“The main item on the Yerevan-Baku agenda is signing a peace agreement”

The Armenian prime minister placed particular emphasis on the fact that no one has been killed or injured in border shootings between Armenia and Azerbaijan for the past two and a half years. He described this as “the greatest achievement of cooperation in recent years”.

“Never before have independent Armenia and independent Azerbaijan experienced such a period, despite centuries of peaceful coexistence between Armenians and Azerbaijanis,” Pashinyan said.

In his view, Yerevan and Baku must build relations between the two states on the basis of this shared experience, respecting each other’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and political independence. This is particularly important given that the two countries have already agreed on these principles and even initialled a peace treaty.

“Signing and ratifying this agreement is the next important item on Armenia and Azerbaijan’s joint agenda. We will continue to work consistently towards this goal,”

“The implementation of TRIPP promises major benefits for all countries in the region”

Pashinyan believes that the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan has opened up new opportunities for the entire region. He said the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP) project would play an important role in this process. He assured his audience that its implementation was “becoming a reality” and would mark a historic milestone for Armenia:

“For the first time since the early 1990s, Armenia will have a railway link with Azerbaijan. This will also connect it to Russia, Central Asia and China.”

The “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) is a transport route that will connect Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory.

The prime minister stressed that Azerbaijan had opened transit routes for Armenia and that rail services between Armenia and Azerbaijan had resumed via Georgia. However, he said, the implementation of TRIPP would establish a direct railway link between Armenia and Azerbaijan:

“In the near future, we will restore the railway sections in Meghri and Yeraskh in Armenia, which existed during the Soviet era but were later destroyed. The railway routes I mentioned will then reopen.”

He said Armenia also expected to restore railway links with Turkey. Alongside TRIPP, he described this as a potential milestone in international logistics, one of the most significant developments in decades:

“This will open up a new railway connection between China, Central Asia, Turkey and the European Union.”

Pashinyan says restoring the railway link between Armenia and Azerbaijan (Nakhchivan) will establish a rail connection between the Persian Gulf and the Black Sea:

“This is an important detail because it shows why and how the implementation of TRIPP promises enormous benefits for all countries in the region. These potential benefits could become a cornerstone of long-term stability and peace, particularly between Armenia and Azerbaijan.”

According to Pashinyan, building pipelines, power lines and roads as part of TRIPP would allow not only Armenia but the entire South Caucasus to become a “crossroads of peace”.

“A plan to seize the state was drawn up”: on elections in Armenia

The prime minister also spoke about the circumstances surrounding Armenia’s recent parliamentary elections. For the second time or more, he openly accused foreign actors of interference:

“Several external and internal forces devised and carried out a plan to seize the state. They used mass disinformation, hybrid and other tools, as well as widespread distribution of election bribes.”

He stressed that Armenia’s state institutions had prevented the seizure of power thanks to their resilience. Pashinyan believes this, in turn, reflects the democratic and institutional reforms that the country has carried out in recent years:

“The people of Armenia voted for peace. And we must consistently work to further strengthen and institutionalise peace.”

Ties with the EU deepen as relations with Russia undergo transformation

Pashinyan also spoke about Armenia’s balanced foreign policy. The prime minister noted that in recent years, his government had established strategic relations with Georgia, France, China, the Netherlands, Kazakhstan, Germany, Luxembourg, the United Kingdom, Bulgaria, Croatia, Lithuania, the United States and the European Union.

“The European Commission has approved a decision to introduce autonomous trade measures for Armenia, marking another sign of the new quality of relations between Armenia and the EU,” he stressed.

Relations between Yerevan and Moscow, meanwhile, are undergoing a transformation, according to the prime minister.

In his view, this is a natural process because the Armenian-Azerbaijani conflict had been the main factor shaping Armenia’s relations with Russia throughout the preceding period. The establishment of peace has fundamentally changed the situation.

“We want our relations with Russia to develop on the principles of friendship and mutual respect,” he said.

Relations with neighbouring countries

Nikol Pashinyan noted that normalising and deepening relations with neighbouring countries is crucial for Armenia:

“We have established high-level dialogue with Turkey. I want to reaffirm President Erdoğan’s remarks from this podium a few days ago. We are firmly advancing the process of normalising Armenian-Turkish relations.”

Good-neighbourly relations with Iran and Georgia are also continuing to develop and deepen. Moreover, the prime minister said, these relations are of “exceptional importance” to Yerevan.

Pashinyan’s UN address

World.title: Сost of childhood: why Azerbaijan has no universal child benefit
World.content:
Child benefits in Azerbaijan

AI-generated illustration. Meydan TV

Azerbaijan has no monthly child benefit paid for every child regardless of their family’s income. For nearly 20 years, the government has followed a different model: it provides support to low-income families and specific social groups instead of making universal payments.

Against a backdrop of persistently falling birth rates, the debate over so-called “child benefits” has returned to the public agenda. The discussion is no longer just about where to find the money. Other questions have also come to the fore: how much a universal child benefit would cost the state budget, how much it would actually help families, and what the long-term social cost of refusing such support might be.

In May 2026, a statement by Gunay Agamali, a member of Azerbaijan’s parliament, sparked a new wave of debate. Speaking on ARB TV, she said that child benefits could make parents “dependent and lazy”. In her view, such payments could reduce some people’s willingness to work.

However, the issue of child benefits is far from new in Azerbaijan. It returns to the public agenda almost every year, and the same questions arise each time. Should the state pay benefits for every child or only for families that genuinely need support? Can the state budget afford such payments? And could child benefits reverse the decline in birth rates?

To answer these questions, it is worth first examining how the current system came about. Read the full article by Meydan TV.

What changed in 2006?

Monthly payments commonly referred to as “child benefits” existed in Azerbaijan before 2006. However, contrary to a widespread misconception, they were not universal either.

● Social assistance is shrinking in Azerbaijan: Is poverty falling, or are low-income people losing support?

● Birth rates decline year by year in Azerbaijan

● Child allowance in Azerbaijan: why is it not paid?

Under the rules in force at the time, families with an average monthly income of less than 16,500 old manats per person (around $3.4–3.5 or €2.7–2.8 at the 2004–2005 exchange rates) received a monthly payment of 9,000 old manats per child (around $1.8–1.9 or €1.5). Payments continued from birth until the child turned 16. For schoolchildren who did not receive a scholarship, payments could continue until the age of 18. Following the redenomination, this amount was equivalent to 1 manat and 80 qəpiks.

In other words, the previous system also took family income into account.

A new phase in Azerbaijan’s social protection system began on 1 January 2006, when the Law on Targeted State Social Assistance came into force. The Law on Social Benefits also took effect on the same date. The new system did not retain a separate child benefit linked to family income.

The government therefore effectively changed its entire approach. Instead of providing a separate payment for each child, it made targeted assistance the main form of social support, with eligibility determined by family income.

In a 2009 interview with Radio Azadliq, Babek Huseynov, a representative of the Ministry of Labour and Social Protection of the Population, said the authorities considered the new system more effective. The previous child benefit, he said, had “lost its economic rationale”. He explained that under the targeted assistance system, payments are calculated based on the difference between a family’s total income and the eligibility threshold.

The same principle remains: assistance for those in need, not everyone

In the following years, the government introduced new types of benefits for children and families and changed payment amounts. However, the underlying principle remained the same: Azerbaijan has no universal benefit paid for every child.

In 2022, Labour and Social Protection Minister Sahil Babayev stated this position explicitly while addressing parliament. According to him, around 600,000 children from socially vulnerable groups receive support through various mechanisms, and social assistance should be targeted rather than universal.

The system in place in 2026 follows the same principle.

Lawyer Fariz Namazly explains:

“We have various benefits for children. Most are designed for socially vulnerable families. There are also one-off payments, such as the benefit paid when a child is born. Low-income families with children under one receive financial assistance, as do parents caring for children under three. Women with more than five children are also eligible for benefits. Separate social payments are available for children with disabilities, children who have lost one of their parents, and other categories.”

Families currently receive a one-off payment of 600 manats (around $353 or €305) when a child is born. Low-income families with children under one receive 140 manats (around $82 or €71) per month. Women with more than five children receive 140 manats (around $82 or €71) per month for each child. The childcare benefit for children under three amounts to 44 manats (around $26 or €22) or 28 manats (around $16 or €14), depending on the child’s age.

In addition, separate payments are available for children with disabilities, those who have lost a breadwinner, children without parental care, and other social categories.

The issue, therefore, is not whether the state provides financial support to families with children at all. Such support already exists.

The main question is who is eligible for it.

Universal child benefits or targeted assistance?

Under a universal system, family income does not matter: if a child meets the eligibility criteria, the family receives a payment.

Under a targeted system, the government first assesses a family’s income, assets and social circumstances before deciding whether it needs assistance.

Fariz Namazly believes both models have advantages and disadvantages:

“There are currently proposals to introduce a universal child benefit — that is, to pay it to all children regardless of family income. Such a system is more transparent. Families would not have to declare their income, the process would be much simpler, and there would be no need to check their financial circumstances. All children would be treated equally.

But this would place a significantly greater burden on the budget. Wealthier families would also receive the benefit. If payments are limited to low-income families, public spending is lower, and the money goes to those who need it most. The problem is that determining a family’s actual income can be difficult, creating opportunities for abuse. Such cases have also occurred in the allocation of targeted social assistance: people have tried to formally give up their jobs or even arrange sham divorces to meet the eligibility criteria.”

The new Law on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 2026, explicitly enshrines a child’s right to social security. Under Article 24 of the law, every child has the right to material support at least equal to the subsistence minimum established by law. The same article states that the government provides social assistance to certain categories of citizens to protect children.

In 2026, the subsistence minimum for a child is 260 manats (around $153 or €132).

However, this provision does not in itself mean that the state is obliged to pay every child 260 manats in cash each month. It establishes a general right to material support, while direct social payments remain available only to specific categories.

Can child benefits make parents “lazy”?

It was against this backdrop that Gunay Agamali argued that parents should not expect financial assistance from the state when deciding to have a child, and that such benefits could supposedly foster dependency.

This argument shifts the debate away from social policy and towards the behaviour of parents themselves.

Yet Azerbaijan’s existing system already provides direct payments to families with children. The debate is therefore not about whether the state should support families financially at all, but whether payments should cover all children or only specific groups.

Earlier, Aygun Gumbatova, the wife of imprisoned opposition activist Agil Gumbatov, called for the introduction of child benefits. She cited her family’s difficult financial circumstances as the reason for her position.

“We have found ourselves in a difficult financial situation. My husband was arrested on false charges. He was the family’s sole breadwinner. Now I am left with three school-age children,” Gumbatova told a Caucasian Knot correspondent.

Her eldest child has autism and requires constant care, making it impossible for Gumbatova to work. According to her, the family’s only stable source of income is the 320-manat disability pension (around $188 or €162) paid for her child’s second-group disability status.

At the same time, supporting a universal child benefit does not necessarily mean that its proponents see it as a solution to all social and demographic problems.

Natig Jafarli, an economist and chairman of the REAL Party, believes the issue is too easily exploited for populist purposes:

“This is a very sensitive issue, and it is extremely convenient for populism. People who do not bear political responsibility can use it simply to score political points. Such promises easily resonate with the public. For example, someone comes out and says: let’s pay 500 manats [around $294 or €253] for every child. Someone with two or three children at home will naturally think: ‘Great, that’s 1,000–1,500 manats’ [around $588–882 or €507–760].”

“That is precisely why the issue often fails to become the subject of serious discussion. It would be far more useful to sit down with government representatives, examine the budget’s capabilities and do the calculations: how much the state can afford, in what form, and under which model such payments could be introduced.

Sometimes populism goes so far that child benefits are presented as almost a solution to every problem. That is also wrong and misleads people. Azerbaijan already faces demographic problems, and the birth rate is falling. But claiming that simply introducing child benefits tomorrow would immediately reverse the situation is also populism. We can see this in European countries. In Poland, for example, families receive 800 zlotys [around $214 or €185] per child — a fairly substantial amount. Yet the demographic situation continues to deteriorate, and the fertility rate has fallen from 1.7 to 1.4.”

According to the World Bank, Azerbaijan’s total fertility rate was 1.7 children per woman in 2020, falling to 1.4 by 2024. The downward trend has continued in more recent statistics. According to Azerbaijan’s State Statistical Committee, 40,798 children were born in the country between January and June 2026. The number of births per 1,000 residents fell from 9.0 in the same period of 2025 to 8.0.

Can the budget afford a universal child benefit?

One of the main arguments against universal payments is their cost.

Natig Jafarli believes that child benefits are economically feasible in Azerbaijan, but that they do not necessarily have to be introduced for all children at once. In his view, the system could be rolled out in stages.

“If the aim is to reverse the demographic situation through child benefits, a benefit alone will not be enough. But from an economic perspective, such payments are possible. We simply need to determine the amount and the stages.

Several years ago, we proposed starting from the assumption that Azerbaijan has around 2.7 million children aged 0 to 18, and approximately 920,000 of them are second-born children in their families. If it is impossible to cover all children under 18 immediately, the programme could at least start with second and subsequent children. If we paid around 100 manats [around $59 or €51] per child, the first stage would require about 1 billion manats a year [around $588 million or €507 million]. That is an amount Azerbaijan’s budget could sustain.

If, on the other hand, we paid 100 manats a month to all 2.7 million children — even if we consider 100 manats a very small amount — the cost would exceed 3 billion manats a year [more than $1.76 billion or €1.52 billion] and reach approximately 3.2–3.3 billion manats [around $1.88–1.94 billion or €1.62–1.67 billion]. Such a burden could create certain difficulties for the budget at the initial stage. So we could start with 1 billion and then expand the programme as the economy’s capacity grows.”

Azerbaijan’s state budget for 2026 has approved revenues of 38.609 billion manats (around $22.71 billion or €19.57 billion) and expenditures of 41.7036 billion manats (around $24.53 billion or €21.14 billion).

Against this backdrop, spending more than 3 billion manats (over $1.76 billion or €1.52 billion) on a universal child benefit would indeed be a substantial expense.

But the scale of the expenditure alone does not settle the debate. A universal payment for every child is not the only possible option. The amount could depend on the child’s age, birth order, or parental income, or the programme could be introduced gradually.

The question, therefore, is not simply whether “the money is available in the budget”. It is also about which model of social policy the government considers a priority.

Birth rates are falling, but benefits are not the only factor

One reason the issue of child benefits has returned to the public agenda is the sharp decline in the number of births.

According to the State Statistical Committee, 122,846 children were born in Azerbaijan in 2022. The figure fell to 112,620 in 2023 and declined further to 102,310 in 2024. In 2025, the country recorded 95,875 births.

This means the annual number of births fell by nearly 27,000 between 2022 and 2025.

In 2025, the number of births per 1,000 residents fell from 10 to 9.4.

The age structure of the population is also changing. At the beginning of 2023, children under four accounted for 6.3% of the population. By the beginning of 2025, their share had fallen to 5.6%. Meanwhile, the proportion of people aged 65–69 rose from 3.9% to 4.6%, while the share of those aged 70 and over increased from 4.6% to 5.3%.

Sociologist Sanubar Heydarli told Meydan TV that support for young families is particularly important in this situation:

“Living standards in Azerbaijan cannot be described as high, and there are many social difficulties. That is why I consider child benefits an important form of support for young families. The figures also point to this: the birth rate is falling sharply, and the population is beginning to age.”

“But child benefits alone cannot solve this problem. We cannot assume that the government will start making payments and the birth rate will automatically rise. Other measures are needed alongside them. The decision to have a child depends on more than a family’s financial situation. Access to the labour market for women, a sense of social security, and the state of healthcare, education and social support systems all matter.

Nevertheless, child benefits provide significant support for young families. After a child is born, one parent temporarily leaves the labour market, reducing the family’s income. The state should therefore support families during childbirth and child-rearing. Child benefits are important, but they are not the only solution to demographic problems.”

What difference would 100 manats make?

Another question is how much the benefit would be worth.

Suppose the government pays 100 manats (around $59 or €51) per child each month. A family with two children would receive an additional 200 manats (around $118 or €101).

Could such an amount solve a family’s main financial problems?

Natig Jafarli believes it could not:

“In Europe, of every €100 spent on food, the figure is around €20 at most. If we spend half our income on food, that points to low living standards in Azerbaijan.

But much depends on the size of the benefit. Imagine a completely unrealistic scenario: the government pays 1,000 manats per child. Such an amount could indeed have a significant impact on poverty. But is that possible? No. If, at best, families receive 100 manats per child and a family with two children gets an additional 200 manats, would that be enough to eliminate poverty? Of course not.”

At the same time, the purpose of a child benefit does not necessarily have to be for the state to provide for a family entirely.

It could also be seen as the government’s contribution towards the additional expenses that inevitably arise when raising a child.

In the long term, Jafarli believes a completely different model would be ideal:

“People should be able to earn a living and support their own families. Small businesses and family businesses should be developed. The economy should move in a direction where people do not need such payments at all. That is the ideal model for me.

In principle, I am sceptical of the idea of the state constantly giving people money, because the more the state finances you, the more it can restrict your rights. We need to build a system, a society and a country where there is no longer any need for such payments. But is there a need for them now? Of course there is.”

Sanubar Heydarli also points to changing attitudes among parents towards raising children. Modern families may consciously choose to have fewer children, preferring to provide one or two children with better education, healthcare and opportunities for development.

What models have neighbouring countries adopted?

The experience of neighbouring countries shows that there is no single model for child benefits. In some countries, payments depend on family income; in others, they depend on the child’s birth order.

In Armenia, from 1 September 2026, every newborn child will qualify for a one-off payment of 500,000 drams, regardless of their birth order. This is equivalent to around 2,341 manats ($1,374 or €1,187). The Armenian government approved the decision on 13 August 2026.

In addition, a monthly payment of 50,000 drams — approximately 235 manats ($137 or €119) — is paid for the third and each subsequent child until the child turns six.

In Turkey, a one-off payment of 5,000 lira is available for the first child born on or after 1 January 2025. This is equivalent to around 176 manats ($104 or €89). For a second child, families receive 1,500 lira per month — around 53 manats ($31 or €27) — until the child turns five. For the third and subsequent children, the monthly payment is 5,000 lira (approximately 176 manats, $104 or €89).

In Georgia, the system is closer to a targeted model. Families with a social rating below the established threshold receive 200 lari per month — around 130 manats ($77 or €66) — for each child under 16. A UN report on social protection in Georgia states that the programme covers children from families with a social rating below 120,001 points.

According to figures for November 2025, more than 250,000 children were receiving these payments.

In Russia, the main unified child benefit is also not universal. When determining eligibility, authorities assess a family’s per capita income and other criteria of need. The payment can amount to 50%, 75% or 100% of the regional subsistence minimum for a child.

These examples show that the choice is not simply between having child benefits and not having them.

A government can provide a one-off payment at birth, introduce monthly benefits until a certain age, offer greater support for second and subsequent children, or limit payments to low-income families.

Azerbaijan currently follows the last model for the most part: targeted assistance and benefits for specific categories.

Is a separate law needed to introduce a universal child benefit?

According to Fariz Namazly, the government would not need to pass a separate law to introduce a universal child benefit:

“There is already a Law on Social Benefits, which could be amended. In addition, a new Law on the Rights of the Child has been adopted, and it could also be supplemented with provisions on new payments and benefits for children. In other words, the necessary provisions could be incorporated into either the Law on the Rights of the Child or the Law on Social Benefits.”

The burden on the budget — what about future costs?

Since 2006, the government’s overall approach has remained largely unchanged: instead of providing the same monthly payment for every child, it offers assistance based on a family’s financial need or a child’s membership in a specific social category.

As noted above, this does not mean the government provides no support to families with children. There are payments at birth, benefits for low-income families, childcare benefits, assistance for women with large families, and support for children with disabilities and those without parental care.

A universal child benefit would mean a shift away from this model.

Clearly, it would require substantial additional spending. At the same time, experts stress that child benefits alone cannot eliminate poverty or automatically reverse the decline in birth rates.

However, the falling number of births and the gradual ageing of the population raise a different question: can social policy be assessed solely in terms of how much money it costs today?

Sanubar Heydarli believes that failing to support families now could leave the state facing much higher costs in the future:

“By refusing to introduce child benefits today, leaving families to cope with their difficulties alone and failing to take responsibility, the state is effectively increasing its future expenditure associated with an ageing population.

Child benefits are a highly visible item of expenditure: when money is paid directly to families and the authorities calculate the total cost, the figures can seem enormous. But this ignores the fact that failing to support children today will translate into unavoidable spending on an ageing population in the future.

The state will have to pay more in pensions and benefits and increase healthcare spending. The proportion of elderly people will grow. As a result, the balance between taxes paid by the younger working population and spending on pensioners will be disrupted. There will be more pension recipients and fewer taxpayers. Ultimately, the burden on the state will only increase.”

With the support of the Mediset

Child benefits in Azerbaijan

World.title: Azerbaijan’s Deputy PM meets with Iranian Minister of Roads and Urban Development
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 29. As part of the visit to the Islamic Republic of Iran of a delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister of Azerbaijan Shahin Mustafayev, a meeting was held between the co-chairs of the Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation between the two countries (Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev on the Azerbaijani side and Minister of Roads and Urban Development Farzaneh Sadegh on the Iranian side.)

The meeting discussed the current state of relations in the economic and trade, transport and communications, and humanitarian fields, as well as other issues of mutual interest and prospects for cooperation.

The sides also discussed the implementation status of the agreements reached, and the measures envisaged in the Memorandum of Understanding signed following the 17th meeting of the State Commission held in Baku in February this year.

The Deputy Prime Minister underlined that the active political dialogue and friendly relations between President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev and President of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian have provided significant impetus to the development of relations between the two countries.

He particularly highlighted the meeting between the leaders held in Bishkek.

Shahin Mustafayev highlighted the progress made over the past period, emphasizing the importance of accelerating the implementation of agreed projects and continuing coordinated efforts among the relevant institutions.

During the discussion, the development of the North-South International Transport Corridor and the enhancement of its throughput capacity in the transport and transit sector were among the key topics.

The completion of the construction of the Aghband–Kelaleh highway bridge was hailed, and issues related to commissioning the border-crossing infrastructure were discussed.

The measures taken to complete work at the Astara cargo terminal and expand its cargo-handling capacity were also reviewed.

The sides exchanged views on promising infrastructure projects between the two countries.

The meeting concluded with an agreement to continue efforts aimed at developing mutually beneficial cooperation between Azerbaijan and Iran, ensuring the consistent implementation of the agreements reached at the 17th meeting of the State Commission, and speeding up the implementation of joint projects.

World.title: Middle Corridor could cut delivery times to 18–19 days by 2040 – WB
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 28. The Middle Corridor could reduce delivery times between Asia and Europe to 18–19 days by 2040.

This was stated in the World Bank report “Integration: World-Class Trade Logistics along the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor.”

It notes that the average delivery time along the Middle Corridor currently stands at around 47–50 days, while the average for maritime routes is approximately 45 days.

The World Bank emphasizes that enhancing the competitiveness of the Middle Corridor will require combining investments in infrastructure and projects that stimulate economic activity with trade facilitation reforms, improved transport services and stronger cross-border cooperation.

According to the World Bank, achieving such performance would also have a significant impact on freight volumes: “Container freight volumes along the Middle Corridor under a scenario in which the necessary improvements are implemented could be more than twice as high as under a scenario in which the development of the route is primarily based on infrastructure expansion without the corresponding improvements.”

The report also notes that enhancing the competitiveness of the Middle Corridor in the Eurasian rail freight market could have a positive impact on other segments of container transportation, including regional and intraregional trade.

According to the World Bank, this, in turn, could become one of the necessary factors for countries located along the Middle Corridor to achieve their economic diversification goals.

It should be recalled that the Middle Corridor is a trade and transport route running through a number of countries in the region and connecting Asia with Europe. It serves as an alternative to the traditional Northern and Southern corridors.

The route starts in China and runs through the countries of Central Asia. It then crosses the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Türkiye, before reaching Europe. The Middle Corridor is a land-based route that bypasses longer maritime routes, connecting the eastern parts of Asia, including China, with Europe.

World.title: Additional investments in Middle Corridor will need to be considered in 2030s – WB
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 28. Additional investments in the Middle Corridor will need to be considered in the 2030s to address operational constraints that may become relevant as freight volumes increase.

This was stated in the World Bank report “Integration: World-Class Trade Logistics along the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor.”

It notes that the development of the Middle Corridor will require not only investment in transport infrastructure, but also improved cross-border cooperation, simplified trade procedures and higher-quality transport services.

According to the report, at the initial stage, railways and roads, seaports, border crossing points and inland ports along the entire route need to be expanded, modernized and upgraded. These investments should be made in accordance with priorities and in a coordinated manner.

The World Bank notes that currently 92 percent of cargo transported across the Caspian Sea consists of commodities such as grain, fertilizers, construction materials and fuel: “For such shipments, the availability of transport capacity and the lowest possible direct transportation costs are of key importance.”

“As the Middle Corridor is still at the development stage, most infrastructure investments are needed in the short term, particularly by 2030. This will help eliminate existing bottlenecks along the route.

At the same time, in the 2030s, additional investments will need to be considered to address operational constraints that may become relevant as freight volumes increase.

However, infrastructure development alone will not be sufficient to improve logistics efficiency and attract new shippers.

As the economies of the corridor's participating countries diversify, and as shippers from East Asia and Europe show growing interest in transporting high-value and time-sensitive goods, the need to improve the quality of transport services and coordinate shipments will increase.

Improving cross-border cooperation, facilitating trade and enhancing the quality of services provided will also be necessary to realize the corridor's full freight and economic potential,” the report says.

The World Bank emphasizes that the relevant reforms and new approaches need to be developed and implemented in the short term: “However, their transformative nature means that implementing these measures will be a long-term process and may take the next 10–15 years.”

It notes that this process will require testing different approaches, sharing accumulated experience, international coordination and improving decision-making mechanisms based on the results obtained and the need to adjust the course.

World.title: Midwest gets first four-wheel-drive ambulance van following emergencies
World.content:
The family of a teenager who was paralysed after a motorcycle crash in an off-road area says the region's first four-wheel-drive ambulance is overdue.

St John WA said Geraldton, 420 kilometres north of Perth, is set to receive a Toyota HiAce four-wheel-drive ambulance in October — the first off-road paramedic van in the Midwest.

Seven of the vehicles are positioned around regional WA, along with 14 troop carriers.

The Hipper family have advocated for the emergency vehicle since James Hipper, then 17, broke his neck and spine in a motorcycle crash at Geraldton sand dunes last year.

An ambulance could not reach the accident, which was about a kilometre from the entrance to the dunes.

James Hipper broke his neck and spine in the crash. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

Instead, his sister Serenity Thorley, then 22, acted as a first responder.

"We were so far in dunes, we knew that no one was coming," she said.

"It was pretty daunting."

'One wrong move'

Ms Thorley said she and other young bystanders used a swag to lift James onto the back of a ute.

James was moved off the beach to a waiting ambulance in a ute. (Supplied/ ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

She said she held his head still as they drove to hard ground to meet the paramedics.

"Just the thought that one wrong move, had I not held him over a bump well enough, I could have lost him then and there," Ms Thorley said.

James was diagnosed as paraplegic, but the move did not contribute to the outcome.

Ms Thorley said she had worried that moving the teenager made his condition worse, until a doctor confirmed the damage was done at the time of impact.

She and her mother, April Hipper, have welcomed the news that the coastal city will soon have an off-road ambulance.

April Hipper's teenage son was paralysed. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

"I really do think it's been left to the wayside for too long," Ms Hipper said.

"At the end of the day, Geraldton is a vast coastline, and we're active people, people like to four wheel drive, people like to bike ride."

Earlier this month, members of the public had to put shark attack victim Mel Ismail in the back of a ute and drive him from the beach to meet paramedics.

Ocean to outback

While the new 4WD ambulance is positive news for the Geraldton area, concerns remain about responses to emergencies in the wider Midwest region.

The Mount Magnet shire, 340 kilometres north-east of Geraldton, is home to stations and mining camps, and a popular destination for self-drive tourists and gold prospectors.

Mount Magnet Shire president Jorgen Jensen said that while most gravel roads were in "fairly good" condition, the large road network was susceptible to damage, making it difficult to traverse.

Prospectors are enticed to the outback bushland near Mount Magnet. (ABC: Chris Lewis)

"A four-wheel-drive ambulance would be invaluable," Cr Jensen said.

" It's really just another example of something that is needed and probably is going to take too long to adequately service. "

Outer areas 'left behind'

Cr Jensen said the Royal Flying Doctor Service transported patients once they were in town, but getting them there could be a challenge.

"Some of the shires nearby would be a bit more vulnerable as far as that goes, from some of their outer limits to get them into town or to a point where they can get medical attention," he said.

Jorgen Jensen says the outer Midwest is often overlooked for essential services. (ABC Rural: Chris Lewis)

Cr Jensen said the region missed out on many essential services, including medical support.

"I think the Midwest is a good area that gets probably a little bit left behind in some aspects, especially the outer Midwest," he said.

St John WA said it continually reviews its regional fleet requirements, taking into account operational demand, geography and local conditions.

A state government spokesperson said there were 28 WA Country Health Service ambulances across the Kimberley, Pilbara and Midwest.

"Locations are chosen based on geography, population distribution, road conditions and health service need," they said.

The spokesperson said multiple agencies may respond to incidents in difficult-to-access areas.

World.title: Parramatta elects youngest lord mayor after Liberal quits party
World.content:
Parramatta City Council has elected its youngest-ever lord mayor the same day a Liberal councillor quit her party because it was becoming more anti-multiculturalism.

Labor councillor Cameron Maclean was elected to the position last night, with the deciding vote cast by Councillor Tanya Raffoul who announced her departure from her party on Monday morning.

The 28-year-old newly elected lord mayor told 702 ABC Sydney there was no deal made with Cr Raffoul.

"She really believes and sincerely believes that the Liberal Party is going the wrong direction, but it's really not for me to put words in Tanya's mouth," Cr Maclean said.

"I thank her for her support and her courage because … it's a big deal; it's a big move to resign from a political party and do something of this nature.

"So I thank her for her support, but there was no deal."

Cr Raffoul published a statement on social media saying the party's "growing policy and values alignment with a divisive political party, and its willingness to marginalise multicultural Australians, particularly across Western Sydney, is disappointing".

Tanya Raffoul announced she was leaving the Liberal Party on Monday morning. (Supplied: City of Parramatta)

"Multicultural communities across Western Sydney are one of our greatest strengths, made up of proud Australians like me who deserve to be represented and respected," she said in the statement.

Cr Raffoul said she was not resigning and would continue to serve as a councillor for the Dundas ward.

Cr Maclean, who was first elected to council in 2021, replaces outgoing mayor Martin Zaiter, who had been in the role since 2024.

Independent councillor Kellie Darley was elected as deputy mayor at Monday night's meeting, just over a year after she won a court battle with the council after it censured her for publishing criticism of a million-dollar partnership with the Parramatta Eels.

Cr Darley pushed for more whistleblower protections in local government during the meeting.

Kellie Darley was elected deputy lord mayor at last night's meeting. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

The council has faced intense scrutiny this year in the Independent Commission Against Corruption's Operation Navarra, which investigated allegations about former CEO Gail Connolly.

The meeting heard from former head of IT at the council, John Crawford, who gave evidence at the public inquiry. He told last night's meeting he had faced retaliation after giving his evidence.

Cr Maclean told 702 ABC Sydney he was committed to greater transparency at the council.

"It shouldn't be that hard to do the right thing and you shouldn't feel that you have to endure punitive measures when you do," he said.

"We have to make staff feel safe and valued within the organisation."

Cr Maclean will hold the position for two years, while Ms Darley will hold hers for one.

World.title: Australian missing in Cambodia allegedly abducted by Vietnamese authorities
World.content:
Pro-democracy group Viet Tan alleges a Melbourne man and his Norwegian Vietnamese colleague, who went missing in Cambodia more than a week ago, were abducted by Vietnamese authorities and forcibly taken to Vietnam, in what it calls "an act of transnational repression".

Hiep Tran, 50, and his colleague Duc Thuan Nguyen, 52, have not been heard from since the morning of September 18.

The pair had travelled to Phnom Penh to meet Vietnamese human rights activists.

They flew into the Cambodian capital from Bangkok on September 15, and were in regular contact with their families until September 18.

They did not board their return flight to Bangkok at 10:30am the next day.

Overnight, Vietnamese state media reported the men had been detained, according to Viet Tan, the group both men belong to and which the Vietnamese government considers a terrorist organisation.

Viet Tan said authorities alleged the pair "illegally entered Vietnam from the Cambodian border".

But the group rejects that account, saying the men had no intention of entering Vietnam and were abducted in Cambodia, then forcibly taken across the border.

The ABC has not seen the state media report but has contacted Vietnamese authorities for comment.

'A blatant fabrication'

Hiep Tran (left) and Duc Thuan Nguyen travelled to Phnom Penh to meet Vietnamese human rights activists. (Supplied)

In a statement, Viet Tan said the claim was a fabrication intended to cover up an abduction that violated Cambodia's sovereignty and international law.

The group said the men were travelling to the Kaoh Andaet area of Cambodia when they went missing.

"Viet Tan is particularly concerned that To Lam's police state is using its security apparatus to pursue and repress activists and foreign nationals even beyond Vietnam's borders," the statement said.

Viet Tan has called on the Australian and Norwegian governments to urgently request direct access to the men to confirm their condition and safety.

It said Mr Nguyen was diabetic and required daily insulin injections, and must be guaranteed access to medication and medical care.

It has also urged both governments and international human rights organisations to pressure the Vietnamese government for the men's immediate and unconditional release.

Family's fears

Speaking before news of her husband's detention, Mr Tran's wife, Chloe Dang, said the couple travelled to Thailand for a holiday before her husband made a side trip to Cambodia.

She said he was a passionate human rights activist but that she feared the men were targeted, or kidnapped, because of their advocacy.

" He always knew there was a risk doing human rights work, but we never thought that this would happen. "

Chloe Dang was waiting for her husband at Bangkok airport, but he and Duc Thuan Nguyen did not show up. (Supplied)

Ms Dang was waiting at Bangkok airport when the pair failed to appear, and was told Mr Tran had never boarded the flight.

"Our last conversation was him checking in on me in Bangkok, making sure I was safe and OK. He always checks in with me," she said.

She said she had lodged a missing person's report in Cambodia, and was liaising with Australian consular officials, but was worried not enough was being done.

"I send DFAT [Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] emails every day and ask for details, but I haven't heard anything since he disappeared," Ms Dang said.

A spokesperson for DFAT said it was providing consular assistance to the family of an Australian reported missing in Cambodia, but could not comment further due to privacy obligations.

Do you know more? If you have any information about the story, contact Victoria Pengilley.

'Not a normal tourist disappearing'

Phong Nguyen, who represents the group in Australia, said Mr Tran was a long-time advocate who trained activists in digital security.

Hiep Tran (fourth from the left) was a passionate human rights advocate. (Supplied)

He previously worked in IT for a large bank and for Telstra, but had left to focus on human rights work.

Mr Nguyen said the men had been supporting human rights activists for more than 20 years and were meeting activists who were not Viet Tan members.

"What's concerning is that this is not a normal tourist disappearing while travelling," Mr Nguyen said.

Hiep Tran previously worked for a large bank and for Telstra. (Supplied)

Rights groups including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have documented the jailing of Vietnamese citizens for online posts and activism.

Mr Nguyen said sentences of 15 or 20 years were not unusual, and that ordinary people were at risk, not only high-profile figures.

He also pointed to a rise in transnational repression, where governments targeted critics abroad, claiming there had been a significant increase in the past year in overseas Vietnamese nationals being "captured, kidnapped" and sentenced.

Mr Nguyen pointed to Australian citizen Chau Van Kham, a Viet Tan member who spent four and a half years in prison in Vietnam after his arrest in 2019.

Mr Nguyen said Mr Tran and Mr Thuan understood the dangers of their work, which made their silence even more alarming.

"Something must have happened very quickly that they couldn't alert," he said.

World.title: Live: ASX to edge higher as US bonds surge
World.content:
The biggest stories are coming together this week, with interest rates today, inflation data tomorrow, and house prices on Thursday, which independent economist Chris Richardson says are all impacted by artificial intelligence, war, and inflation.

"The biggest shift in many ways in the last little while has been the increase, globally, in the long-term interest rates in the borrowing costs of government bond yields," he says. "This is the biggest market in the world, and it's getting grumpier and grumpier."

Currently, the Australian bond market is 5.42%, and the US bond market is 5.24%.

"And as the cost of the future goes up, which is what it means, as long-term interest rates rise, that changes all sorts of equations," says Richardson. "I would certainly say it's part of the ongoing pressure on real estate in Australia, commercial as well as residential, and I suspect it's the next reckoning for share markets as well."

Despite the pain, Richardson pointed out that long-term interest rates are returning to what they used to look like.

"They used to be roughly the level economies grow over time, nominal GDP, the dollar size of economies," he says. "And the reason is fairly simple: you want interest rates - the sort of financial economy - to help balance the real economy, the factory economy."

But after 15 years of low interest rates, it's coming as a shock to many.

Richardson says what is happening, no matter how painful, "is not that unusual; it's a return to the old normal".

Given it's also driven by government borrowing, and tech companies borrowing for the AI boom, we may just need to get used to this "normal".

"It's not going away, regardless of what the Reserve Bank does in the next year, markets are saying interest rates in Australia ... aren't going to be going down for a while, and not much when they do."

World.title: TikTok tourists blamed for visitor damage at Victoria's Pink Cliffs
World.content:
Social media has inspired a swag of tourists to visit a fragile land formation in central Victoria, prompting warnings about damaging the unique site.

Photos and videos showing people standing on the Pink Cliffs at Heathcote have spread on TikTok and Instagram, with each platform featuring dozens of posts on the attraction.

Recent posts highlighting the site as a unique photo spot have garnered more than 100,000 views.

A visitor climbing in the Pink Cliffs, posted on social media. (Supplied: TikTok)

But Parks Victoria is concerned visitors may be ignoring signs and barriers to get the perfect picture.

"Social media has probably highlighted what has been a trend [of going off track] for a while," ranger Peter Barrow said.

The cliffs are a remnant of local gold mining in the 1800s.

Mr Barrow said visitors were welcome to explore the reserve, but needed to stay on designated walking tracks and behind barriers to protect the area's unique geology.

He said the exposed formations were particularly vulnerable because people could accelerate erosion by walking over them.

"It may not impact on the current generation, but the following generations will lose the ability to see this really unique geology," he said.

Why people ignore the signs

Victoria University School for the Visitor Economy director Naomi Dale said social media had the power to influence how people behave at tourist attractions.

She said repeatedly seeing photos of people enjoying a location can create a fear of missing out, even when signs tell people they shouldn't be there.

"People are really driven now with that perfect shot," she said.

Another visitor documents a Pink Cliffs visit on social media. (Supplied: TikTok)

Professor Dale said people could also underestimate the impact of their actions, believing one person climbing on a formation would not make a difference.

But when many people do the same thing, the cumulative impact can be significant.

More than just an Instagram backdrop

Geologist Clive Willman said the Pink Cliffs were created when miners used high-pressure water to wash away large volumes of soil and rock in search of gold.

The process exposed the layers underneath, leaving behind the distinctive gullies and formations seen today.

Clive Willman says the Pink Cliffs might be spectacular, but they're a devastated landscape. (ABC News: Molly Paynter)

He said the site was visually spectacular, but also evidence of significant environmental damage caused by the gold rush.

"People see an amazing moonscape. It's a feast for the eyes but, really, it's the site of a devastated landscape," he said.

Mr Barrow said signage at the reserve had been replaced in the past year, and there was a balance between protecting the formations and allowing visitors to experience them without being surrounded by signs.

Signs warn visitors not to stray from paths at the Pink Cliffs. (ABC News: Molly Paynter)

World.title: Cornell University gang-rape allegations to be reinvestigated
World.content:
A United States prosecutor has reopened an investigation into allegations a woman was plied with alcohol and drugs and gang-raped by seven students at a Cornell University fraternity.

The woman, identified only by a pseudonym, filed a lawsuit on September 16, saying she was sexually assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house on the Ivy League campus in October 2024.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said on Monday, local time, his office would present evidence to a New York grand jury as he faced questions from the public about why there were no criminal prosecutions in the case.

The alleged victim said the incident occurred after she was pressured into snorting ketamine, smoking marijuana and drinking alcohol, then became completely incapacitated while frat members sexually assaulted her.

The lawsuit, the reopening of the investigation and Cornell's response have sparked a flood of commentary on social media.

Many people have criticised the school and the district attorney's office in their posts, while some have expressed doubt about the lawsuit's allegations.

Others have posted photos of the seven fraternity members online.

The university has defended its handling of the allegations, saying it has conducted its own investigation and expelled or suspended students. (AP: Heather Ainsworth)

The accuser is suing the men, the Chi Phi fraternity, the university, an Ithaca bar and others, seeking undisclosed damages.

Her attorney did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment on the prosecutor's decision.

The woman went to campus police at the time, but Mr Van Houten said the accuser did not make any claims of being gang-raped or drugged in her initial sworn statement to authorities.

The prosecutor also said he was never contacted by the woman's attorney about her statement or about reconsidering the decision not to prosecute, but he reached out to the attorney recently.

"Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence," Mr Van Houten said in a statement.

"I have been asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members.

"I have already begun that process, starting with our conversation with Jane Doe and her attorneys."

Cornell responds to criticism about its handling of allegations

The university said in a statement it supported the decision to reopen the investigation.

The school said it conducted its own investigation and issued sanctions, including expelling some students and suspending others.

It also said the on-campus Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remained barred from campus.

A 2025 Cornell University taskforce survey report found 35 per cent of undergraduate women and 8 per cent of undergraduate men reported experiencing sexual assault during their time at Cornell. (AP: Seth Wenig)

School officials on Monday declined to release more information on the sanctions, including how many students were expelled and suspended.

Cornell said last week that federal privacy law barred it from disclosing specific information on individual students.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," the university said.

"A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the under-reporting of sexual assault."

The national chapter of Chi Phi did not return phone and email messages.

The school said it conducted an internal disciplinary investigation in 2024. It said a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, and both the woman and the people accused had the opportunity to testify and present evidence.

Lawsuit alleges student was assaulted during night of celebration

The woman's complaint accused the university of not preventing the alleged assaults and failing to properly address sexual violence on campus.

It included a photo that it said showed a group chat between frat members discussing the night's events.

The woman, who was a 20-year-old Cornell student at the time and a sorority member, went to campus police about three weeks later, according to the lawsuit.

Around 30,000 students, staff and laureates attend Cornell University. (Reuters: Supplied/Mary Chao/USA Today Network)

The fraternity and seven of its members were placed on temporary suspension that same day, the lawsuit said.

The complaint said the seven were given "the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell".

Cornell said "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement", noting the expulsions and suspensions.

Over the weekend, New York Democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned what she called a "culture of rape" that was protected at elite institutions.

"When I read what happened at Cornell, those men posted in a group chat. That means it was normal to them," she said on Sunday at a forum packed with young people near Cornell's campus.

"That means it was acceptable to them. This is a culture.

"And what we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore."

School says it has taken additional action to address sexual violence

Cornell said a school taskforce on campus sexual assault formed in 2025 made recommendations earlier this year, several of which had been implemented while others were in development.

The taskforce report said a 2025 school survey showed 35 per cent of undergraduate women and 8 per cent of undergraduate men reported experiencing sexual assault during their time at Cornell.

The university said the on-campus Chi Phi fraternity was closed in 2024 and remained barred from the campus. (AP: Heather Ainsworth)

Mr Van Housten said that since the lawsuit was filed, his office had been flooded with phone calls, voicemails and emails about the case from people seeking answers and others making insults and threats.

"The community outrage stemming from the incomplete news and social media coverage requires that I provide an answer to why the investigation resulted in a lack of criminal charges," he said.

World.title: Live: Chalmers does not want to see workers 'carry the can' for Middle East war
World.content:
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland has been asked about the rapid review into the OpenAI agent breach of the Medicare statistics portal last week on ABC Radio National Breakfast.

It's unclear if a breach of this kind can be prosecuted under existing law, and Rowland said the taskforce will look at any gaps in legislation.

At this stage, the attorney-general says it's too early to tell if an offence has occurred and if the Australian Federal Police should investigate.

"We need to look at all the evidence first," Rowland says. "There's a lot of forensics that still needs to be gathered and assessments made on that."

She said while this is a novel technology and the breach itself has been described as "minor" in terms of cybersecurity, "Australians are rightly concerned".

She added that if the tech companies responsible were operating in Australia, the government could regulate them more easily, but it was more complicated when they were located overseas.

"We've had issues of extra-territoriality and certain platforms challenging the jurisdiction of the e-safety commissioner as a regulator, for example — that complicates it more."

World.title: Cleary defends Crossland after gruesome injury as hearing locked in
World.content:
Nathan Cleary has leapt to the defence of Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland, pleading with fans to stop peppering the embattled Knight with social media abuse as he prepares to plead his case to the NRL judiciary tonight.

Cleary confirmed on Monday night that Crossland had apologised for the hip-drop tackle that left him needing emergency surgery for a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle.

But less than 24 hours before Crossland was due to launch a desperate bid to play in the grand final, Cleary posted on Instagram from his hospital bed to offer support to the Knights number nine.

"Please don't be one of those people writing comments like this to Phoenix," Cleary posted alongside a graphic of some of the abuse Crossland had received.

Cleary vows 'I'll be back' Nathan Cleary says "I'll be back" in an upbeat Instagram post after successful surgery on his badly broken leg.

"It was a complete accident, and he doesn't deserve the unwarranted hate. He reached out to apologise, and I have nothing but respect for him.

"He's a competitor, and our game is made up of split-second moments that sometimes lead to unfortunate circumstances.

"Comments like this are so unfair. Spread love, not hate."

The comments against Crossland included accusations the tackle was deliberate and threats to maim the Knights dummy-half. Several are not suitable for print.

Crossland had almost appeared close to tears as Cleary was stretchered off Stadium Australia after the tackle and appeared to have accepted his fate even before referee Gerard Sutton sent him off.

He cut a dejected figure in the dressing room after being dismissed, before the Knights held on for a famous 22-14 win to qualify for the grand final.

Crossland seemed to accept his fate before it was even decided. (Supplied: Fox League)

Crossland was referred straight to the judiciary over the incident, with a hearing set for 6pm AEST tonight.

The New Zealander will almost certainly be rubbed out of Sunday's grand final against the Sydney Roosters, with a question of how much of a ban extends to the World Cup.

The longest suspension handed down for a hip-drop tackle is five weeks. That would keep Crossland out of the World Cup final, if they qualify.

"He was disappointed, we've got to try and get him upbeat," Knights coach Justin Holbrook said after Sunday's game.

"He's an emotional guy. He's been so great for us every week this year. Hopefully Nathan's OK."

World.title: ‘Exclude her’: British Jews urge UK to bar entry for Australian author over October 7 remarks
World.content:
WorldEuropeUK ‘Exclude her’: British Jews urge UK to bar entry for Australian author over October 7 remarks David Crowe September 29, 2026 — 8:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Britain’s peak Jewish group has urged the UK government to prevent Australian author Randa Abdel-Fattah from visiting the country after an outcry over her past remarks about the October 7 attacks on Israel. The Board of Deputies of British Jews said it was concerned at plans for Abdel-Fattah to promote her new novel in the UK when she had previously described the Hamas attacks as “exhilarating” and a sign of hope. Randa Abdel-Fattah with her novel, Discipline. “At a time when Jewish communities are remembering the victims of 7 October, providing a platform to someone who has spoken of that day in such terms is profoundly insensitive,” the board said. “We urge the Home Secretary [Shabana Mahmood] to use her powers to exclude her from the UK.”



The statement heightens the debate about the author’s visit next week after a Conservative Party frontbencher, Chris Philp, called on the UK government to consider refusing or cancelling any visa or travel clearance she might have. Related Article Review A bold exploration of media censorship around the Israel-Palestine conflict Mahmood has not made any public comment on the case but the Home Office said it was committed to “rooting out antisemitism” and anyone spreading hatred. Abdel-Fattah, who is Palestinian-Australian, was dropped from the Adelaide Writers’ Week this year due to her remarks about Israel, leading 180 writers to quit the literary festival. While South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas strongly criticised Abdel-Fattah, the Adelaide Festival board later apologised to the author and offered her a place at its 2027 events.



The cover of Abdel-Fattah’s novel Discipline. The controversy centres on social media posts and statements by Abdel-Fattah about the October 7 attacks, when Hamas crossed into Israel and killed 1195 people. Those killed included 36 children and hundreds of adult civilians, such as 364 people attending the Nova music festival. Survivors of the attack reported sexual violence against victims, but Abdel-Fattah dismissed this as “rape atrocity propaganda” despite a detailed investigation reporting a pattern of rape, mutilation and extreme brutality against women on October 7. Hamas is listed by Australia and other nations as a terrorist organisation. One year after the October 7 attacks, Abdel-Fattah wrote about the events using messages that described it in positive terms.



“If you ask me about hope, there was a glimmer on October 7,” she wrote. “It was palpable, real, and exhilarating. If you ask me about confusion, fear, and expectations, they were there in the early hours and days.” Abdel-Fattah’s novel, Discipline, concerns the personal and public debates about Israel and Palestine and is published outside Australia by London publisher OneWorld. The writer is due to speak at events in the UK and Ireland from Wednesday night, although Cambridge University’s Newnham College Literary Festival chose in early September to cancel her planned appearance. OneWorld lists five speaking events in Dublin, Manchester and London. Philp wrote to Mahmood on Sunday to ask her to look at ways to stop the book tour going ahead, although he said this would depend upon the legal power to do so. “The government cannot say that it is determined to confront extremism while failing to scrutinise overseas speakers whose rhetoric appears to celebrate or excuse the events of October 7 and refuse to describe a proscribed terrorist organisation for what they are,” he wrote.



Related Article Investigations ‘Create tension and disruption’: Randa Abdel-Fattah’s road to festival fiasco “The timing makes this visit particularly concerning. Ms Abdel-Fattah’s tour falls around the anniversary of the October 7 atrocities, at a time when British Jewish communities continue to face acute security. “I therefore urge you to review Ms Abdel-Fattah’s case as a matter of urgency and, if the relevant legal threshold is met, refuse or cancel any Electronic Travel Authorisation, entry clearance or other permission required for her to enter the UK.” Abdel-Fattah made a brief remark on Instagram when the Cambridge festival stopped plans for her appearance this month: “Another literary festival, another cancellation.” She has not made any public response to Philp’s request for her to be banned from Britain, and she could not be reached by this masthead. Her publisher, OneWorld, did not respond to a request for comment.



In her response in January to the Adelaide Festival, however, she argued for the right of authors to speak despite attempts to silence them. Related Article Exclusive

Israeli-Palestinian conflict The denial and disinformation facing October 7 survivors “To be Palestinian in this world is to confront the violence of erasure, gaslighting and dehumanisation over and over again,” she wrote. “It is heartbreaking to think about the lost opportunities that marginalised and debut writers will face with such boycotts especially in circumstances when so many had debut books. “We must do everything we can to hold decision makers accountable for callously abdicating their duty of care towards us all.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.
