A teenager caught flying a drone near the south-west Sydney home of an underworld figure warned by police to fear for his life has been charged over an alleged murder plot. Jimmy Schulz, 18, is due to face court on Tuesday charged over the alleged conspiracy to murder a man linked to the Haouchar crime family. Jimmy Schulz has been charged over an alleged murder conspiracy following his arrest earlier in September. NSW Police Earlier this month, Schulz was charged with murder over a separate incident, after allegedly flying a drone used in the mistaken identity shooting of Joshua Macdonald, 40, on September 2. But police allege Schulz was also conducting drone surveillance as part of a separate murder plot on the day of his arrest. He was arrested in a car on September 11 alongside 19-year-old Ratu Viliame James Koroitamana, who was charged with driving while disqualified and participating in a criminal group to contribute to criminal activity.



Schulz was further charged on Monday with conspiring and agreeing to murder any person, participating in a criminal group contributing to criminal activity, possessing a dedicated encrypted criminal communication device to commit serious criminal activity, and failing to operate unmanned aircraft within visual line of sight. Last week, stood down PE teacher Ashleigh Ann Seeney, 28, was charged in relation to the same plot. Ashleigh Ann Seeney, 28, was arrested over the alleged gangland murder plot. Nine News Seeney was allegedly in “constant contact” with the two teens at West Hoxton, relaying information about police movements and leaving the area shortly after they were arrested. Detective Superintendent Jason Box said the alleged murder plot Seeney and Schulz have been charged over targeted a man living nearby.



“He has been warned about this threat to life … as with most of the persons that we do warn, they’re – a lot of them – very dismissive of what we tell them,” Box said. “He has been spoken to numerous times about his connections with organised crime, potential threats, and he was warned yet again after this.” Detective Superintendent Jason Box. Sam Mooy The alleged plot is said to stem from an internal dispute within the Haouchar crime family and is not believed to be related to ongoing conflict between the Alameddine organised crime network and rival group the Coconut Cartel. Police allege the Haouchar crime family once controlled an international billion-dollar drug, gun and tobacco trafficking syndicate, commanded by Bilal Haouchar. Haouchar, who remains wanted by NSW Police, fled Australia for Lebanon, where he has been jailed.



Seeney and Schulz have both been charged in relation to Macdonald’s death at Merrylands West. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on September 2. Nine News Schulz has been charged with murder and participating in a criminal group to contribute to criminal activity in relation to Macdonald’s killing. Seeney has been charged with accessory after the fact to murder, participating in a criminal group contributing to criminal activity and failing to comply with a digital evidence access order direction. Both remain in custody and before the courts. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth
World.content:
NationalNSWData centres Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth Cindy Yin and Jessica McSweeney September 29, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An industrial property giant’s plan for a hyperscale data centre on Sydney’s north shore has been abandoned after outrage among residents, in a case that has become a flashpoint for the spread of artificial intelligence infrastructure across the country. Goodman Group had placed state-significant plans for the construction and 24/7 operation of an $800 million, 81-megawatt data centre on public exhibition in March, which would have required the demolition and excavation of four existing warehouses. A concept view of the data centre’s facade from Mars Road, Lane Cove. Urbis In a letter to the NSW government on Monday, Goodman’s head of planning Guy Smith confirmed it was withdrawing the application and cited “emerging federal and state policy” as among the reasons for abandoning the development. “During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly,” it said.



“Goodman has carefully considered these changes together with feedback received through the planning process, including the views of the local community.” The proposal not only sparked backlash from residents: utility providers Sydney Water and Ausgrid were concerned the development would strain existing infrastructure and increase electrocution or fire risks. Goodman Group was also asked about the proposal in federal parliament, but the appearance of senior leaders via audiovisual link was plagued by technical problems. The 28-metre-tall “Project Mars” data centre would have been located within the Lane Cove West industrial area, which is bordered by a park, low-density homes 50 metres to the east, and Lane Cove West Public School about 160 metres north-east of the site.



Related Article Data centres Data centres are popping up all over Sydney. But what impact do they have on our suburbs? In a letter to the planning department in May, Ausgrid raised issues about the compatibility of the data centre with existing infrastructure, requiring “due consideration be given … particularly in relation to risks of electrocution, fire risks”, citing other noise and visual amenity impacts. Data centres are large, energy-intensive facilities requiring uninterrupted power and a constant supply of potable water to cool servers. At capacity, Goodman had anticipated Project Mars would have used about 35 litres of water per second during peak times and about 1.4 million litres per day. Sydney Water said in a submission it was “unable to support progression” of the data centre without more detailed planning assessments of water demand and wastewater impacts. The state-owned corporation said Project Mars would have heaped pressure on the existing drinking water system, which in its view had “limited capacity to service the development”. Both utility providers’ doubts illustrate a pattern of concerns that emerge when data centre developments outpace upgrades to critical infrastructure, strained by population growth and climate change. The global AI boom has boosted demand for data centres with greater capacity in Sydney: there are 41 state-significant projects across the city in the development pipeline, of which 18 have been approved. World.title: ASX to open flat ahead of RBA rate call; Wall Street wobbles as bonds spike
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX to open flat ahead of RBA rate call; Wall Street wobbles as bonds spike Staff writers September 29, 2026 — 6:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket is set for a cautious start on RBA day, with investors looking to the Reserve Bank’s press conference after its expected decision to raise interest rates for clues on whether a follow-up hike will be needed. ASX futures were up 2 points at 8722 as of 6.39am AEST. The local bourse rose 0.2 per cent on Monday, with a slump in miners counterbalancing rallies in banks, and defensive sectors such as utilities and health care. The Australian dollar traded at US70.17¢. Investors’ focus will be on the Reserve Bank’s interest rate call and subsequent press conference. Oscar Colman The Reserve Bank’s nine-member policy board will increase the cash rate by a quarter-percentage point to 4.6 per cent, the highest level since November 2011, in its decision announced at 2:30pm in Sydney, economists widely predict. Traders are also pricing an end to the RBA’s two-meeting pause, against a backdrop of spiralling energy prices across the global economy. Investors will closely scrutinise both the rate statement and RBA Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference an hour later. They’ll be seeking clues on whether the central bank is prepared to deliver back-to-back hikes in November or prefers to watch and wait through the rest of the year.



“The risk sits with the need to tighten monetary policy further beyond September given the inflation backdrop,” said Belinda Allen, head of Australia Economics at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “But it is not an easy decision to push monetary policy further into restrictive territory.” Related Article Opinion

Bonds Wall Street’s multitrillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The central bank has stood pat at 4.35 per cent since May after opening the year aggressively, with rate rises at each of its first three meetings. On Wall Street overnight, yields in the US bond market cranked up and again reached their highest levels in roughly two decades, which knocked stocks further from their record high. The S&P 500 fell 0.8 per cent and gave back much of its gain from last week, which had brought it to the brink of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished down 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.9 per cent.



US stocks felt pressure as the yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.23 per cent from 5.17 per cent late on Friday. That’s a considerable move for the centrepiece of the US bond market, taking the 10-year yield back to where it was in 2007, before the global financial crisis sent yields toward zero. Treasury yields have been jumping for a range of reasons, from worries about Washington’s massive debt load to rising energy costs from the Iran war, which boost inflation. That pressures the economy because it prompts higher interest rates, making borrowing money more expensive for everyone, while also undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Monday’s rise in yields followed the latest swings for oil prices, which have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide. The latest turns came after President Donald Trump over the weekend rejected an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program. “I’d like to make a deal, too,” Trump said Saturday. “But that deal would not be acceptable.”



West Texas Intermediate futures settled below $US93 a barrel, up 0.5 per cent, after a day of choppy trading, which saw it rising by as much as 4.5 per cent during the session. Brent was up 1.3 per cent at $US105.71 a barrel. Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds for concrete progress on the nuclear issue, according to a US official. Iran’s nuclear program is a key sticking point for both sides. Traders have been parsing conflicting signals on progress towards a US-Iran ceasefire and a reopening of the vital waterway. Bloomberg reported that Iranian officials have privately expressed pessimism about reaching a deal to before the US midterm elections in November. Trump said that talks with Iran were held on Monday through mediators. The US president earlier rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen Hormuz if Washington made some concessions. The stark shift in tone over the span of a day highlights the whiplash-inducing rhetoric traders have had to navigate since the conflict began seven months ago. “Without a concrete deal or conclusion to the conflict, the market is quickly fading initial headline reactions and higher prices are becoming harder to shake,” said Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities. “The market is increasingly worried about escalation via Iran or the Houthis prior to midterm elections, or from the US post midterms.”



Related Article AI Nvidia unveils security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue On Wall Street, stocks of airlines and other companies with big fuel bills sank because of the rise in oil prices. American Airlines fell 2.5 per cent, and United Airlines lost 2.2 per cent. Gold miners were also weak after the price of gold sank 3.9 per cent. Gold has a reputation for helping to protect its investors from high inflation, but its price tends to weaken when rising yields mean bonds are paying investors more in interest. Gold struggles to keep up because it pays its investors nothing. Nvidia, Wall Street’s most influential stock, rose 1.7 per cent. The chip company said it approved a plan to send up to another $US150 billion to its shareholders in a stock buyback plan, bringing the program’s total remaining size to $US235 billion. Nvidia has the power to do so after the frenzy around its chips used for artificial-intelligence technology helped it more than double the amount of cash on its books in the first half of its fiscal year. The company also on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue.



AI stocks have broadly come under pressure after leaders of the industry said it needs to slow its development to give safety measures time to catch up. In other international markets, European indexes were mixed following weaker performances across much of Asia. Indexes dropped 2.7 per cent in Seoul and 1.7 per cent in Shanghai for two of the world’s bigger moves. with AP, Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: Nvidia unveils security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Nvidia unveils security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue Kelvin Chan and Anne D'Innocenzio September 29, 2026 — 6:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue. The company on Monday said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open-source software that “sets boundaries for agents,” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organisations. The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia says its new security platform can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue. Bloomberg Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face.



“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. Related Article Exclusive

AI Anthropic boss to skip Senate grilling into rogue AI agents The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI’s models including breaching Australia’s Medicare website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organisations on their own. Nvidia’s software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said. Because it’s open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.



The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behaviour,” Boitano said. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has argued it’s up to AI companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Bloomberg Nvidia said more than 100 organisations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture, and JPMorgan Chase.



The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. But others including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterised AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address. Biggest share buyback ever Also overnight, Nvdia said its board approved expanding its share buyback program by $US150 billion as the chipmaking giant looks to make use of more of its stellar revenue growth fuelled by demand for its high-end artificial intelligence chips. The company said Monday the share buyback increase, which it touted as the largest buyback in history, brings its stock repurchase program to $US235 billion. Its shares rose 1.6 per cent.



Companies use repurchases, in part, to return cash to investors and support the stock’s price. Earnings per share can increase because there are fewer shares outstanding. Buybacks also signal confidence from leadership about a company’s financial prospects. Related Article AI Inside the elite meeting where OpenAI lectured on security, a day before the hack was revealed “NVIDIA’s growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing,” said Huang. “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders. This authorisation reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead.” Nvidia’s high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI, and are highly sought after. The company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion late last month. While AI has powered stock market gains and US economic growth in recent years, there’s been growing scepticism about whether AI will justify the trillions of dollars being spent to develop the technology.



The AI industry also faces increasing pushback amid objections to the expansion of data centres and fears that the rapid speed of AI adoption could lead to widespread job losses worldwide. World.title: This city is banning drones and owners aren’t happy
World.content:
WorldAsiaInside China This city is banning drones and owners aren’t happy Lisa Visentin September 29, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: At authorised buyback stores across Beijing, residents are reluctantly surrendering their drones to comply with a new ban that has sparked a rare venting of frustration from some owners in the usually tight-lipped city. Under rules announced this month, Beijing authorities imposed a total ban on the possession of drones inside the capital, forcing owners to sell them or move them out of the city by November 15. For the past fortnight, a steady procession of drone owners have queued at drone maker DJI’s stores and other designated buyback sites across the city to offload their devices, as complaints have circulated about low resale values and property rights. A man negotiates the sale of his drone at an official buyback retailer in Beijing ahead of a citywide ban on drones coming into effect on November 15. Fairfax Media “My freedom’s been restricted,” said Li, who spoke to this masthead outside a store in the city’s financial district using a pseudonym.



“This is not a fair and normal request for the government to ask citizens to take. It’s my property; I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to sell it.” Li said he originally paid about 5000 yuan ($1060) for his drone and only used it to take photos of friends and family and while travelling. It was now a “write-off”, he said. Chinese drone maker DJI is the global leader in consumer drones, but it can no longer sell the devices in Beijing. Bloomberg The September regulations extend and even override drone rules introduced only in May. Those earlier measures banned new drone sales and imposed a no-fly zone over Beijing without prior approval, but had allowed existing owners to keep their devices as long as they registered them with police. To comply with the May rules, DJI – a global leader in consumer drones and a Chinese company success story – and other sellers had to clear out stock from the shelves of their Beijing stores. It underscores an underlying tension in government policies, as Beijing tightens security measures over the capital while championing the low-altitude economy as one of the country’s key strategic industries.



The latest crackdown comes after a pilot flew a small recreational aircraft into Beijing’s tallest skyscraper in June, killing himself and injuring 13 people, in an incident that exposed security vulnerabilities over the city’s airspace. Related Article Updated

Air accident ‘An earthquake in the security system’: How did a plane crash into Beijing’s tallest building? Drones can still be purchased and flown outdoors in other parts of the country, provided they are registered with authorities. In Shenzhen, a tech hub in China’s south, drones regularly buzz over the CBD skies, delivering food to designated sites operated by takeaway giant Meituan. To cushion the blow, Beijing authorities are offering subsidies to owners who resell or recycle their devices through designated buyback platforms. Residents can also ship the drones out of the capital free of charge, or sell them to buyers in other Chinese cities on second-hand trading sites. Despite the November deadline, some owners have reported being contacted by police urging them to offload them more quickly. Others have taken to Chinese social media to lament low-ball offers on the second-hand market as buyers capitalise on the forced sales.



“I’m really reluctant to let it go,” one owner commented on Red Note, a video platform. “It comes with three batteries, and the system has only gone through a single charge cycle. A lot of people don’t see the value – they just treat it like a joke and are looking to snap it up at a bargain-basement price.” “I’m speechless,” said another said, who sold their device for a quarter of its retail value. “Literally bought it last August and flew it less than five times.” In the tech hub of Shenzhen, in southern China, consumers can have food delivered by drones to designated drop-off sites. Fairfax Media And selling to individuals outside Beijing can come with other hurdles. Li said he received a text message from his local residents’ committee – neighbourhood groups that are often closely affiliated with the Communist Party – advising that if he transferred the drone outside the city, he would need to provide photographic evidence of the buyer holding the drone in front of a prominent landmark.



“If I send it to Shanghai, the person would have to hold it on the Bund, or somewhere like that,” he said. Related Article Inside China Working from sun up to sun down, China’s delivery drivers caught in a price war At another buyback shop in Beijing, 26-year-old Chen said he was offered about 1400 yuan for his four-year-old DJI drone, about $125 less than he might get via a second-hand online retailer. But if the second-hand buyer disputed the purchase after receiving the drone, Chen wouldn’t be able to have the drone sent back to him in Beijing, potentially leaving him with nothing. Chen said he was dismayed by the policy, but believed it was trying to regulate irresponsible behaviour by drone flyers in the past.



“That eventually led to the situation we have now, where we’re no longer really able to fly drones even as a personal hobby. I think that’s quite a shame,” he said, giving only his surname. “We hope the government can continue improving the regulations, so that people can have ways to fly them.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

The controversy centres on social media posts and statements by Abdel-Fattah about the October 7 attacks, when Hamas crossed into Israel and killed 1195 people. Those killed included 36 children and hundreds of adult civilians, such as 364 people attending the Nova music festival. Survivors of the attack reported sexual violence against victims, but Abdel-Fattah dismissed this as “rape atrocity propaganda” despite a detailed investigation reporting a pattern of rape, mutilation and extreme brutality against women on October 7. Hamas is listed by Australia and other nations as a terrorist organisation. One year after the October 7 attacks, Abdel-Fattah wrote about the events using messages that described it in positive terms.



“If you ask me about hope, there was a glimmer on October 7,” she wrote. “It was palpable, real, and exhilarating. If you ask me about confusion, fear, and expectations, they were there in the early hours and days.” Abdel-Fattah’s novel, Discipline, concerns the personal and public debates about Israel and Palestine and is published outside Australia by London publisher OneWorld. The writer is due to speak at events in the UK and Ireland from Wednesday night, although Cambridge University’s Newnham College Literary Festival chose in early September to cancel her planned appearance. OneWorld lists five speaking events in Dublin, Manchester and London. Philp wrote to Mahmood on Sunday to ask her to look at ways to stop the book tour going ahead, although he said this would depend upon the legal power to do so. “The government cannot say that it is determined to confront extremism while failing to scrutinise overseas speakers whose rhetoric appears to celebrate or excuse the events of October 7 and refuse to describe a proscribed terrorist organisation for what they are,” he wrote.



Related Article Investigations ‘Create tension and disruption’: Randa Abdel-Fattah’s road to festival fiasco “The timing makes this visit particularly concerning. Ms Abdel-Fattah’s tour falls around the anniversary of the October 7 atrocities, at a time when British Jewish communities continue to face acute security. “I therefore urge you to review Ms Abdel-Fattah’s case as a matter of urgency and, if the relevant legal threshold is met, refuse or cancel any Electronic Travel Authorisation, entry clearance or other permission required for her to enter the UK.” Abdel-Fattah made a brief remark on Instagram when the Cambridge festival stopped plans for her appearance this month: “Another literary festival, another cancellation.” She has not made any public response to Philp’s request for her to be banned from Britain, and she could not be reached by this masthead. Her publisher, OneWorld, did not respond to a request for comment.



In her response in January to the Adelaide Festival, however, she argued for the right of authors to speak despite attempts to silence them. Related Article Exclusive

Israeli-Palestinian conflict The denial and disinformation facing October 7 survivors “To be Palestinian in this world is to confront the violence of erasure, gaslighting and dehumanisation over and over again,” she wrote. “It is heartbreaking to think about the lost opportunities that marginalised and debut writers will face with such boycotts especially in circumstances when so many had debut books. “We must do everything we can to hold decision makers accountable for callously abdicating their duty of care towards us all.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Teen drone pilot charged over second alleged gangland murder plot
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Teen drone pilot charged over second alleged gangland murder plot Jack Gramenz September 29, 2026 — 8:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A teenager caught flying a drone near the south-west Sydney home of an underworld figure warned by police to fear for his life has been charged over an alleged murder plot. Jimmy Schulz, 18, is due to face court on Tuesday charged over the alleged conspiracy to murder a man linked to the Haouchar crime family. Jimmy Schulz has been charged over an alleged murder conspiracy following his arrest earlier in September. NSW Police Earlier this month, Schulz was charged with murder over a separate incident, after allegedly flying a drone used in the mistaken identity shooting of Joshua Macdonald, 40, on September 2. But police allege Schulz was also conducting drone surveillance as part of a separate murder plot on the day of his arrest. He was arrested in a car on September 11 alongside 19-year-old Ratu Viliame James Koroitamana, who was charged with driving while disqualified and participating in a criminal group to contribute to criminal activity.



Schulz was further charged on Monday with conspiring and agreeing to murder any person, participating in a criminal group contributing to criminal activity, possessing a dedicated encrypted criminal communication device to commit serious criminal activity, and failing to operate unmanned aircraft within visual line of sight. Last week, stood down PE teacher Ashleigh Ann Seeney, 28, was charged in relation to the same plot. Ashleigh Ann Seeney, 28, was arrested over the alleged gangland murder plot. Nine News Seeney was allegedly in “constant contact” with the two teens at West Hoxton, relaying information about police movements and leaving the area shortly after they were arrested. Detective Superintendent Jason Box said the alleged murder plot Seeney and Schulz have been charged over targeted a man living nearby.



“He has been warned about this threat to life … as with most of the persons that we do warn, they’re – a lot of them – very dismissive of what we tell them,” Box said. “He has been spoken to numerous times about his connections with organised crime, potential threats, and he was warned yet again after this.” Detective Superintendent Jason Box. Sam Mooy The alleged plot is said to stem from an internal dispute within the Haouchar crime family and is not believed to be related to ongoing conflict between the Alameddine organised crime network and rival group the Coconut Cartel. Police allege the Haouchar crime family once controlled an international billion-dollar drug, gun and tobacco trafficking syndicate, commanded by Bilal Haouchar. Haouchar, who remains wanted by NSW Police, fled Australia for Lebanon, where he has been jailed.



Seeney and Schulz have both been charged in relation to Macdonald’s death at Merrylands West. Joshua Macdonald was killed in a shooting at Merrylands West on September 2. Nine News Schulz has been charged with murder and participating in a criminal group to contribute to criminal activity in relation to Macdonald’s killing. Seeney has been charged with accessory after the fact to murder, participating in a criminal group contributing to criminal activity and failing to comply with a digital evidence access order direction. Both remain in custody and before the courts. Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth
World.content:
NationalNSWData centres Project Mars set off a war of words. Now the AI data centre is wiped off the face of earth Cindy Yin and Jessica McSweeney September 29, 2026 — 8:07am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An industrial property giant’s plan for a hyperscale data centre on Sydney’s north shore has been abandoned after outrage among residents, in a case that has become a flashpoint for the spread of artificial intelligence infrastructure across the country. Goodman Group had placed state-significant plans for the construction and 24/7 operation of an $800 million, 81-megawatt data centre on public exhibition in March, which would have required the demolition and excavation of four existing warehouses. A concept view of the data centre’s facade from Mars Road, Lane Cove. Urbis In a letter to the NSW government on Monday, Goodman’s head of planning Guy Smith confirmed it was withdrawing the application and cited “emerging federal and state policy” as among the reasons for abandoning the development. “During this time, the policy and regulatory environment for large-scale data centre development has evolved significantly,” it said.



“Goodman has carefully considered these changes together with feedback received through the planning process, including the views of the local community.” The proposal not only sparked backlash from residents: utility providers Sydney Water and Ausgrid were concerned the development would strain existing infrastructure and increase electrocution or fire risks. Goodman Group was also asked about the proposal in federal parliament, but the appearance of senior leaders via audiovisual link was plagued by technical problems. The 28-metre-tall “Project Mars” data centre would have been located within the Lane Cove West industrial area, which is bordered by a park, low-density homes 50 metres to the east, and Lane Cove West Public School about 160 metres north-east of the site.



Related Article Data centres Data centres are popping up all over Sydney. But what impact do they have on our suburbs? In a letter to the planning department in May, Ausgrid raised issues about the compatibility of the data centre with existing infrastructure, requiring “due consideration be given … particularly in relation to risks of electrocution, fire risks”, citing other noise and visual amenity impacts. Data centres are large, energy-intensive facilities requiring uninterrupted power and a constant supply of potable water to cool servers. At capacity, Goodman had anticipated Project Mars would have used about 35 litres of water per second during peak times and about 1.4 million litres per day. Sydney Water said in a submission it was “unable to support progression” of the data centre without more detailed planning assessments of water demand and wastewater impacts. The state-owned corporation said Project Mars would have heaped pressure on the existing drinking water system, which in its view had “limited capacity to service the development”. Both utility providers’ doubts illustrate a pattern of concerns that emerge when data centre developments outpace upgrades to critical infrastructure, strained by population growth and climate change. The global AI boom has boosted demand for data centres with greater capacity in Sydney: there are 41 state-significant projects across the city in the development pipeline, of which 18 have been approved. World.title: ASX to open flat ahead of RBA rate call; Wall Street wobbles as bonds spike
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX to open flat ahead of RBA rate call; Wall Street wobbles as bonds spike Staff writers September 29, 2026 — 6:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket is set for a cautious start on RBA day, with investors looking to the Reserve Bank’s press conference after its expected decision to raise interest rates for clues on whether a follow-up hike will be needed. ASX futures were up 2 points at 8722 as of 6.39am AEST. The local bourse rose 0.2 per cent on Monday, with a slump in miners counterbalancing rallies in banks, and defensive sectors such as utilities and health care. The Australian dollar traded at US70.17¢. Investors’ focus will be on the Reserve Bank’s interest rate call and subsequent press conference. Oscar Colman The Reserve Bank’s nine-member policy board will increase the cash rate by a quarter-percentage point to 4.6 per cent, the highest level since November 2011, in its decision announced at 2:30pm in Sydney, economists widely predict. Traders are also pricing an end to the RBA’s two-meeting pause, against a backdrop of spiralling energy prices across the global economy. Investors will closely scrutinise both the rate statement and RBA Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference an hour later. They’ll be seeking clues on whether the central bank is prepared to deliver back-to-back hikes in November or prefers to watch and wait through the rest of the year.



“The risk sits with the need to tighten monetary policy further beyond September given the inflation backdrop,” said Belinda Allen, head of Australia Economics at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. “But it is not an easy decision to push monetary policy further into restrictive territory.” Related Article Opinion

Bonds Wall Street’s multitrillion-dollar question: Could bonds end the AI boom? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The central bank has stood pat at 4.35 per cent since May after opening the year aggressively, with rate rises at each of its first three meetings. On Wall Street overnight, yields in the US bond market cranked up and again reached their highest levels in roughly two decades, which knocked stocks further from their record high. The S&P 500 fell 0.8 per cent and gave back much of its gain from last week, which had brought it to the brink of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished down 0.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite lost 0.9 per cent.



US stocks felt pressure as the yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.23 per cent from 5.17 per cent late on Friday. That’s a considerable move for the centrepiece of the US bond market, taking the 10-year yield back to where it was in 2007, before the global financial crisis sent yields toward zero. Treasury yields have been jumping for a range of reasons, from worries about Washington’s massive debt load to rising energy costs from the Iran war, which boost inflation. That pressures the economy because it prompts higher interest rates, making borrowing money more expensive for everyone, while also undercutting prices for stocks and other investments. Monday’s rise in yields followed the latest swings for oil prices, which have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide. The latest turns came after President Donald Trump over the weekend rejected an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program. “I’d like to make a deal, too,” Trump said Saturday. “But that deal would not be acceptable.”



West Texas Intermediate futures settled below $US93 a barrel, up 0.5 per cent, after a day of choppy trading, which saw it rising by as much as 4.5 per cent during the session. Brent was up 1.3 per cent at $US105.71 a barrel. Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds for concrete progress on the nuclear issue, according to a US official. Iran’s nuclear program is a key sticking point for both sides. Traders have been parsing conflicting signals on progress towards a US-Iran ceasefire and a reopening of the vital waterway. Bloomberg reported that Iranian officials have privately expressed pessimism about reaching a deal to before the US midterm elections in November. Trump said that talks with Iran were held on Monday through mediators. The US president earlier rejected a proposal by Tehran to reopen Hormuz if Washington made some concessions. The stark shift in tone over the span of a day highlights the whiplash-inducing rhetoric traders have had to navigate since the conflict began seven months ago. “Without a concrete deal or conclusion to the conflict, the market is quickly fading initial headline reactions and higher prices are becoming harder to shake,” said Ryan McKay, senior commodity strategist at TD Securities. “The market is increasingly worried about escalation via Iran or the Houthis prior to midterm elections, or from the US post midterms.”



Related Article AI Nvidia unveils security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue On Wall Street, stocks of airlines and other companies with big fuel bills sank because of the rise in oil prices. American Airlines fell 2.5 per cent, and United Airlines lost 2.2 per cent. Gold miners were also weak after the price of gold sank 3.9 per cent. Gold has a reputation for helping to protect its investors from high inflation, but its price tends to weaken when rising yields mean bonds are paying investors more in interest. Gold struggles to keep up because it pays its investors nothing. Nvidia, Wall Street’s most influential stock, rose 1.7 per cent. The chip company said it approved a plan to send up to another $US150 billion to its shareholders in a stock buyback plan, bringing the program’s total remaining size to $US235 billion. Nvidia has the power to do so after the frenzy around its chips used for artificial-intelligence technology helped it more than double the amount of cash on its books in the first half of its fiscal year. The company also on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue.



AI stocks have broadly come under pressure after leaders of the industry said it needs to slow its development to give safety measures time to catch up. In other international markets, European indexes were mixed following weaker performances across much of Asia. Indexes dropped 2.7 per cent in Seoul and 1.7 per cent in Shanghai for two of the world’s bigger moves. with AP, Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Liberal MP Aaron Violi says the only way Australia will be able to defend itself from cyberattacks is to obtain the best frontier artificial intelligence models from the United States.

“Many of the big four banks, many large organisations, are using AI tools to identify risks and patch those risks in their company because, in a very simple way, AI allows users to find vulnerabilities that the human eye can’t see,” the opposition’s spokesman for the digital economy and cybersecurity told Radio National.

Liberal MP Aaron Violi. Alex Ellinghausen

“We have to embrace and use AI from a cybersecurity perspective. It’s already happening, and that’s why we need to have access to the frontier models because as they get better, the ability to defend gets better, but also the ability to attack obviously improves as well.”

Violi said the joint select committee on artificial intelligence, which he sits on, would examine how strong to make mandatory reporting requirements for breaches after OpenAI agents got into a Medicare portal, as well as how government departments could better communicate a breach.

“[The Medicare breach] looks like it’s on the relatively minor end. But we can improve that process, particularly if it is a major situation that we’re dealing with in the future,” he said.

World.title: Nvidia unveils security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Nvidia unveils security platform to stop AI agents from going rogue Kelvin Chan and Anne D'Innocenzio September 29, 2026 — 6:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nvidia has unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue. The company on Monday said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open-source software that “sets boundaries for agents,” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organisations. The disclosures sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control. Nvidia says its new security platform can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue. Bloomberg Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face.



“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” said the company’s vice president of enterprise AI, Justin Boitano, referring to companies at the forefront of AI. Related Article Exclusive

AI Anthropic boss to skip Senate grilling into rogue AI agents The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed the safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI’s models including breaching Australia’s Medicare website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organisations on their own. Nvidia’s software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more,” Boitano said. Because it’s open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.



The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said. “It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said. “OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behaviour,” Boitano said. Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has argued it’s up to AI companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Bloomberg Nvidia said more than 100 organisations are using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture, and JPMorgan Chase.



The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up. But others including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release. Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterised AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address. Biggest share buyback ever Also overnight, Nvdia said its board approved expanding its share buyback program by $US150 billion as the chipmaking giant looks to make use of more of its stellar revenue growth fuelled by demand for its high-end artificial intelligence chips. The company said Monday the share buyback increase, which it touted as the largest buyback in history, brings its stock repurchase program to $US235 billion. Its shares rose 1.6 per cent.



Companies use repurchases, in part, to return cash to investors and support the stock’s price. Earnings per share can increase because there are fewer shares outstanding. Buybacks also signal confidence from leadership about a company’s financial prospects. Related Article AI Inside the elite meeting where OpenAI lectured on security, a day before the hack was revealed “NVIDIA’s growth is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing,” said Huang. “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders. This authorisation reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead.” Nvidia’s high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for AI, and are highly sought after. The company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion late last month. While AI has powered stock market gains and US economic growth in recent years, there’s been growing scepticism about whether AI will justify the trillions of dollars being spent to develop the technology.



The AI industry also faces increasing pushback amid objections to the expansion of data centres and fears that the rapid speed of AI adoption could lead to widespread job losses worldwide. World.title: This city is banning drones and owners aren’t happy
World.content:
WorldAsiaInside China This city is banning drones and owners aren’t happy Lisa Visentin September 29, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beijing: At authorised buyback stores across Beijing, residents are reluctantly surrendering their drones to comply with a new ban that has sparked a rare venting of frustration from some owners in the usually tight-lipped city. Under rules announced this month, Beijing authorities imposed a total ban on the possession of drones inside the capital, forcing owners to sell them or move them out of the city by November 15. For the past fortnight, a steady procession of drone owners have queued at drone maker DJI’s stores and other designated buyback sites across the city to offload their devices, as complaints have circulated about low resale values and property rights. A man negotiates the sale of his drone at an official buyback retailer in Beijing ahead of a citywide ban on drones coming into effect on November 15. Fairfax Media “My freedom’s been restricted,” said Li, who spoke to this masthead outside a store in the city’s financial district using a pseudonym.



“This is not a fair and normal request for the government to ask citizens to take. It’s my property; I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to sell it.” Li said he originally paid about 5000 yuan ($1060) for his drone and only used it to take photos of friends and family and while travelling. It was now a “write-off”, he said. Chinese drone maker DJI is the global leader in consumer drones, but it can no longer sell the devices in Beijing. Bloomberg The September regulations extend and even override drone rules introduced only in May. Those earlier measures banned new drone sales and imposed a no-fly zone over Beijing without prior approval, but had allowed existing owners to keep their devices as long as they registered them with police. To comply with the May rules, DJI – a global leader in consumer drones and a Chinese company success story – and other sellers had to clear out stock from the shelves of their Beijing stores. It underscores an underlying tension in government policies, as Beijing tightens security measures over the capital while championing the low-altitude economy as one of the country’s key strategic industries.



The latest crackdown comes after a pilot flew a small recreational aircraft into Beijing’s tallest skyscraper in June, killing himself and injuring 13 people, in an incident that exposed security vulnerabilities over the city’s airspace. Related Article Updated

Air accident ‘An earthquake in the security system’: How did a plane crash into Beijing’s tallest building? Drones can still be purchased and flown outdoors in other parts of the country, provided they are registered with authorities. In Shenzhen, a tech hub in China’s south, drones regularly buzz over the CBD skies, delivering food to designated sites operated by takeaway giant Meituan. To cushion the blow, Beijing authorities are offering subsidies to owners who resell or recycle their devices through designated buyback platforms. Residents can also ship the drones out of the capital free of charge, or sell them to buyers in other Chinese cities on second-hand trading sites. Despite the November deadline, some owners have reported being contacted by police urging them to offload them more quickly. Others have taken to Chinese social media to lament low-ball offers on the second-hand market as buyers capitalise on the forced sales.



“I’m really reluctant to let it go,” one owner commented on Red Note, a video platform. “It comes with three batteries, and the system has only gone through a single charge cycle. A lot of people don’t see the value – they just treat it like a joke and are looking to snap it up at a bargain-basement price.” “I’m speechless,” said another said, who sold their device for a quarter of its retail value. “Literally bought it last August and flew it less than five times.” In the tech hub of Shenzhen, in southern China, consumers can have food delivered by drones to designated drop-off sites. Fairfax Media And selling to individuals outside Beijing can come with other hurdles. Li said he received a text message from his local residents’ committee – neighbourhood groups that are often closely affiliated with the Communist Party – advising that if he transferred the drone outside the city, he would need to provide photographic evidence of the buyer holding the drone in front of a prominent landmark.



“If I send it to Shanghai, the person would have to hold it on the Bund, or somewhere like that,” he said. Related Article Inside China Working from sun up to sun down, China’s delivery drivers caught in a price war At another buyback shop in Beijing, 26-year-old Chen said he was offered about 1400 yuan for his four-year-old DJI drone, about $125 less than he might get via a second-hand online retailer. But if the second-hand buyer disputed the purchase after receiving the drone, Chen wouldn’t be able to have the drone sent back to him in Beijing, potentially leaving him with nothing. Chen said he was dismayed by the policy, but believed it was trying to regulate irresponsible behaviour by drone flyers in the past.



“That eventually led to the situation we have now, where we’re no longer really able to fly drones even as a personal hobby. I think that’s quite a shame,” he said, giving only his surname. “We hope the government can continue improving the regulations, so that people can have ways to fly them.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: The arrival of John Longmire may be the most significant addition to Essendon in decades
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 The arrival of John Longmire may be the most significant addition to Essendon in decades Michael Gleeson September 29, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

John Longmire is one of Essendon’s most significant appointments in decades; in fact, he could be the most important. With unimpeachable football credentials as both player and coach, he is exactly the sort of person Essendon have needed, yet have been unable to attract for years. Essendon have pulled off a huge coup landing Sydney premiership coach John Longmire as their new head of performance. Getty Images His appointment as Essendon’s new head of performance instantly reshapes the image of the club. It changes the image of an organisation that has been smashed in recent years as amateurish. He gives authority to a football department and, by extension, to the club. He is not a messiah; he won’t single-handedly change Essendon on the field. What he is and what his appointment does is enhance the idea of Essendon bringing in football people of gravitas.



The Pullman sexual assault investigation has hurt the Sydney Swans’ reputation, but for decades, stretching back to Paul Roos then Longmire, the club had a football program and a playing culture that was the envy of other clubs. Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 Inside the ‘redemption campaign’ to reinstall James Hird Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age For two decades, the same could not be said of Essendon. The club has struggled to attract elite players and staff while being plagued by off-field factionalism. When the senior coaching position was vacant, some candidates pulled out fearing either a boat race for a pre-ordained candidate in James Hird, or were dissuaded by Essendon’s simmering factionalism. Club president Andrew Welsh and the board’s appointment of Mark McVeigh offered dual benefits: it secured a long-term assistant with multi-club experience, a current trend in modern coaching, while bringing a popular former Bomber back to the club.



Critically, he is also a friend and teammate of Hird’s and tightly connected with that generation of Essendon players. So if the club was not going to appoint, or re-appoint, Hird then hiring a person of McVeigh’s standing would silence any further agitation over Hird not being chosen. To bring in Longmire, the man McVeigh worked under at Sydney, to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with him at Essendon is as politically smart as it is a clever football appointment. It projects a mature image of the club to be embraced by such a respected figure. New Essendon coach Mark McVeigh was an assistant coach under Longmire at Sydney. Jason South Longmire does not come in as general manager of football, nor as coaching director. He is general manager of performance, which is a hybrid role blending parts of both coaching director and some responsibilities carved away from the general manager of football role. He will oversee not only coaching but player development, where the club has just hired Brent Prismall as their new head of development. Essendon is still looking for a new general manager of football. The belief at the club is that the role of the senior coach has become so big it is unreasonable to expect one person to cover everything without burning out.



The idea is that Longmire can ease some of the burden of media, corporate and commercial work that the senior coach would normally do, while also being involved in coaching, strategy, mentoring the coaches and overseeing player development. They insist he is not coming in as de facto head coach. Whether Longmire will be in the coaches’ box on match day with McVeigh or whether McVeigh coaches from the boundary while Longmire is in the box is yet to be decided. But it will be McVeigh’s decision – he is the head coach. Essendon now appear to have a blend of two coaching types. One, in McVeigh, is the 45-year-old assistant who has done a long apprenticeship in good programs and is ready for a senior gig like Craig McRae and Damien Hardwick were, and like Josh Fraser is. In Longmire, on the coaching panel and in football management, they have something of the avuncular Chris Fagan type. Loading The appointment of Longmire furthers what has been a wholesale turnover of the football department over two years, started by former CEO Craig Vozzo and who, after stepping down for personal and family reasons, has continued to consult the club on how a football department should look and be structured.





They got veteran CEO Greg Swann in and set about making sure they had in place good people in key roles across coaching, football management and list management. The playing side was the slowest piece because young talent coming in, moving players out to turn the list over, and then instituting a cultural change can take time to filter through before you see results on the field. Essendon have been trying to do something similar. David Barham started the process before passing it over to Welsh, who has worn some political heat, but he has made some big decisions. Securing Longmire is the biggest of them. Get around our AFL finals coverage Post mortem: Is ‘Wharfie Time’ dead?

World.title: Legal action hovers over restart to FENZ restructure
World.content:
Two unions are threatening legal action against Fire and Emergency over its proposed restructure.

The PSA and Professional Firefighters' Union wrote to FENZ chairman Raveen Jaduram asking him to immediately suspend the restructure but he refused.

"We have prepared legal proceedings, but we are hoping that they will not be necessary," PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons wrote 11 days ago.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons. Supplied

The unions argue that with FENZ's leadership in strife - a recent inquiry faulted it and information withheld by the chief executive Kerry Gregory has been referred to the Serious Fraud Office - the plan they came up with almost a year ago to overhaul the agency should at least be paused or ditched entirely.

Jaduram pushed back to Fitzsimons.

"The issues you raise in relation to Mr Gregory are distinct, and do not warrant suspension of the current restructuring process."

FENZ chief executive Kerry Gregory. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

FENZ told RNZ it was going ahead, talking with a "small number of our people through targeted re-consultations over the next few weeks".

It would then look at all the feedback and make final decisions.

Last November it proposed axing about 140 jobs and changing about 700 other roles among its 3000 staff. Controversy over changes to the likes of wildfire response roles followed.

But a court found FENZ did not consult properly. Since then, its plan has been held up and is still in limbo.

The United Fire Brigades' Association that represents 14,000 volunteers said on Monday it was "fully consulted by FENZ leaders many months ago on the reasons for the change" and awaited the further consultation on amendments.

The Government says it's an operational matter and up to FENZ. Labour repeated this on Tuesday, adding "the situation at FENZ has become untenable".

At the same time, National has announced a plan to reset the agency if re-elected; and Labour says it will hold an independent review of it.

Head of the professional firefighters' union, Wattie Watson, said all these were reasons to hit pause.

Head of the professional firefighters' union Wattie Watson. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"For them to pursue a restructure that was driven by Kerry Gregory is foolhardy and could have some serious ramifications where they lose people that have a capability needed or they spend a lot of money and cause a lot of grief," she said on Monday.

But Jaduram thought otherwise.

"A substantial number of people from Fire and Emergency have been involved in developing the proposals and the process to date, including all of the executive leadership team, and Fire and Emergency has received considerable input from staff and the unions to inform its current thinking," he wrote to the unions.

Brooke van Velden. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

FENZ said on Tuesday it had received a letter from minister Brooke van Velden expressing no confidence in Gregory.

"The board is having discussions in relation to the minister's concerns and has been in touch with the chief executive to convey this, noting that he is currently out of the country. The board chair has met with the minister."

World.title: EVs being trialled as giant batteries to power homes for less in Auckland
World.content:
A trial to test how EVs can be used as giant batteries that could power households for less is being launched in Auckland.

The Energy Efficiency and Conservation Authority said up to 100 two-way chargers will be installed in homes and businesses in the city and other urban areas, to explore how the technology could save households money and make the energy system more resilient.

Two-way chargers allow EVs to charge as usual, but then discharge that electricity back to a home, business, or even back to the national grid at times of peak power use.

That means households can charge their EV when power is cheap, and either use the stored energy themselves at peak times, or sell any surplus back when the price is high.

A charged EV with a two-way system could also help a household to get through power outages caused by storms or other severe weather.

The technology - known as vehicle-to-household or vehicle-to-grid - is gradually rolling out internationally.

Australia has already run large trials and two-way charging is now available in certain circumstances in New South Wales and South Australia.

However, EECA said that two-way chargers that can discharge to the grid are not widely available in New Zealand, and the technology is relatively untested here.

The new trial will build on a smaller trial that is already underway and expanding in Queenstown.

"The findings will help build an evidence base to inform future policies and guidance that enable two-way chargers to be rolled out effectively across New Zealand," EECA policy and regulation manager Murray Bell said.

Most people with EVs charged them at home, he said.

"This means there is potential to use parked vehicles for energy storage while they are charging."

There were lots of possible benefits for households, including lowering their electricity bills.

The potential upsides also extended to lines companies and the national grid, by reducing peak electricity demand, EECA said.

Less strain on transmission and distribution networks would reduce the need for costly upgrades.

The Ministry for Business, Innovation and Employment expects New Zealand's electricity demand to increase by between 35 and 82 percent by 2050, as the economy - including transport and industry - shifts from fossil fuels to low-emissions energy sources.

Counties Energy, which runs national EV charging service OpenLoop, would be EECA's partner for the trial, overseeing participant recruitment and charger deployment.

As well as passenger EVs, the trial could include a small number of heavy vehicle chargers.

Findings from the trial would be published regularly, EECA said.

It had just published a market study from its Queenstown trial, setting out some of the hurdles that exist in New Zealand.

World.title: Wellington Indoor Sports to close one of its sites
World.content:
A Wellington indoor sports centre is shutting one of its sites after nearly two decades.

Wellington Indoor Sports (WIS) announced it would be closing its City Station location on 31 October after KiwiRail ended its lease.

The company's director Mukesh Dayal said it was "pretty much the end of an era".

He said the venue had served 200 sports teams.

He said the company's Shed 1 location would remain open, but this didn't have space for indoor cricket or netball. He was looking for another venue that was the right size and height for to accommodate a court.

"It's hard to find locations like that within Wellington."

Dayal said he wanted to relocate some staff to Hutt Indoor Sports, but others would need to find other jobs.

"I just feel sorry for the staff, really."

Wellington Indoor Sports and KiwiRail had the property revalued separately a couple of years ago, Dayal said.

He said KiwiRail renewed a two-year lease with a 20 percent rent increase in line with Wellington Indoor Sports' valuation - the lesser of the two.

He said KiwiRail offered to renew the lease for another year, with the agreement it could break the lease if it found a tenant who would pay rent in line with KiwiRail's higher valuation of the property.

A spokesperson for KiwiRail said details about the arrangement were commercially confidential.

"KiwiRail has finalised a lease agreement with a new tenant. The new tenancy is also sports related," the spokesperson said.

Dayal said he had tried to get help from Wellington City Council and Associate Minister for Sport Chris Bishop, who he said passed the request on to Minister for Sport Mark Mitchell.

But he said nobody was able to intervene in the negotiation of a commercial lease.

He said he would have been willing to break even on the location but not take a loss and so had to close.

Fans expressed their disappointment online.

One wrote in the comments of WIS' Facebook announcement: "This is so sad. But thank you to the amazing team behind the scenes who kept things so fun for so long."

World.title: Are healthcare workers obligated to help you during a medical emergency?
World.content:
The death of a man on a footpath outside an Auckland medical centre earlier this month has prompted questions about the obligations of health staff.

Several members of the public had tried to save the man, who was in his late 60s or early 70s, after he was discovered outside the Mt Albert Medical Centre with a faint pulse and unusual breathing.

Do you know more? Email melanie.earley@rnz.co.nz

Witnesses said staff at the clinic declined to help or let members of the public use their defibrillator, before the man died on September 10.

Now, another Auckland man has come forward to allege he was also denied help during a medical emergency.

Sam Behzadi said he experienced a sudden loss of motor function in his feet and was unable to walk, requiring help from a member of the public, after giving blood at Awanui Labs in Onehunga in March.

The Good Samaritan went back into the lab to seek help, Behzadi said, and a nurse and senior manager came outside.

"They told me my condition was not related to the blood test, and I should return home and call an ambulance.

"I couldn't walk, so the member of the public drove me home and my wife took me to hospital."

Behzadi spent eight weeks in hospital and was diagnosed with a spinal stroke associated with spinal injury.

"It left me questioning the clinical response and more broadly, the responsibility of healthcare practitioners to appropriately assess and respond when a person presents with acute and serious medical conditions.

"I would have expected the response to be focused first and foremost on ensuring the immediate safety of a person."

Awanui labs' chief operations officer Nick Champness said Awanui staff were trained to respond to medical events at the centres and teams assisted patients experiencing adverse reactions including fainting or other medical episodes.

In Behzadi's case, two staff members went outside to help- but his symptoms were outside the scope of their clinical training and expertise, Champness said. The staff went to the neighbouring medical centre for additional help.

He said incident record notes had shown medical centre staff at The Doctors Onehunga suggested Behzadi go home and call an ambulance rather than Awanui staff.

"While we don't have further information about the circumstances of the medical event, we can confirm that our staff responded to a request for assistance and sought additional medical support when the situation presented was beyond their scope of clinical practice."

General manager of The Doctors, Wayne Woolrich said his team member's recollection differed from Behzadi's and the lab workers.

"Our team member recalled going to the individual's car and offering to provide an assessment in the clinic and offering to call an ambulance."

Woolrich said the team member noted they were given "limited information" by Behzadi and the lab staff member and did not know a medical event occurred.

Behzadi claims while staff approached the car, they stayed five metres away and did not help or ask what he was experiencing.

"They didn't approach me or carry out any physical examination."

What is a healthcare worker expected to do in a medical emergency?

Dr Ken Clark is the chairperson for the Medical Council, the official body responsible for regulating doctors - making sure they're "competent and fit to practice" - to protect the health and safety of the public.

Dr Ken Clark. (File photo)

Doctors had an ethical obligation to respond promptly if needed, he said.

If they chose not to attend, they needed to be able to justify their decision.

"Good Medical Practice provides additional information for doctors in an emergency, that they should offer to help, taking account of their own safety, competence and the availability of other options for care."

The council's standards only applied to doctors, Clark said, while the Nursing Council advised on nurse's obligations and healthcare providers on reception staff and clinic procedures.

"We take seriously any concerns about a doctor's competence, conduct or fitness to practise," he said.

"Concerns about the care or treatment a person received can be raised with the Health and Disability Commissioner. HDC can refer matters to Council where concerns about a doctor require our consideration."

Anyone concerned about the competence of a doctor, their conduct or their fitness to practise could notify the council using an online form on its website.

The Nursing Council said its job was to regulate nurses and set standards of practice and conduct expected of the profession.

Its code of conduct included an expectation that nurses offer assistance in an emergency, taking into account competence, safety and the availability of other options.

"Whether a nurse's actions were appropriate in a particular circumstance depends on the specific facts of the situation," a spokesperson said.

World.title: Multicultural groups demand Ethnic Communities Ministry rethink
World.content:
Multicultural New Zealand has called on political parties to rethink the role of the Ministry for Ethnic Communities as the country moves closer to a general election.

The organisation wanted responsibility for cultural diversity to sit across all government portfolios instead of sitting with a single ministry.

The call came as part of a declaration released at the New Zealand Federation of Multicultural Councils' annual general meeting in the capital earlier this month.

It was attended by 23 regional multicultural councils from across New Zealand, which are all part of Multicultural New Zealand.

Pancha Narayan, president of Multicultural New Zealand, pointed to what he said was a "unanimous agreement [at the annual meet] that New Zealand needs a new approach to recognise and serve [its] cultural diversity".

"That's why we are calling for a fundamental review of the Minister for Ethnic Communities' portfolio and the Ministry for Ethnic Communities," Narayan said.

"Cultural diversity is not the responsibility of one ministry," he said.

"It affects every part of government, including health, education, employment, housing, justice, economic development and public services," he said.

"The ministry has valuable functions that should be retained and strengthened, particularly community engagement, evidence, advice, advocacy and improving the responsiveness of government services.

"But responsibility for outcomes should sit across government. Every minister and agency should be accountable for how their policies and services respond to New Zealand's cultural diversity."

Established in July 2021, the Ministry for Ethnic Communities is the government's chief advisor on ethnic diversity and inclusion in the country.

It succeeded the Office of Ethnic Affairs, which was set up in 2001 and worked as a stand-alone unit within the Department of Internal Affairs.

The proposed "new approach to cultural diversity", Narayan said, meant separating religion from culture.

"People from the same culture can have different religions or no religion," Narayan said. "[Similarly] religious communities also cross ethnic, cultural and national boundaries.

"[That's why] Multicultural New Zealand is calling for the establishment of an independent Crown entity for religious affairs.

"It will provide impartial advice on religious freedom, and the relationship between religion and the state, within New Zealand's human rights and constitutional framework."

In similar vein, Narayan didn't believe the term "ethnic communities" reflected contemporary New Zealand.

"It has increasingly become shorthand for immigrants, former refugees and recent migrants," he said.

"That is too narrow. The time has come to move beyond 'ethnic communities' as the overarching government policy framework."

The regional multicultural councils present at the meeting also pledged to build respectful relationships with tangata whenua and deepen their understanding of Te Ao Māori.

Ethnic Communities Minister Mark Mitchell RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Ethnic Communities Minister Mark Mitchell praised the ministry for its "outstanding work supporting a wide range of communities across New Zealand".

"I am proud of the services they deliver - from helping ethnic communities access government services, working on social cohesion and providing advice, information and support in relation to foreign interference," Mitchell said.

The minister agreed the entire government was responsible for the welfare of ethnic communities in New Zealand, not just one ministry.

"Multicultural New Zealand is correct that responsibility for outcomes should sit across government, and it does," he said.

"The ministry's role is primarily as chief advisor on the perspective of ethnic communities, a job which they do very well."

Separately, ruling coalition partner ACT said in March it wanted to abolish the ministry and fold its functions into other ministries.

Todd Stephenson, finance spokesperson for ACT, claimed the Ministry for Ethnic Communities funded political activism through its Ethnic Communities Development Fund.

"The ministry was set up to support social cohesion and help us understand each other. Instead, they're funding divisive political activism," Stephenson said.

"ACT would end the Ethnic Communities Development Fund tomorrow, saving New Zealanders $4 million a year. In fact, we would abolish the Ministry for Ethnic Communities and fold any functions that are actually delivering value into other ministries."

World.title: Hallenstein Glasson delivers sharp lift in annual earnings
World.content:
Hallenstein Glasson continues to defy the retail gloom on the high street, posting another strong set of results for the full year ended August.

Net profit after tax rose by 49.9 percent from the year before to $59.2 million, and total group sales climbed nearly 20 percent to $563.0 million.

Key numbers for the year ended 1 August 2026 compared with a year ago:

Net profit $59.2m vs $39.5m

Revenue $563.0m vs $470.7m

Operating profit $87.4m vs $61.0m

Gross margin 61.7% vs 59.3%

Final dividend 40 cents per share

The company's Australian operations continued to be the engine room of growth.

Glassons Australia's sales rose by 29 percent to $324.4 million.

The group operates 41 stores across the Tasman and says it continues to evaluate new store opportunities, and its new Sydney warehouse has commenced operations.

Sales of the Glassons brand in New Zealand rose by 11.5 percent to $124.8 million from the year before, as the company refurbished and expanded town-centre stores in Hamilton and Porirua.

The Hallensteins side of the business - including Australia - had slower sales growth of 6.1 percent, taking revenue to $113.8 million, but its pre-tax profit more than doubled to $10.9 million.

The result was also backed by tight stock control and strong cash generation.

Inventory slipped to $30.4 million despite the rise in sales, while operating cash flow increased 38 percent to $122.2 million.

The group ended the year with $88.2 million in cash and short-term deposits, and no interest-bearing bank debt.

The company declared a final dividend of 40 cents per share, partially imputed, bringing full-year dividends to 69.0 cents per share.

Update on trading

The company said sales in the first eight weeks of the new financial year were 18.4 percent ahead of the same period last year, as new and refurbished stores came online.
