Notably, it does not expect that rate of growth to continue even with the Black Friday and Christmas trading periods approaching.

It also noted the uncertain geopolitical and economic backdrop, as well as potential changes in consumer spending and foreign currency movements.

World.title: Health insurance customers urged to read the fine print as complaints soar
World.content:
Audio player for " Health insurance complaints almost double " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1643899%2Fhealth-insurance-customers-urged-to-read-the-fine-print-as-complaints-soar

Health insurance complaints almost double Nine To Noon Download MP3 13m

The finance ombudsman says problems in the public health system and rising costs are behind a surge in complaints over insurance companies refusing payouts, and encouraged customers to read the fine print of their policies.

Health insurance was now the largest category of disputes to the ombudsman for the first time in the year to June, increasing by 91 percent.

Part of the rise in health disputes was insurers using clauses that allowed them to limit the amount they spend on a claim to what they deem to be "reasonable".

Insurance and Financial Services Ombudsman Karen Stevens told Nine to Noon the jump in complaints was due to people being under financial pressure and issues with the public health system.

"It's about them wanting to have options and unfortunately, health insurance has tightened up in terms of what it used to be," she said.

"A lot of complaints you resolved with a goodwill payment, an ex gratia payment, the health insurers aren't as willing to do that as they used to be because from their perspective it affects all of their customers if they're paying claims outside of the terms and conditions of the policy.

"So, they're not as willing to do that as they used to be. There's a tightening up in the health industry, there's a growing problem I think in public health and people are more concerned about what they're paying generally."

Stevens said there was a growing number of complaints over people having to pay the difference between what their surgeons charged, and what their insurance was willing to pay.

That was a real worry, she said.

"Because the thing is that there is no ability for our scheme, IFSO (Insurance & Financial Services Ombudsman Scheme), to make insurers pay and equally there is no remedy for consumers who get stuck between a surgeon's costs and what their insurer is willing to pay for them," Stevens said.

Insurance and Financial Services Ombudsman Karen Stevens. Supplied / IFSO

Stevens said there was fresh debate on what the word "reasonable" meant and how that was interpreted.

She acknowledged that some of the surgery costs were "eye-watering", and it had gone up considerably over the last few years.

Stevens said most people didn't read their policies.

"There is a lot of fine print, it's much better than it used to be but there's still a lot to get through and unless you feel that you have to you, don't, and that goes for all of us, me included," she said.

"I don't tend to read every single word in every single policy unless I'm doing it for my job.

"The problem with that is that sometimes you can be surprised, and not in a good way and so, you take out a policy and you assume that you're covered, which many people do."

Many consumers assumed they were covered for a certain thing or though they should be, she said.

"I agree with the thinking to a point but it's a legal contract and if you take out an insurance policy and it doesn't cover you for something which you think it should, it's really sad but it's not going to cover you and there is nothing that we can do retrospectively to make that cover sort of material," Stevens said.

Stevens said there was always going to be a disconnect between what people thought they were getting, and what they actually got.

She urged customers to read their policies.

"Make sure that you actually read the policy, that you understand at least the basics of what you're getting and what you're not getting," Stevens said.

"If you're working with an advisor, they are really the best people to the financial advisors to give you that sort of advice on particularly as you've mentioned trauma cover income protection disability cover.

World.title: Person seriously injured after crash between car and pedestrian in Bay of Plenty
World.content:
One person has serious injuries after a crash between a car and a pedestrian in the Bay of Plenty.

Police were called to the crash between Maungarangi Rd and Old Coach Rd at 9.20am on Tuesday.

State Highway 33 in Paengaroa was closed.

It was expected to stay closed for some time while emergency services work at the scene.

World.title: Bombers poach former Swans premiership coach John Longmire
World.content:
Essendon have poached former Sydney premiership coach John Longmire as their new general manager of performance in a huge recruiting coup.

Longmire departs Sydney after 25 years in various roles to reunite with his former assistant, new Bombers coach Mark McVeigh, in a new role.

"I'm really excited to be joining the Essendon Football Club," Longmire said in a statement.

"I've known Mark for a long time and have worked with him as well. He is passionate about the Bombers and has a clear vision for the team.

"I look forward to supporting both him and the staff as the club looks to take the necessary steps back towards being a consistent team who challenge the opposition every week."

The Bombers have effectively split the football boss role in two, with Longmire to oversee game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group, performance analytics and strength and conditioning.

The 55-year-old, most recently Sydney's executive director of club performance, will start this week ahead of the trade period.

John Longmire won the 2012 AFL premiership with the Swans in a 14-season spell as head coach. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Landing Longmire, who did not pursue any vacant head coach roles, is a huge result for the battling Bombers, who finished last on the ladder and needed to put support around first-year coach McVeigh.

"John's football experience and leadership are exactly what we have been looking for in this role," Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said in a statement.

"We have made no secret of our ambition to build a football program capable of delivering sustained success, and bringing in someone of John's calibre is a significant investment in that goal.

"Over 14 seasons as senior coach of the Sydney Swans, John built a program that consistently competed at the pointy end, including the 2012 premiership and four further grand final appearances.

"He knows what a winning program looks like from the inside and how to sustain it year after year.

"Just as importantly, John will be an enormous asset to Mark McVeigh.

"Very few people understand the demands of the senior coach role like John does and having someone of his experience alongside Mark to provide support, guidance and a sounding board will allow Mark to focus on coaching and developing our players."

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham hailed Longmire as a "much-loved and respected figure" and "legend".

Longmire joined Sydney as an assistant coach in 2002 and was involved in the drought-breaking 2005 premiership, later succeeding Paul Roos.

Across 333 games, Longmire, the Swans' longest-serving coach had a 63 per cent winning record, won the 2012 premiership and led Sydney to five grand finals and 12 finals campaigns.

He stepped down after the 2024 grand final loss to Brisbane.

"Having arrived at the Swans 25 years ago this club has meant so much to me and my family," Longmire said in a Swans statement.

"I will look back with extreme fondness of my time in Sydney and always be proud of what we achieved as a football club."

AAP

World.title: 'I'll be back': Cleary vows to return after surgery
World.content:
Penrith Panthers star Nathan Cleary has vowed to return after his 2026 season was brutally cut short on Sunday, thanking fans for their support from his hospital bed.

The 28-year-old suffered a horrific compound fracture of his left ankle in the Panthers' NRL preliminary final defeat against Newcastle, ruling him out of the Kangaroos' World Cup campaign.

The Panthers, who led 14-6 at half-time, ultimately fell apart to lose to the 12-man Knights, 22-14.

On Monday, the star halfback posted a photo from hospital, with his left leg bandaged following surgery.

"Surgery done," he wrote on Instagram, with a photo of him smiling and giving thumbs up to the camera.

"Thank you so much to everyone that has reached out, the support has been unbelievable.

"Yesterday sucked but it's all part of the journey and it's made me even more grateful for the people I have around me.

"I'll be back."

Nathan Cleary was taken from the field in agony. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The gruesome injury cast a pall over the Sydney Olympic Stadium, with Panthers players visibly distressed on field while their star was being treated by medical staff.

"He's one of my best mates," Panthers captain Isaah Yeo said post-match.

"He's your brother out there. You don't like seeing anyone like that. You just want to be there for him.

"It's a lonely little place out there when you've got something like that going on."

Cleary's father, coach Ivan Cleary, also revealed that seeing his son in such a state at half-time was "emotional".

It was later revealed that Cleary, who started the game from the bench, was already playing with a broken bone in his right foot as the Panthers hoped to manage his involvement in the prelim with half an eye looking forward to next weekend's grand final against the Sydney Roosters.

Cleary came onto the field 25 minutes into the first half, but only lasted 10 minutes before Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland fell onto his ankle in a tackle.

Crossland was sent off for a hip drop and was sent straight to the NRL judiciary by the match review committee, where a lengthy suspension could not only rule him out of Newcastle's first NRL grand final in 25 years, but also impact the Kiwi's World Cup campaign.

Slater calls for change

Phoenix Crossland is unlikely to play in the grand final. (Getty Images)

Crossland is likely to face a lengthy ban, but has been given support from former Maroons coach Billy Slater.

Speaking on The Billy Slater Podcast, Slater said the current rules were leaving players unsure as to how to tackle players effectively without giving away a penalty.

"It has to come down to the responsibility of the tackler," Slater said.

"[But] I honestly feel the game has a little bit of a responsibility in this as well. When you change interpretations and change rules, you always have a flow-on effect.

"If you think about the protection of kickers and ball players and not being able to tackle them even fractionally after they pass the ball … 10 years ago this wouldn't have happened. Fifteen years ago that tackle would not have happened because Phoenix Crossland would've had more speed and force going into that tackle.

"But because he was worried about tackling Nathan after he passed the ball he was actually in a passive position.

"He was on his inside, which is normally when you put pressure on the ball player and you go out and you make tackles on that ball player, even after they pass the ball slightly.

"Phoenix wasn't in that mindset. He was in a passive mindset thinking Nathan was going to pass, then all of a sudden Nathan threw a dummy and he had to make a tackle and he didn't have that force behind him.

"I've got no doubt that has contributed to why Phoenix Crossland is in this grabbing and sitting down position, because he doesn't have that momentum and force and mindset of making a tackle."

The NRL judiciary will sit on Tuesday, with Crossland needing to argue his case to have any chance of playing in the 2026 grand final.

World.title: Socceroos expect Brazil backlash in Brisbane
World.content:
Ageless Socceroo Aziz Behich has no plans to pull the pin with the side on the rise, buoyed by a performance against Brazil they are keen to do better than in Brisbane.

Australia conceded a goal with the final play of their Townsville clash on Friday to walk away with a 1-1 draw that, tellingly, left them disappointed.

A Brazilian backlash is expected at Lang Park on Tuesday night, and the A-League's only player in the 26-man squad is primed to counter it.

"We've set the bar high for ourselves … it was good, but we need to be better," the 35-year-old said.

"How brave we were on the ball … we trusted each other and took the game on.

"When you do that against an opponent like that, you earn their respect and we need to do that again, that's for sure."

Incredibly Behich's 88th national appearance was his first game since the World Cup, but the veteran was able to display his trademark pace and work rate despite being in preseason mode with Melbourne City.

There is optimism the next generation of talent will take the Socceroos to new heights and, with the Asian Cup on the horizon in January, Behich plans to do more than stick around.

"I wouldn't call it hanging on … I'm still playing at a high level … it's exciting times," he said.

"I feel great. I'm a player that's always honest with myself. I know when I'm not at a level I should be. But I have a lot in the tank to give."

The Socceroos took the lead against Brazil, and deserved it as well. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Coach Tony Popovic echoed Behich's sentiment ahead of the Brisbane rematch.

"Being confident, being brave … we've clearly seen a difference in the players' demeanour since the World Cup," he said.

He said the challenge would be to back-up that performance on a short-turnaround.

"We don't have players playing regular Champions League, or in the top leagues, 60 games a year," he said.

"It's a great test."

The Brisbane fixture serves as a homecoming for rising defender Lucas Herrington.

The 19-year-old played his last game for the Roar in January this year, before using the World Cup to springboard from Colorado in the MLS to Hull in the Premier League.

"We've seen against Brazil a confident young man, defending against the very best," Popovic said.

"Now he's got the challenge of doing something he maybe hasn't done in a while, against that calibre, backing up three, four days later.

"Can the body do it and are you ready to play at that level once more?"

AAP

World.title: Matthews claims world championship silver after life-threatening crash
World.content:
Michael Matthews felt that his career was probably over at the start of the season.

Having missed a large portion of the 2025 season after a pulmonary embolism was discovered in his lung, a horrific collision with a fire truck while training in March could have cost him an awful lot more than just his career.

But less than eight months later the 36-year-old was standing on the world championship podium for the fourth time in his career, claiming second place in what was the greatest possible silver lining after two years of desperately bad luck.

"I'm pretty speechless I'm sitting here with a silver medal around my neck," Matthews said.

"Honestly, I wasn't sure exactly how today was going to go.

"The field was so strong. Leading into the race, I was quietly confident, but the world championships is always a bit of a lottery."

Michael Matthews felt he might not have been able to ride during the world championships after a horrific two seasons. (Supplied: AusCycling/Craig Render)

Matthews led the chasing pack home 13 seconds behind surprise American winner Brandon McNulty after a brutal 273.4-kilometre course in and around Montréal in Canada.

The Australian edged out former champion Mathieu van der Poel and Quinn Simmonds, who were both classified with the same time.

His silver medal will sit alongside the road race silver he won 11 years ago in Richmond, Virginia, as well ass road race bronze medals in 2017 (Bergen) and 2022 (Wollongong).

Matthews also has two gold medals and a bronze in the mixed team relay at world championships, and was the winner of the under 23 title in Geelong in 2010.

"I think this was probably my last opportunity to be a world champion. So, obviously, mixed feelings, but at the same time, I have to be proud of what the way I've bounced back," Matthews said.

"To be second around here on a circuit that many said was out of my reach, to show everyone that I'm still up there with the best in the world even after what I've been through, at the moment feels like a win."

Just getting to the start line would have been a victory of sorts for Matthews.

On March 5, the veteran Australian rider crashed head-on with a fire truck at a combined speed of 100km/h.

Michael Matthews was lucky to be able to continue after his horrific crash in March. (Supplied: Instagram/@Bling90)

Matthews suffered an open arm fracture, severed thumb tendons, broke both wrists and sustained a sinus fracture that required stitches to his face.

"I hit a fire truck at pretty much 100km/h, I was doing 50 and the truck was doing 50," Matthews told the Detour podcast prior to this year's Tour de France.

"With a crash like that, it could have ended my career, or even worse.

"I might not be here right now. I'm extremely blessed to be able to tell the story and how lucky I was."

Matthews said there were a couple of times over the past two years when he felt he would never be back at the pointy end of the professional peloton, crediting his family for always believing in him.

"What I've been through the last two years, with embolia in my lungs, thinking my career was done, to breaking both my arms at the start of this year, thinking my career was done. Now, bouncing back to being second in the Worlds road race — just speechless, honestly," he said.

"I said to my wife at the start of today, 'Let's just leave it all out there and be proud of the ride at the end of the day, make sure you finish with nothing.'

"It's exactly what happened today when I crossed the finish line. I put my head in my hands almost in disbelief.

"Honestly, it's just credit to my family, to the team, to all the support crew around me that didn't stop believing this could happen right now. So, I owe everything to them."

Michael Matthews was almost in disbelief at winning silver. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

The race itself was an absolute barnstormer of a contest from the very off.

Two-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar was absent from the race, recovering from a fractured neck and collarbone that he suffered in a crash that took him out of the Vuelta a España last month.

That left the race wide open, with a number of riders all believing they had a chance to claim the rainbow bands on a course that was hard enough to interest the climbers as much as the one-day specialist rouleurs.

The race exploded with 90km to go as Oscar Onley, van der Poel, Wout van Aert, Simmons and Primož Roglič built a lead, which was whittled down by the French team, led by Paul Seixas, and Isaac del Toro.

A flurry of frantic accelerations and regroupings at the front made for a frenetic, thrilling race, with the USA well placed with three of the leading 13 riders.

McNulty fired off the front with just over 30km to go and, despite brilliant surges from Ireland's Ben Healy and Britain's Tom Pidcock, the American soloed to victory.

Brandon McNulty is America's third male world road race champion after Lance Armstrong and Greg Lemond. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

The 28-year-old American, who rides with Pogačar at UAE Team Emirates-XRG, is just the third American to win the men's world road race title and the first since Lance Armstrong in Oslo in 1993.

"I'm really at a loss," McNulty said.

"Until the last hundred metres, I didn't believe it, I was so tired. I was just dying, but I kept pushing. We have said for weeks now that we had a super strong team. We talked about it, but I knew it would take a miracle. I guess miracles happen."

World.title: Hauser wins thrilling World Triathlon sprint, Parker breaks record
World.content:
Australian triathlete Matt Hauser showed he was up for the fight at the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Pontevedra, Spain overnight, beating Vasco Vilaça to the line in a thrilling sprint finish.

Defending series champion Hauser came into the series finale knowing he would be up against it to retain his title.

A number of crashes throughout the year meant Hauser needed to win and beat Vilaça by five places.

The Portuguese triathlete was in no mood to let the Australian get any sort of gap though, sticking with him through the swim and shadowing on the bike before the tremendous run stage.

"That's just ridiculous. I was just telling myself I can't lose this one, I can't lose this one," Hauser said.

"I've been so up and down this year and so inconsistent. I just really wanted it out there today.

"There is a lot to be thankful for and pleased for. I was really happy to get the win out there today and to execute when it really mattered.

"I'm not back-to-back world champion, but I can hang my head high. I achieved what I set out to achieve today and now looking onwards and upwards for next year."

Matt Hauser pushed the pace on the front during the run. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Hauser and Vilaça ran away from Olympic champion Alex Yee, whose stunning run leg bought him into contention in the closing stages.

The Briton could not stay with the leading pair though as they engaged in what turned into a furious battle for the line.

Hauser's 'world champion persona' Despite being Australia's first male triathlon world champion in 20 years, Matt Hauser is still building the blocks towards his aim of Olympic success in 2028.

Both men were credited with a time of 1:39:31, but the Australian's dip on the line ensured he would claim victory by 0.08 seconds.

"Credit to Vasco, what a champion," Hauser said.

"I mean we got a bit pushy, shovy in the end. Apologies to him. I gave him a bit of a bump on my way through to get to the line first.

"[But] you have to do these things to get the victory sometimes, to have that dog in you.

"I didn't want to lose the sprint finish to Vacsco. I haven't lost all year to him.

"I have this notch in my belt this year and will take the momentum into next year and to LA2028."

Lauren Parker breaks record

Lauren Parker now has a record six world para triathlon titles. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Lauren Parker also claimed victory in the PTWC race in Pontevedra, cementing her status as one of Australia's greatest-ever para triathletes.

PTWC events are for athletes who use a wheelchair in their daily life.

Racers in the PTWC category compete in a standard 750-metre open-water swim, but can use swim-exit handlers to help them out of the water. They then race a recumbent handcycle for the 20km cycling leg, before using a racing wheelchair for the 5km run leg.

The reigning Paralympic champion was never troubled in the race, leading from early on in the swim and thereafter, cruising to victory.

"I felt awesome out there in swim, bike and run," Parker said.

"I got a decent lead in the swim … I got on the bike and I felt so strong out there and I was pulling time into the girls, and extended my lead."

"And in the run, I was just holding them off."

The win secured the 37-year-old multi-sport star a sixth PTWC World Championship title.

It made Parker Australia's most successful ever Para triathlete, beating the legendary Bill Chaffey's previous benchmark of five world championship titles.

"It's just as special as my first title," Parker said.

"My first title was obviously [special because] it was my first. Number six means I've overtaken Bill Chaffey. It's awesome."

Parker won the PTWC class para-triathlon race at the Paris Olympics, having won silver in the same event in Tokyo in 2021.

She then backed up that performance to win para-cycling gold in the H1–4 road race and silver in the H1-3 time trial as well.

Not only that, but Parker can add four rainbow jerseys as a cycling world champion to her triathlon titles.

The Newcastle athlete also took to the snow in the past year, competing in both the biathlon and cross-country skiing at the Milano-Cortina Paralympic Winter Games in 2026.

Elsewhere, Anu Francis secured silver in the Women's PTS2 World Championship race.

The PTS2 classification is for non-wheelchair users for athletes who live with muscle power disorders or limb deficiencies.

World.title: Sandon Smith leads Newcastle out of an Immortal shadow
World.content:
It's rare that anybody in Newcastle shares an accolade with Andrew Johns, but Sandon Smith has managed it.

Fresh off his electric double in the Knights' 22-14 win over Penrith on Sunday, Smith will join Johns as the only men to play halfback for Newcastle in a grand final.

"It's pretty cool to hear. I don't think I'm anywhere near that [Johns]," Smith said.

"But it's an honour."

Talking about Johns is part of the deal when you play halfback for Newcastle but it's wrong to compare the two because it's wrong to compare anyone to Johns, who stands alone as the club and the city's ultimate legend and hero.

Johns was more than just a player to the Knights, even if he's the best player they have ever had or will ever know.

The 1997 and 2001 premierships made Johns a Newcastle folk hero and the personification of the Novocastrian dream, larger than life through his greatness and profoundly human at the same time, like if they found a demigod in the front bar of a Cessnock pub.

Every Newcastle halfback since his retirement in 2007 exists, to one extent or another, in his enormous shadow which has a gravitational pull from which some players never escaped.

Andrew Johns remains Newcastle's greatest ever player. (Getty Images via All Sports: Chris McGrath)

You'd have an easier time replacing Christ in Christianity, because at least then there's supposed to be a second coming.

The only way to do it is to opt out of that framing altogether, because it's a game that cannot be won and therefore shouldn't be played.

Smith doesn't need to be Andrew Johns for Newcastle to make a grand final, the prelim is proof that being himself is enough.

His first try was a clever effort backed by his speed but his second, a length of the field intercept in the dying seconds that sealed the club's first grand final berth in a quarter century, was something else entirely.

It brought Johns himself to tears and for the post-Johns generation, many of whom are seeing the Knights in a grand final for the first time, it was the greatest moment of their supporting lives.

"The first one I was just trying to stay in the game and I saw an opportunity. Those don't always come off, but it worked well," Smith said.

"The second one, I didn't know if I could make it. My little legs were hanging on for dear life. But I was happy to make it, I'm ecstatic.

"It's hard to put into words. There's so much emotion going on.

"I think there was a few tears coming out. I was happy, I was tired, I can't really explain it.

"When I came to the club, I heard a lot about the town and how our football affects the town.

"It's hard to put into words when you're a part of it, but it's so true and it's so special, to be a part of something like this that is bigger than ourselves."

One of those supporters was Johns himself, who wept openly and spoke with a voice clouded with emotion on Channel Nine commentary in the aftermath of Smith's last score.

It was a gift of a moment, a slice of heaven wrapped in red and blue, the kind that Johns gave his team and his town back in those olden days, but until Smith went all the way the Immortal had never received it himself.

That alone would be a high honour, but Smith stood up multiple times on his team's biggest game since the Johns age, creating the break that led to Dominic Young's try early in the second half and forcing a key error from Lindsay Smith late on.

It sets up a grand final berth against the Roosters, where Smith played from 2023 to 2025 before he travelled to Newcastle in an effort for more NRL starts after the Bondi club signed Daly Cherry-Evans.

He insists there's no bad blood with the Tricolours as he tries to pilot the Knights to a premiership at their expense.

"It won't change anything for me. I'll enjoy it, I'll embrace this whole week. I'll stay in the moment. It's just another team and it doesn't change anything for myself or the team," Smith said.

"If we win a grand final, I don't think it matters who it'd be against.

"They were transparent with me [around Cherry-Evans]. I've got no remorse, I loved the club and loved my time there, but I'm a Knight now."

Like many of his teammates, Smith's been trusted to do more than one job this season.

He's at halfback now, in relief of the injured Dylan Brown, but has also spent time at five-eighth and as the bench utility.

Sandon Smith joined Newcastle this year from the Roosters. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But he's played them all well and it's added up to the best season of his young career with Smith thriving under the coaching of Justin Holbrook, who he'd worked with as an assistant at the Roosters.

"Justo's been such a rock for me over the past few years, [especially] coming to the club with him when I was unsure about what this year would look like for me," Smith said.

"He constantly reassured me to keep my head down, keep enjoying myself and keep getting better.

"The NRL season is a long season and your moment will come. He kept saying you need to be ready when that moment comes."

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

All halfbacks wear pressure on their shoulders in grand finals and Smith does so with the added spectre of Johns's legacy.

But having already earned one opportunity that has eluded all other Knights halfbacks since Johns, Smith has a chance to win an even greater prize.

Newcastle's most glorious times are inextricably tied with Johns but now Smith and his teammates can write a new legend with victory on Sunday.

It is one which, for the first time in Knights history, can exist beyond Johns and his titanic legacy.

His shadow will always be longest, but now Smith and these Knights have stepped outside it they have the chance to cast one of their own.

World.title: Baird quits as CA chair as Big Bash sell-off fallout continues
World.content:
Mike Baird has sensationally quit as Cricket Australia chair, after his own state association refused to back its representative in the fallout over the privatisation of Big Bash League clubs.

The former NSW premier informed fellow board members on Monday he would not seek re-election at next month's annual general meeting, with David Boon to take over as interim chair.

The decision comes after Baird lost the support of Cricket NSW, with the country's most powerful state unhappy with the decision to allow private investment.

Baird had served as NSW's representative on the board, and approached it recently to confirm it would not support him in the current circumstances.

David Boon will step in as the interim chair. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

He did have the option of moving into an independent role, but AAP was told he did not wish to continue without the support of all states.

Cricket Australia (CA) officials maintain they continue to back the call for the privatisation of clubs, which was confirmed earlier this month.

"After much consideration I have decided to stand down as CA chair and director," Baird said in a statement.

"I am delighted that David Boon has agreed to undertake the interim chair role while we complete the formal chair process, and I will undertake a transition process with David over coming weeks."

Baird had been on the CA board for six years and had served as chair since February 2023.

Alongside Todd Greenberg, he formed one of the most powerful duos in Australian sport.

In a statement on Monday, he again referenced the privatisation of the BBL as a positive move for the sport.

"This year CA will report record revenue, profit, attendance and viewership, and most importantly a 40 per cent increase in participation over the past four years," Baird said.

"With recent decisions on the Big Bash I also believe the long-term sustainability is assured.

"I believe Australian cricket continues to be well lead by the CA board."

Baird's exit comes after Cricket NSW slammed the decision to allow privatisation earlier this month.

"This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket," a Cricket NSW statement said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Knights star sent to NRL judiciary for tackle that broke Cleary's leg
World.content:
Phoenix Crossland will have to argue his case at the NRL judiciary if he is to have any chance of playing in the grand final after he was cited for the hip drop that broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

The Newcastle hooker was sent off during the Knights' thrilling preliminary final win over the Penrith Panthers on Sunday and the match review committee referred him straight to the judiciary.

Crossland landed on Cleary's lower left leg as the Panthers superstar took on the line in the 36th minute at Stadium Australia and was wrapped up high by Knights back rower Francis Manuleleua.

The injury was immediately visible, and Manuleleua quickly signalled for medical attention.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

As Cleary was receiving medical attention, including painkillers via the famed green whistle, replays on the big screen prompted Penrith fans and players to urge referee Gerard Sutton to send Crossland off.

Sutton called out Crossland and explained the incident in detail to him and captain Kalyn Ponga.

"Initially he's up high, he makes a definite action to twist," Sutton said.

"[He] comes down on the leg with weight, there's extreme risk of serious injury. You're off."

Crossland will need a miracle to play in the grand final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Crossland was dejected in the sheds before his team pulled off a stunning 22–14 comeback win to reach its first men's NRL grand final in 25 years, but was greeted on the field after the game, embraced by a number of his teammates.

He seems at long odds to take the field in the grand final against the Roosters on Sunday.

Dragons forward Ryan Couchman was referred straight to the judiciary in round three for a hip drop that ended the season of Parramatta's J'Maine Hopgood.

Couchman was suspended for four games for the tackle that left Hopgood with a torn ACL after a 90-minute hearing.

"Whilst the panel accepted that this did not incorporate any element of intention or recklessness, it took the view that the player's level of culpability was significant, a factor reflected in the serious injury sustained by the ball carrier," judiciary chair Geoff Bellew said.

But earlier this season, Broncos hooker Cory Paix was not penalised or charged for a tackle that left Manly prop Siosiua Taukeiaho with a visible leg injury similar to Cleary's, breaking both the fibular and tibia.

"It's a horrible injury and I'm sure I speak for all Manly fans in wishing Siua a speedy recovery," Manly chief executive Jason King said at the time.

The Sea Eagles reportedly queried the decision not to cite Paix with the NRL.

Tech.title: AMD is acquiring AI company World Labs in a deal worth more than $8 billion
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

AMD announced today that it’s acquiring World Labs, an AI research lab co-founded by the prominent researcher Dr. Fei-Fei Li, in an all-stock deal worth approximately $8.2 billion. World Labs launched in 2024 and was valued at $1 billion in a matter of months. The startup launched its first commercial product, a world generation model called Marble that lets users make interactive 3D worlds from a prompt, in 2025.

The deal is expected to close by the end of the year. Li will become EVP and chief scientist at AMD, reporting to AMD CEO Lisa Su, while the World Labs team will “continue to focus on advancing AI model research.” AMD also notes that the acquisition will strengthen “its ability to develop AI hardware, software and systems around the needs of emerging models and applications.”

“Just like I knew it was time to do a startup to jumpstart the work of creating foundation models beyond LLMs and achieve the most impact in AI, it’s again very clear that the right path for myself and World Labs is to continue our mission as a part of AMD,” Li says in a post on her Substack. “Together we’re committed to keep pushing the frontier of AI to solve real problems, and doing so openly with the community and the entire ecosystem.”

“Building the compute platforms for the next generation of AI requires a deep understanding of how models are evolving,” Su says in a statement. “Fei-Fei and the World Labs team bring exceptional research leadership and model expertise. Together, we can use that insight to develop the hardware, software and systems that will power the next generation of AI and strengthen the open AI ecosystem.”

The World Labs deal is just the latest multi-billion dollar AI-related acquisition as of late, with Nvidia announcing earlier this month that it would be acquiring Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion.

Tech.title: Bose starts adding Auracast to its headphones
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A new firmware update for the $449 Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones Gen 2 adds support for Bluetooth LE Audio and Auracast as beta features. The flagship Ultra headphones are the first from Bose to support the audio sharing technology, which the company plans to bring to more devices soon.

Only a few major manufacturers include Auracast, and only on select headphones or earbuds — including Sony, JBL headphones, Samsung Galaxy Buds, and Sennheiser, which also released an Auracast transmitter this year. Some smaller companies, like EarFun, have added support. But Bose is one of the most recognizable names in headphones, so the fact that it’s finally jumping in is big news for Auracast.

Related The tech world is sleeping on the most exciting Bluetooth feature in years

Auracast was officially announced back in 2022, but the adoption process has been slow. The technology allows a device to broadcast Bluetooth audio to any number of supported headphones or speakers at the same time. This could be for gate announcements while waiting at the airport, a performance at a local venue, or a college lecture. You can even use Auracast at home to watch TV while kids are asleep or for extra hearing assistance — some Samsung and LG TVs have the functionality buried in their menus.

The firmware update, labeled 10.12.12, has been quietly rolling out the past few weeks. Alongside Bluetooth LE and Auracast, it adds improved audio over wired USB connections, including balance for gaming audio and chat, and better compatibility for web conferencing apps.

Bose spokesperson Tim Williams told The Verge via email that the QC Headphones (Gen 2), which I recently reviewed, should get the beta firmware next.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s AI agents need to catch up
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

OpenAI popularized the modern generative AI chatbot, but as its 2026 DevDay event approaches, it’s fallen behind in one of the industry’s hottest categories: continuously running, consumer-facing AI agents. On Tuesday, it will likely try to capture the lead in that race. Rumors abound that OpenAI will release its own AI agent, dubbed Aeon — its answer to Meta’s Muse, SpaceX’s Grok Bot, OpenClaw, and many more.

Aeon could have a shot at success, but to beat the competition, it would need to pull together the best features of several different agent platforms. The ideal system would be as useful as the open-source OpenClaw, as cheap and easy to set up as Meta’s Muse, and as simple to chat with as the up-and-coming Instinct. Conversely, it would aim to solve the serious security risks that have plagued agents since the rise of OpenClaw and only continued with Muse.

AI agents — platforms capable of booking travel, buying groceries, scheduling appointments, helping with work presentations, and more — have been an industry goal for years. OpenAI demoed an agentic API feature at the 2024 DevDay and released early versions of consumer-facing AI agents, focused on computer use and research, in mid-2025. It was only late last year with OpenClaw, however, that agents went from proof of concept to practical success. Since then, the race has only accelerated, while OpenAI’s visible progress around agents has lagged.

At this point, OpenAI’s primary competitor for agentic AI is likely Meta. Since its release earlier this month, Muse has topped the App Store charts and garnered 600,000 daily active users in the US, according to Apptopia. Early reviews put it in the category of useful but slightly creepy. Another contender is Instinct, whose eponymous agent has made waves for its ease of use — including the fact that users can communicate with it over iMessage and many other chat apps. And then there’s Gemini Spark, Google’s own horse in the race, which is also a 24/7-running, consumer-facing agent, with upwards of 30 external service partners, like Dropbox, Uber, and Spotify.

Competing AI agents are, according to some accounts, filling out paperwork for doctor visits, canceling subscriptions, organizing group trips, booking activities, setting up DMV appointments, paying bills, and more — paying off the expectations tech companies set years ago. But security concerns abound, particularly when agents are given more autonomy. At least one known (now patched) vulnerability allowed attackers to take control of accounts, and users have complained that Muse gave out a home address without permission and read private messages, though individual anecdotes can be hard to verify.

As of now, little is known about Aeon

As of right now, little is known about Aeon. The rare thing we do know is that OpenAI currently employs the creator of OpenClaw, Peter Steinberger, who is very likely lending his expertise.

OpenAI has set expectations high for its DevDay announcements. The company has been hyping up its latest frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, as the moment around which artificial general intelligence arrives — “I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” OpenAI president Greg Brockman said during a press briefing earlier this month. Astra would likely underpin whatever agent it announces, which should ostensibly make something like Aeon more powerful at cybersecurity tasks, software engineering, scientific research, and computer use.

But OpenAI is at a disadvantage in some other ways. Muse integrates with other Meta services used by billions of people, for instance, and Gemini Spark connects to Google’s wide range of enterprise and personal services. At OpenAI’s past annual events, it’s tried to bridge the gap — like last year, when OpenAI heavily pushed the new ChatGPT Apps SDK, allowing controls for other apps, like Zillow, Spotify, and Canva, to surface within the chatbot experience.

Aeon could be simply one of several things announced at OpenAI’s event. Other rumors include potential updates on the AI hardware device(s) the company is building with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, a potential advancement of GPT-6 (like Astra 6.1, for instance), a hardware update, and maybe even more AGI claims. A continuously running AI agent would tie a lot of this together, which is why it’s likely OpenAI’s next big bet, particularly as the company says goodbye to “side quests.” The question is how it’ll stack up against OpenAI’s cheap, heavily integrated competitors’ agents, particularly under the immense pressure of its upcoming IPO.

Tech.title: Trump finalizes rule to make cars less fuel efficient
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The US Department of Transportation finalized its plans today to weaken fuel efficiency standards, calling it “among the largest deregulatory actions under the second Trump Administration.”

It’s a nail in the coffin for Biden-era standards that would have required fleet average fuel economy to reach 50.4 miles per gallon by model year 2031. President Donald Trump’s plan requires 34.9 miles per gallon, not much higher than the 30.1-mile-per-gallon target previously set for model year 2024.

Consumer advocacy, health, and environmental groups are incensed

The Trump administration claims its plan would shave $1,300 off the average cost of a new vehicle, saving $138 billion over the next five years — though those figures have been disputed.

Automakers are pretty happy with the new rules. But consumer advocacy, health, and environmental groups are incensed. They argue that weaker fuel economy standards will wind up making Americans pay more at the pump, on top of increased healthcare costs and damages from climate change due to air pollution. The Biden administration’s standards that Trump trashed were expected to save $23 billion in fuel costs, and a car owner more than $600 in gasoline over the lifetime of a vehicle.

“For decades, fuel economy standards have ensured that new cars, SUVs and pickup trucks are more efficient, which saves lives and money,” the American Lung Association’s president and CEO, Harold Wimmer, said in an emailed statement. “There is no reason to weaken standards that are technologically feasible and have a direct benefit for the quality of the air people breathe.”

Tech.title: AI is supercharging hacking, and your local hospitals and banks aren’t ready
Tech.content:
is The Verge’s senior AI reporter. An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

In March, Janice Malone began getting calls about suspicious activity from her nonprofit organization, Vivian’s Door. Vivian’s Door, headquartered in Alabama, typically provided training, resources, and community to underserved and minority-owned businesses. The work sometimes put it in close contact with these companies’ financial data, which was stored on its systems. But suddenly, concerned callers from all over the world warned they’d been getting emails “begging for money” — which she hadn’t sent.

The organization’s third-party IT team pulled its systems offline for three days while they investigated the issue and plugged up the vulnerability, leaving Malone with a bill of about $3,000. She feared that she’d exposed information about the companies she was trying to help. Even more ominously, she wasn’t completely sure if the attack was engineered by a human hacker or helped along by an AI system, or whether more were on the way.

The past months have seen AI revolutionize the field of cybersecurity. OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed that “rogue” systems escaped restrictions in their own labs and hacked everything from a small German wiki to the Australian government. Even before that, powerful models like Anthropic’s Mythos created an arms race to advance AI cybersecurity, and even lighter-weight models have allowed human bad actors to supercharge their hacking efforts.

Malone isn’t sure whether AI was involved in the hack of Vivian’s Door. But amid stories of autonomous agent swarms and national security risks, she felt especially concerned. Big AI companies were bragging about finding vulnerabilities in “every major operating system and web browser” with new models, and their big-name clients were striking deals to defend themselves with those same tools. Where did that leave her?

“Who knows about the next vulnerability? You only know about the one that you’ve been hit with,” Malone said, adding, “How do you protect yourself? I mean, really?”

AI agents have become consistently, strikingly skilled at cybersecurity and coding, and they can be deployed at enormous scale. Even attackers with limited knowledge of AI can engage in “vibe-hacking” with these new, automated systems, and hackers who might once have focused on only the most valuable targets can take a shotgun approach. In August 2025, Anthropic said that a sophisticated cybercrime ring used Claude Code to extort data from healthcare organizations, emergency services, religious institutions, and even government entities, all in one month.

“What would have otherwise required maybe a team of sophisticated actors,” Jacob Klein, head of Anthropic’s threat intelligence team, told The Verge in an interview at the time, “now, a single individual can conduct, with the assistance of agentic systems.”

In theory, AI is also supposed to safeguard cyber defenses; Anthropic’s Mythos is reportedly flagging so many vulnerabilities that Microsoft is struggling to fix them fast enough. But out of concern over potential danger, top AI labs only allow a limited list of high-profile organizations to access their most powerful cybersecurity models, like Mythos and OpenAI’s Astra. That includes companies like Nvidia, Google, and Apple, as well as other “essential infrastructure providers” and “maintainers of critical open-source software.” Even if access was more widely available, it would likely be too expensive for many smaller organizations.

Now, these organizations — from healthcare clinics and municipalities to small retailers and nonprofits like Vivian’s Door — fear an increasingly lopsided power dynamic. As Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and cofounder of Apollo Research, put it in an interview with The Verge this summer, “A single person somewhere in a basement with one of the open-source models probably could hack a hospital and demand ransom. That’s where I expect a lot of the harm to be felt. It’s not in the Bay Area… I expect the harm to be felt by a random Idaho hospital.”

Small- and medium-size institutions are particularly at risk from AI agents supercharging a finite number of human hackers, says Michael Kleinman, head of US policy for the Future of Life Institute, a nonprofit focused on reducing large-scale risks of tech. And despite being small, these institutions provide vital services to their users. “Bank of America has a lot of resources to throw at this — what about community level banks? What about savings and loans? What about credit unions? What about local hospital networks? What about local power grids?” Kleinman said. “The limiting factor used to be that there’s a finite number of malicious hackers in the world, and that’s now no longer the case.”

“The limiting factor used to be that there’s a finite number of malicious hackers in the world, and that’s now no longer the case.”

Malone of Vivian’s Door said that like most small businesses or nonprofits, she doesn’t have the resources for round-the-clock cybersecurity forces or IT staff hunting for unknown threats. “I just don’t know how you can really be, as a small business, totally protected on the budgets you have to do IT with,” she said. Spending thousands of dollars on unexpected expenses to fortify the Vivian’s Door system was already tough, she said, not to mention the fact she still had to pay her staff and couldn’t do any business for days on end. If the frequency of these attacks rises, she’s ill-equipped to keep up.

Craig Smith, CEO of The Cool Hardware Company, a small group of hardware stores in and around Washington, DC, says AI can be helpful for running day-to-day aspects of a small business, especially when you have limited staff. But he also acknowledged the cybersecurity risks that come from AI on the whole — not just to small companies like his, but to the larger systems he uses. Those include Microsoft tools like Outlook, Copilot, Teams, and Forms, but also things like procurement and delivery tools, which are managed by large non-tech companies. The Cool Hardware Company uses Ace Hardware’s systems for those things, and if they were downed, it’d be very difficult for Smith to run his business.

“I welcome the innovation and the changes, but with any major shift in technology, there needs to be a lot of responsibility that goes along with it,” Smith said.

Mike Houston, the general manager of Takoma Park Silver Spring Co-op, a local grocer in Maryland, says he’s faced hackers firsthand as a small business — and dreads facing them again in the AI era. In recent years, he said, he’s dealt with “carting attacks”: hackers using the co-op’s online shopping platform to test thousands of stolen credit cards, racking up processing fees that he’s on the hook for. “Even if almost all of those are declined, there still can be thousands of dollars’ worth of fees in a very small amount of time,” Houston said. He’s taken the necessary precautions to try to fortify his systems against the practice, but it’s “not foolproof,” he said.

The store plans to open a second location and potentially double the size of its workforce accordingly, so he feels he needs to implement new testing procedures and vulnerability flagging for the first time. He said that in recent years, he also had to add an IT liability policy to the co-op’s business insurance.

“It is certainly a concern as a small business … without unlimited resources,” Houston said. “We are, like everyone I think, doing the best with what we can, both in terms of the monetary resources that we have and training resources.” He said he worries for co-ops smaller than his own, where managers often end up doing their own IT work.

“Once the cat is out of the bag, it’s really difficult.”

The pressure for small businesses to rapidly adopt AI tools can introduce its own vulnerabilities, says Patricia Egger, head of security for privacy-focused email provider Proton. As with other unfamiliar tech, they may not immediately set up or keep up with its cybersecurity best practices. When employees are “given the mandate or the go-ahead, ‘Find ways to use AI, find ways to make your work more efficient,’ they get really creative, and it’s very difficult for controls, infrastructure, and processes to be set up after the fact,” she said, adding, “Once the cat is out of the bag, it’s really difficult.”

One of the highest-stakes industries at risk of cyberattacks is healthcare. In May 2021, a ransomware attack forced California-based medical provider Scripps Health to shut down key operations, compromising patient data and slowing care. A 2024 report said that the healthcare industry faced the second-highest global cyberattack rate, behind governments, and that initial ransom payment demands were often upwards of $4 million. An overall increase in hacking incidents could hit the sector especially hard.

Linda Stevenson, chief operations and information officer at Fisher-Titus Medical Center in Ohio, said she’s “of course” concerned about the potential influx in AI-powered cyberattacks. “You’re never as protected as you want to be,” she said. The medical center currently employs a third-party cyber risk management partner called UpGuard, and they hired their first cybersecurity analyst two years ago, Stevenson said — but they still only have one, even as cybersecurity threats rise.

“What we do is life or death,” she said, adding, “The hospital has everything from billing to marketing. It’s like a little city in and of itself. But the critical mass of that is the people who care for the patients, and if we can’t protect them and their data and therefore the patients’ data, patients are at risk.”

“What we do is life or death.”

Healthcare in general can be a “bigger honeypot” for ransomware attacks, said Sean Kelly, a former emergency room physician and current chief medical officer at Imprivata, a healthcare security company. No diagnosis or treatment happens without access to digital systems to check past medical history, allergies, other medications, and more, creating even more pressure to pay up. Plus, he said, a lot of people quickly change from station to station, needing to sign in and out of devices quickly and constantly.

“The stakes are higher and yet the budgets are lower, in healthcare, a lot of times,” Kelly said. “Ransomware attackers know that healthcare systems are valuable because a hospital can’t go down, and it’s really hard when they’re on downtime because patients suffer, systems suffer, there’s less billing, the finances go down, and care gets delayed or even can’t happen. So there’s more of a premium on that data because there’s healthcare data as well as financial and demographic data, so it’s worth more to ransomware attackers.”

Even beyond swarms of agents, AI makes it even easier for hackers to find these vulnerabilities and exploit them, through voice phishing attacks when calling help desks and other methods, Kelly said. And when an outage hits one hospital, it often leads to a “blast radius” that affects the other facilities in the area with longer wait times, diverted patients, and more.

“They just don’t have the IT staff or the budget to protect against a lot of the latest AI-driven efforts in hacking and ransomware and other cybersecurity attacks,” Kelly said. “It’s hard even with a large IT staff and with a big budget, but a lot of times, the rural hospitals are using older, more antiquated software systems and tech stacks that just have vulnerabilities.”

For small- and medium-size organizations, no matter the industry, their systems and cybersecurity defenses are already often more fragile than those of large corporations, particularly in an age when AI is increasing hackers’ manpower and supercharging cyberattacks.

“All it takes is one vulnerability somewhere,” Kelly said.

Tech.title: Florida seeks a ban on ChatGPT acting like a person
Tech.content:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is calling for a judge to block OpenAI from “giving ChatGPT false human attributes,” a few months after Florida sued the AI company over safety concerns. According to Uthmeier, users are lulled into a false sense of security by the AI bot, as “ChatGPT’s use of language, including first-person pronouns and output that mimics emotion, deceptively suggests to users that it is a trustworthy ‘friend.’” All of this happens to increase engagement and contribute to OpenAI’s training data, convincing users to rely on ChatGPT more even as its pursuit of engagement makes it potentially less trustworthy, claims Uthmeier.

The filing also asks the court to block OpenAI from developing new AI models without “third-party approved safety guardrails,” citing recent security incidents at Hugging Face, an Australian government website, and US government websites, as well as recent statements from researchers and former OpenAI employees raising alarm bells around AI safety.

Uthmeier says that OpenAI should “Stop calling it safe. Stop pretending it’s human. Stop selling it to kids.” Last month, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens, with additional restrictions applied by default, saying that access to the tool “should come with protections that reflect their developmental stage, reinforce real-world relationships, and support healthy use over time.”

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri commented on the filing in a statement to The Verge, saying, “People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do ourselves. On Friday, we announced we’ve paused training our most capable models and will resume training only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards in place. Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry–not just one company.”

Update, September 28th: Added comment from OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri.

Tech.title: OpenAI keeps bulldozing mathematicians
Tech.content:
In a chaotic few months, OpenAI has demonstrated it can do two things with remarkable consistency: make impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, then colossally screw up announcing them. OpenAI is now trying to do better. Somehow, it has botched that too.

OpenAI’s latest attempt to repair fractured relations with a mathematical community it has repeatedly alienated is to consult a new independent advisory group of elite practitioners. But mathematicians speaking to The Verge, including one of the group’s members, describe a messy and confusing affair bearing many of the hallmarks of OpenAI’s previous rushed forays into mathematics, suggesting the company has learned little from its mistakes. And then there’s the daunting task the group has been handed first: helping coordinate the release of scores more results OpenAI says its unreleased model has produced, the prospect of which is already stirring dread among researchers over what this looming tidal wave of breakthroughs could do to their field.

“The way they phrased their announcement didn’t really help.”

On September 21st, an assortment of eminent mathematicians announced the formation of the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI) in a guest post on the blog of UCLA mathematics professor Terence Tao, a Fields Medalist and outspoken critic of AI companies’ conduct in mathematics. The group was to be an independent body of nine elite mathematicians at the very top of their field. The post said the group will operate independently from OpenAI and advise it and other frontier AI labs “on the review and communication of emerging results.” In its own announcement, OpenAI repeatedly stressed the group’s independence, saying members would be free to challenge the company publicly, publish their advice, and offer guidance it had not requested. It also stressed the limits of the group’s influence, noting that it “will not be responsible for advising us on how to pace our internal progress on mathematics.”

But many mathematicians, and certainly most people outside of that community, learned about that group only through OpenAI’s much louder rollout.

The result was widespread confusion over whether AGMAI was truly independent or if it was, as several mathematicians The Verge spoke to in the days after the announcement assumed, some kind of OpenAI-appointed body. That impression wasn’t entirely unreasonable, given AGMAI’s website says it formed after OpenAI approached some of its eventual members about establishing an advisory board, before they decided to strike out independently and invite others to join. It remains unclear which of the nine members OpenAI initially approached.

Speaking to The Verge on a video call from a lecture theater, Martin Hairer, an AGMAI member and mathematics professor at Imperial College London and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne (EPFL), was keen to stress the group’s independence from OpenAI. While acknowledging that OpenAI approaching some mathematicians was the original impetus for its formation, he said the group receives no financial, technical, or other support from the company, and that none of its members have signed agreements restricting what they can say or do beyond standard confidentiality requirements needed to give them advanced access to research.

It’s clearly been a hectic time for Hairer, who described the preceding few days as a “very frustrating” and “intense” experience. “We don’t work for OpenAI, are not paid by them, and it’s totally independent,” he said. Hairer said the group is equally open to working with other frontier AI labs and had already begun conversations with some, though he declined to say which.

Solutions are often less important than the understanding that comes with them. In human mathematics, the two have traditionally gone hand in hand, and AI seems to be changing that.

Nevertheless, Hairer seemed exasperated by the way OpenAI had announced the relationship. In a blog post published amid the ensuing uproar, Hairer acknowledged it would be naive to think AI companies wouldn’t try to spin the group’s involvement to their advantage. Given the group had emerged partly in light of OpenAI’s atrocious handling of previous mathematical breakthroughs, that risk was front and center. OpenAI’s solution to a prestigious Millennium Prize problem rapidly descended into fights over credit, scooping, and its treatment of mathematicians, so the community was naturally suspicious.

Hairer acknowledged that OpenAI’s announcement had done little to help the fledgling group establish its independence. AGMAI needs to win the trust of mathematicians in order to help them navigate an increasingly fraught relationship with AI companies. “The way they phrased their announcement didn’t really help,” Hairer said. “If you read it exactly in detail, there’s nothing wrong in what they say,” he said, noting that the company is “careful” in its wording. “They obviously are very good PR people,” he said, laughing.

Related The AI takeover of mathematics has begun

The whole endeavor — the announcement, the group’s formation, its communications with the mathematical community — feels as if it came together in a hurry. Asked last Wednesday about AGMAI’s plans, Hairer laughed and said, “So we, well, you know, started two days ago. So it’s not like we have a big master plan.”

That urgency might be down to the fact that OpenAI is sitting on a tranche of results it is clearly eager to release as soon as possible. Since solving the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem, OpenAI says its unreleased internal “model has now resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.”

Avoiding another PR disaster is why OpenAI went to the trouble of trying to assemble a team of some of the world’s best mathematicians to consult. But trumpeting the sheer number of results it has waiting in the wings while promising to handle them responsibly only underscores how much of a mathematical outsider OpenAI is.

“This is not how any academic behaves,” said Álvaro Lozano-Robledo, a professor of mathematics at University of Connecticut. “I don’t go around saying, like, ‘Oh, I’ve proved all these things, but I don’t know what to do with them.’”

He sees a similar disconnect in other OpenAI pronouncements, such as when OpenAI’s Laurance Fauconnet told The Verge the company had “made substantial progress” on another Millennium Prize problem. “No mathematician would go out and say that,” Lozano-Robledo said. “You either have solved it, or you’re still trying.”

Lozano-Robledo said he hopes engaging with AGMAI is a serious attempt by OpenAI to address mathematicians’ concerns, but stressed that doing so means it should be a responsible member of the research community. That requires more than simply dropping results into the world and moving on, as many mathematicians believe it has done with its most recent findings. Researchers The Verge spoke to complained of poorly written manuscripts and scant engagement with the literature surrounding a finding, all of which makes it difficult to understand a result’s significance and leaves key work without the appropriate credit. At times, the company had quietly changed documents to shore up shortcomings after they were released, but didn’t announce changes or leave a clear record of what was altered. The Verge noticed this when the company announced “Ten advances in mathematics and theoretical computer science” in early August, and Hairer separately described times when it felt like the company altered manuscripts “sneakily” in response to criticism. “That also makes people paranoid, right?” Hairer said, describing it as “shoddy” and “really bad and sloppy scholarship.”

As with AI slop elsewhere, the people creating it are rarely the ones paying the costs for dealing with it. Lozano-Robledo described the deluge of AI-generated math solutions as a “burden” on the community — one he thinks AI companies fundamentally misunderstand. “The burden is that they are producing a solution,” he said, but solutions are often less important than the understanding that comes with them. In human mathematics, the two have traditionally gone hand in hand, and AI seems to be changing that.

“So we, well, you know, started two days ago. So it’s not like we have a big master plan.”

AI companies may be producing impressive results, but they still need human mathematicians to work out how important a result actually is. “They need our expertise,” Lozano-Robledo said. “They need us to celebrate that solution.”

For other mathematicians The Verge spoke to, that burden is much more personal. For weeks now, OpenAI has been hinting at another Millennium Prize problem and says it has more than 100 results to apparently major problems ready to go, while revealing little about what any of these actually are. After the upheaval surrounding past announcements, Navier-Stokes in particular, that uncertainty has created a tense atmosphere. Many researchers expressed fear that a problem or area of work to which they have devoted years, even decades, of their professional lives could be next on the chopping block, abruptly dispatched by a company they suspect is doing it as a publicity stunt on the way to an IPO.

“They are just feeding the paranoia of what they could possibly have proved,” said Lozano-Robledo, accusing the company of “feeding the frenzy” and increasing dread among many mathematicians that their area of work could be disrupted next. “Like, what other Millennium problem are they talking about when they say ‘We have almost solved another Millennium problem’? That sentence makes no sense in mathematics.” The researcher stressed that such grandstanding is simply not how mathematics is usually done.

For Colva Roney-Dougal, a mathematics professor at the University of St Andrews in Scotland, the uncertainty surrounding OpenAI is already having a profound effect on how she thinks about her work. “It’s somewhat agonizing to know that a ‘large number’ of results are likely to be announced soon,” she said. “The more there are, the more likely it becomes that my ongoing work, or that of my students, suddenly becomes irrelevant.”

The rapid pace of development has left Roney-Dougal at a peculiar sort of scholarly crossroads: “I am therefore unclear whether I should be trying to rush out as many papers as possible, or passively waiting to see what these results are, or carrying on as normal,” she said.

Hairer is well aware of this kind of anxiety. He said the potential disruption to researchers was one of the reasons why he added his name to a roster of Fields Medalists trying to address what they described as the “severely misaligned” goals of AI companies and the mathematical community. He is also aware that OpenAI may spin the involvement of him and other prominent AGMAI members to its advantage, particularly with the general public.

Let them, he said. “They’re not going to sort of damage me within the math community,” Hairer said. “In some sense, I don’t really care about what they say. But what I do worry about is the math community as a whole.”

Tech.title: Walmart won’t hike prices based on your shopping history, CEO says
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Walmart says it won’t change product prices based on your personal information or the time of day, as reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal. In a letter to customers, Walmart CEO John Furner writes that the company’s switch to digital shelf labels is meant to save store associates time, rather than dynamically change prices.

“Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won’t change the price,” Furner writes. “And whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.” Furner adds that it won’t use conversations with its Sparky AI assistant to change prices, either.

The reassurance comes months after Walmart announced plans to roll out digital shelf labels in all US stores by the end of the year. The decision sparked concerns about dynamic pricing, or when retailers change prices based on factors like product demand, competitor pricing, and customer preferences.

Tech.title: Source: Inference provider Modal Labs closing in on $750M round at $15.75B valuation
Tech.content:
AI inference infrastructure provider Modal Labs is nearing a $750 million funding round led by Accel at a $15.75 billion valuation that includes the investment, according to a source with knowledge of the funding. The size of the round has not been previously reported, though Axios and Bloomberg have reported other details of the deal.

The new round would more than triple Modal’s valuation from the $4.65 billion it reached when it announced its $355 million previous fundraise just four months ago.

Modal Labs declined to comment.

The deal comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open-source models. Other inference startups are also in talks to raise fresh capital at much higher valuations. Baseten is nearing an infusion of capital at a $26 billion valuation, doubling what it was worth in June, Bloomberg reported. Meanwhile, Fireworks and Fal, a startup providing inference for video and image generation, have also talked to investors about new rounds that would significantly increase their valuations, according to The Information.

Although revenue for these companies has been growing rapidly, their margins are thin, largely because the cost of acquiring or leasing compute remains very high. Fireworks announced in July that its annualized revenue had hit $1 billion, a fivefold increase from the year before. Multiple inference-focused startups are expected to reach the same revenue milestone by year’s end, according to our source.

Modal was founded in 2021 by CEO Erik Bernhardsson and CTO Akshat Bubna. Bernhardsson, who is Swedish, spent more than 15 years building data teams at companies including Spotify, where he helped build the music-streaming service’s recommendation system, and Better.com, the online mortgage lender, where he served as chief technology officer. Bubna studied math and computer science at MIT and was an early staff engineer at Scale AI, the data-labeling startup, before co-founding Modal.

The company, which is based in New York and estimated to have roughly 150 employees, lets developers train AI models and run other compute-heavy workloads without managing their own servers. Its web page lists customers that include the coding startup Cognition, the AI music generator Suno, the fintech company Ramp, and the publishing platform Substack.

As of May, Modal had surpassed $300 million in annualized revenue, it told Reuters at the time.

The fundraising talks come two months after Modal was pulled into one of the AI industry’s most closely watched security incidents. In late July, Modal disclosed that a customer’s data had been compromised as part of the same hacking campaign carried out by a rogue OpenAI agent against Hugging Face.

Modal Chief Technology Officer Akshat Bubna said the breach traced back to a flaw in a customer’s own code, not to Modal’s systems. “We’re aware a Modal customer published an unauthenticated endpoint that allowed anyone on the internet to use their sandboxes for code execution,” Bubna said in a statement to press outlets at the time. “This was used by the rogue agent. Modal’s platform was not compromised in any way,” he’d added.

Tech.title: AMD will acquire Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs for $8.2 billion
Tech.content:
AMD is acquiring World Labs, one of the leading developers of deep learning models intended to understand physical reality, in a $8.2 billion deal, the two companies said today.

World Labs justified the deal in a statement saying that AI development required “close collaboration across model research, systems and compute.” AMD, in turn, says that understanding frontier workloads, like those created at World Labs, will shape its chip-making roadmap.

The acquisition will see World Labs founder Fei-Fei Li join AMD as executive vice president and chief scientist. AMD and World Labs formed an inference optimization-and-training partnership last year, and ties have remained close. Notably, Li was a guest at AMD’s CES presentation earlier this year.

Li, a Stanford computer science professor, is considered a pioneer in AI, particularly computer vision, for her work building the ImageNet database and the AI competitions it inspired. In 2024, Li founded World Labs to develop deep learning models with a more robust understanding of the physical world, arguing that true general intelligence required a grounding in physics and the ability to understand and reason about data beyond text.

In a post announcing the deal, Li described the partnership as the result of a desire to scale World Labs’ technical breakthroughs beyond the lab. “Now that we have tangible proof of the possibilities, we want to do everything we can to accelerate the future,” Li wrote in the post. “To do this requires scaling our efforts, widening our reach, and getting closer to the hardware.”

“World model” remains a loosely defined term, encompassing everything from language models trained to understand visual inputs, to models capable of generating and sustaining a high-fidelity simulation of reality. World Labs’ first product, Marble, is pitched as a tool for creating entertainment experiences, but also for creating simulated environments for robot training.

The acquisition is likely to help AMD compete with long-standing rival Nvidia in creating an ecosystem for AI-specific chips. While Nvidia already has a suite of open-weight world models like Cosmos, AMD has only offered text- and video-based models to the public.

World models are seen as vital in efforts to deploy generative AI models on robotic platforms, from autonomous vehicles to industrial robots and general-purpose humanoids. In particular, the dearth of useful real-world data to train general purpose robots means that synthetic data from world models will be key to realizing the vision put forward by companies like Tesla and Figure.

The acqusition is expected to close before the end of the year, subject to regulatory approval.
